items.text:
Denmark: Top court backs hardline law against 'non-Westerners'
November 23, 2026
Denmark's Supreme Court on Monday ruled in favor of a housing association that terminated 91 leases in order to prevent the label "hard ghetto" being applied to their housing complex. The decision align's with Copenhagen's hardline approach to immigration.
The court on Monday upheld Denmark's 2018 "ghetto law," which allows for the relocation of "non-Western" residents from minority-heavy neighborhoods in order to foster integration. The Danish court ruling diverges from a top EU court decision last year that found application of the law could amount to discrimination.
The Danish laws requires social housing estates to rebuild, renovate and adjust their social mix if these become minority heavy, stipulating that 60% of apartments be rented to "Westerners" at market value by 2030.
Denmark's hardline immigration policies making it a role model in the EU
Denmark's pioneering role in spearheading tougher immigration rules has made it a model for some in the EU. Denmark was also one of five countries that last week announced its intent to set up an asylum seeker deportation hub in Rwanda.
Danish Housing Minister Jacob Mark welcomed Monday's decision, saying it "strengthens security, social cohesion and integration."
The court's decision upheld a 2022 lower court ruling against seven tenants who fought their evictions in Nojsomhed, Helsingor, just north of Copenhagen.
In Monday's ruling, the law was found to be non-discriminatory when it comes to the eviction of "immigrants and descendants from non-Western countries" as it is not broadly based on ethnicity. The EU ruling focused on this particular aspect, saying the law would be discriminatory if criteria were race based, while ultimately allowing national courts to have the last say in the matter.
"The Supreme Court notes that applying the criterion of the law involves dividing people into two groups [immigrants and descendants from non-Western countries, and all other persons]. Both groups include a very large majority of different ethnic origins, and there will simultaneously be persons with the same ethnic origin in both groups," read the Danish court's ruling.
Who is a 'non-Western' resident?
Tenants' associations estimate that 11,000 people across Denmark will have to be relocated to comply with the law.
The housing association in question issued a written statement saying that it was aware that the evictions would impact those affected, adding that it undertook measures to insure that residents found new homes.
According to Statistics Denmark's definition, "non-Western" countries include every country other than the 27 member states of the European Union, as well as Andorra, Australia, Britain, Canada, Iceland, Liechtenstein, Monaco, New Zealand, Northern Ireland, Norway, San Marino, Switzerland, the United States and the Vatican.

items.text:
Anthropic is launching some new Claude AI features to help software engineers ship code. As part of a new Claude Ship product being announced today, Claude now can review, fix, and approve pull requests.
Claude AI can review pull requests and ship fixes on its own now
Anthropic is bringing new AI tools to software engineers with Claude Ship.
Engineers have already been able to take advantage of Claude’s code review capabilities thanks to the Code Review feature, which was announced in March and became generally available in October. What’s new alongside Claude Ship are the PR Steward and Claude Approvals agents, which are launching in beta today.
PR Steward “jumps in on failing CI checks, merge conflicts, and review feedback from Code Review, other review tools, or team members” and leaves comments on what it changed, according to Anthropic. Claude Approvals can approve routine changes if an organization’s policy allows it. “Teams can have Claude Approvals consider a variety of signals in its decision-making process, including Code Review findings or their own classifiers using natural language,” Anthropic says.
Claude Ship is now available for Claude Team and Enterprise customers and works with repositories on GitHub.

items.text:
The Jensen Huang era of Nvidia nearly came to an end this month. Huang, who three decades ago co-founded what’s come to be considered one of the most important companies in AI, resigned from his role on November 12th over mounting scrutiny around his alleged affairs. Huang admitted he had been “unfaithful” to his wife and that he “created problems for the board.”
How Jensen Huang ended up as Nvidia CEO again
In the span of less than a month, Nvidia lost and reinstated its CEO.
How Jensen Huang ended up as Nvidia CEO again
In the span of less than a month, Nvidia lost and reinstated its CEO.
Huang’s resignation came after weeks of escalating problems, both personal and professional. First, reporting from The New York Times said he had a “close relationship” with a woman passing intelligence to China. Subsequent reporting said that China’s intelligence agency had enlisted that woman, Alice Huang, then an executive at Nvidia customer Megaspeed, to spy on Nvidia’s leader, and that the Singapore-based company was under investigation for potentially smuggling AI chips to China. Stories followed that indicated Huang was having an affair with Alice as well as an Nvidia executive, vice president of healthcare Kimberly Powell.
So when Huang resigned less than two weeks ago, the decision seemed final. Even Nvidia’s board appeared unwilling to budge. “The Nvidia board unanimously accepted his resignation and does not intend to reinstate Jensen as CEO,” board chair Harvey Jones said during an earnings call last week.
But in the days following Huang’s resignation, the founder’s allies — including President Donald Trump — mounted a pressure campaign that brought him back to the company he created and sent Nvidia’s share price rocketing upward, almost as though he had never left.
The campaign in support of Huang began almost immediately after his resignation. A coterie of tech leaders began posting in support of Nvidia’s founder: Epic Games CEO Tim Sweeney questioned the motives of journalists who broke the stories about his affairs. Tesla CEO Elon Musk likened Huang’s departure to “kicking Michael Jordan off your team when you’re on a winning streak.” OpenAI CEO Sam Altman later said on stage, “it’s hard to imagine the AI revolution without Jensen.”
“If I didn’t get involved, you’d probably have a very sad Nvidia for a long time to come,” Trump said.
Meanwhile, some of those tech leaders began questioning aspects of the reporting that led to Huang’s exit. Venture capitalist and former White House AI czar David Sacks cast doubt that Alice Huang was a spy, citing a lack of confirmation from US officials. Trump exacerbated the uncertainty, telling reporters, “I don’t know that she is a spy,” despite reports saying the assessment had relied on US intelligence sources.
Nvidia’s board, meanwhile, found itself in a tough position. The company’s shares crashed following Huang’s departure, and they didn’t pick up even after a rosy earnings report. The board was also scrambling to find a new CEO, something industry analysts speculated would prove exceptionally difficult. Reports indicated that Nvidia was considering hiring Arm CEO Rene Haas and Apple hardware chief Johny Srouji, both of whom already have powerful roles in the chip industry.
Trump quickly warmed up to Huang’s return, too. The president — whose investment accounts traded up to $97 million worth of Nvidia stock since returning to office — initially floated the idea of having former Apple CEO Tim Cook take Huang’s place, before saying that it “certainly isn’t a bad idea” to bring Huang back.
This past weekend, Trump appears to have inserted himself into the situation directly. A report from The New York Times says that Trump asked Vice President JD Vance to work with Huang and Nvidia’s board to “resolve the situation,” while the Trump administration reassured the board that it “did not believe that Mr. Huang himself posed a national security risk.” Semafor reports that Trump even called into Nvidia’s board meeting to advocate for Huang’s reinstatement. Sunday evening, Trump said in a post on Truth Social that he hopes Nvidia’s board “rehires Jensen Huang.”
Hours later, Nvidia’s board did just that. The board announced on Monday that it reinstated Huang as its CEO, president, and board member. In its statement, the board said that it received input “from senior levels of the United States government,” and determined that “Huang’s reinstatement poses no national security risk.”
Trump immediately took credit for Huang’s reinstatement, with White House spokesperson Steven Cheung saying the president “was totally involved” in the decision. “If I didn’t get involved, you’d probably have a very sad Nvidia for a long time to come,” Trump said during an interview with CNBC. He added in a post on Truth Social that the US Attorney General confirmed that it doesn’t have evidence that Huang “engaged in any unlawful conduct.”
Nvidia’s shares rose on the news of Huang’s reinstatement, while tech leaders celebrated his return on social media. But the saga is likely far from over. The board said it will finish its investigation into Huang, the Securities and Exchange Commission is looking into Nvidia’s “accounting practices,” and Megaspeed is being investigated by the Justice Department. Even Trump has said that Nvidia should continue its internal investigation about export controls compliance.
Trump’s apparent involvement also leaves plenty of room for scrutiny from Democratic lawmakers, who will control the House and Senate next year. Sen. Elizabeth Warren (D-MA) called Nvidia’s decision “reckless” and urged the Trump administration to explain the “input” government officials provided to the company’s board
Huang’s stunning reinstatement still leaves many questions unanswered. Though the backing of Wall Street, the White House, and Silicon Valley may have brought Huang back as CEO, a new wave of scrutiny from federal regulators and lawmakers is just getting starte

items.title: Are Man Utd genuinely in a relegation battle?
items.summary:
Are Manchester United in a relegation battle? Gary Neville and Jamie Carragher assess their survival chances
After Manchester United's 4-0 thrashing at Liverpool, Mauricio Pochettino's side officially have the worst defence in Europe and have endured their worst start to a season in over half a cent
items.text:
Are Manchester United in a relegation battle? Gary Neville and Jamie Carragher assess their survival chances
After Manchester United's 4-0 thrashing at Liverpool, Mauricio Pochettino's side officially have the worst defence in Europe and have endured their worst start to a season in over half a century - so are they going down?
Monday 23 November 2026 19:56, UK
What started as a blip has become a problem far more systemic for Man Utd.
"If the name wasn't Man Utd and you're watching their performances, you'd say they are a team in a relegation fight. They're conceding lots of goals, a comedy of errors, red cards - they've won one game all season," said Sky Sports' Jamie Carragher.
Only Ipswich beaten in 11 attempts, the worst defence in Europe - and a 4-0 hammering at Liverpool on Sunday to wipe the gloss off Mauricio Pochettino's arrival within 12 first-half minutes.
Carragher added: "This Manchester United back four can't cope with pace. They're a million miles off it in terms of coming up against what they are in the Premier League."
The unthinkable is beginning to become thinkable. Are United in an actual relegation battle now?

- Man Utd fixtures & scores | FREE Man Utd highlights▶️
- Got Sky? Watch Premier League games LIVE on your phone📱
- Not got Sky? Latest Sky Sports deals or stream PL games with no contract📺
"They're in a relegation fight right now because of where they are in the table," said Carragher after a fifth defeat of the season left them with their lowest points tally at this stage of a season since 1972. "You can't say anything else when you look at their record this season.
"We don't believe it will happen over a 38-game season, but they haven't had the most difficult of starts. They've played a lot of promoted teams; they haven't played the best team in the league, Arsenal, yet.
"I don't think they'll go down, but this idea that they haven't got a scrap on their hands, they have."
It seems unfathomable. But should it? The numbers don't give Pochettino any grounds for optimism. Only 26 teams - barely one a season - have picked up eight points or fewer from their opening 11 games in the history of the Premier League and only 13 of those, exactly half, avoided the drop.
Of course, most of those were not clubs anywhere near the size and stature of Manchester United. But even the Opta supercomputer, which provides far more contextualised feedback, is losing faith and gives them a 24 per cent chance of going down - though it does still back them to stumble to safety and finish 16th.
"You wonder how low it can get," said Gary Neville after Sunday's defeat. "It's embarrassing. I don't believe they're in a relegation fight, they'll get out of this, but this is the worst Man Utd have been in 53 years. The worst defensive team in Europe, second-bottom in the league, they've never started this badly.
"Mauricio Pochettino's options aren't great."
That may be putting it lightly. As well as the worst defence in Europe's top-five leagues across all competitions, United also have the third-worst performing attack in the Premier League, falling below their xG tally by 4.2 goals already.
In an immediately infamous tweet in 2014, then-boss David Moyes was quoted as saying United "must improve in a number of areas, including passing, creating chances and defending".
Pochettino is unlikely to admit it publicly, but behind closed doors must have similarly widespread concerns even at this early stage. United have not found themselves in the bottom two after 11 games in 40 years.
Sir Alex Ferguson was brought in as their eventual saviour that winter, but turning the tide on this United side is a significantly bigger ask.
Are there personnel at his disposal who could improve matters? Potentially. Neville did pinpoint a back four of Luke Shaw, Harry Maguire, Lisandro Martinez and Diego Dalot who could at least get United out of their defensive slump.
"It's a poor back four, but it's their best back four. It could compete," he added. "But the one that started today and finished against Villa a few weeks ago, that'll get you relegated."
There is good news and bad news. Neville's quartet are unbeaten in every game they have started together since the start of 2023/24 - and can boast a 70-per-cent win ratio. Unfortunately for Pochettino, that only amounts to 10 games across more than three seasons, owing largely to availability.
But that still does not solve the problem of their limp attack. Of the 22 players to have attempted a shot for the club this season, 19 have under-performed their xG, and the three who have not, Benjamin Sesko, Joshua Zirkzee and Youri Tielemans, have scored only a solitary goal apiece.
There remain huge question marks over the Man Utd dressing room, its commitment and a lack of leadership which permeated into the public sphere in the final weeks of Michael Carrick's reign. Though Pochettino's players have shown they can perform when they want to. Carrick himself knows that better than anyone.
But his successor barely has time to address it over the next few weeks, with only one free midweek between now and the end of 2026 - and even then he has a trip to the Emirates, live on Sky Sports on December 20, to face at the end of his first uninterrupted week on the training pitch.
By that point United will be almost half-way through the Premier League season - and alarm bells will be ringing even louder if they still find themselves in the quagmire, especially with rock bottom Crystal Palace and promoted Coventry to come before then.
But might even that prove problematic for Pochettino?
"If you look at the strength of the Premier League this season, in terms of what we would call the teams you'd expect to be mid-table or near the bottom - it's probably as strong as it's ever been," said Carragher.
"There's no poor teams. There's not many great teams, but there's no poor teams.
"And that's a problem for Man Utd."

items.text:
As tech outages mount, some New Yorkers prepare for the worst
As digital disruptions raise concerns about essential services, some residents are preparing for prolonged outages.
New York City, New York – When a series of technology outages struck services across the United States this month, Kristyn Lavery began thinking about what might happen if the disruptions lasted longer.
The 67-year-old retired fashion designer, who has lived in Manhattan’s East Village since 1981, started keeping cash and extra water in her 32.5-square-metre (350-square-foot) apartment. She also looked into ways to keep warm but says she cannot afford a generator, which can cost hundreds of dollars.
Lavery is part of a trend of US citizens stocking up on essential supplies over fears that the technology outages could presage other vulnerabilities — or even a tech collapse.
Public concern began to grow on November 13, after a malfunctioning flight communication system led to a nationwide halt to air travel. Experts later credited the ground stop to a tech update gone awry.
The flight delays happened around the same time that the tech giant Microsoft announced problems with its services, including the email platform Outlook.
In the following days, the US National Security Agency, the tech company Apple and banks including JPMorgan Chase all reported service disruptions.
Last week, authorities said they were also investigating a suspected hack of the National Crime Information Center and the US Department of Agriculture.
While there is no evidence that the episodes are connected, residents like Lavery say they are worried.
For Lavery, the recent outages have heightened fears shaped by major events like the attacks on September 11, 2001, and the COVID-19 pandemic.
Now, with US officials warning about further disruptions, she is determined to take the possibility of another emergency more seriously.
“I feel vulnerable. And I don’t want to be a victim. Yet I feel like, if this happens, it will be on me for not preparing,” she told Al Jazeera.
She remembers what happened in 2012, when flooding from Hurricane Sandy disrupted transport and power in parts of Manhattan. Her neighbourhood went without heat and hot water for days, and residents had to rely on one another.
“I got no help from the government,” Lavery said. “It was neighbours helping neighbours.”
A surge in emergency preparedness
The growing interest in emergency preparedness has become a trend on social media in recent weeks.
On TikTok, a New Yorker, identified only as Nat, posted a video on Tuesday showing the canned food and water she stocked up on for her Lower Manhattan apartment.
“There’s some weird s*** going down in the US. And we don’t really know what’s going on, but I’ve been convinced to stock up,” she said. “I’d rather be crazy than sorry.”
Moderators of Reddit’s r/preppers community — an emergency preparedness forum — said on Sunday that the group had gained nearly 12,000 members in the past month. It recorded 4.2 million views over the same period, up by 2.4 million from the previous month.
There are also signs of increased emergency spending in recent months, even before the tech outages began. Sales from the wholesale retailer Costco, for instance, rose 8.1 percent in October, excluding fuel.
Analysts at Mizuho Securities, a financial firm, estimated that the company’s growth accelerated to about 12 percent in the final week of the month and continued into early November.
They attributed some of the increase to emergency-preparedness purchases due to what they called “apocalyptic concerns” on social media.
Separately, sales of water-purification tablets rose 154 percent and disinfecting wipes 72 percent in the four weeks ending November 1, compared with a year earlier, according to Circana data.
Joel Smernoff, CEO of the New York-based emergency-preparedness company Black Umbrella, told Al Jazeera that his sales had nearly doubled over the past two weeks, largely from new customers.
He explained that the recent outages have made the vulnerabilities of everyday infrastructure feel more tangible.
“It’s the drumbeat of every day: Another huge brand is going down,” Smernoff said.
He also brought up New York’s experience with Hurricane Sandy. After the storm struck, his apartment building near Union Square lost power and running water for six days.
He said older residents on upper floors who could not manage the stairs needed the building superintendent to bring them bottled water.
“We don’t know where or when an unexpected event is going to hit, whether it’s a storm, a cyberattack or infrastructure going down,” Smernoff said. “The rapidity and the frequency of it can be surprising.”
Cybersecurity experts have pointed out that artificial intelligence has made it easier to discover potential flaws in software, forcing companies to proactively seek out and patch vulnerabilities.
But emergency updates can themselves introduce disruptions when they are rolled out across complex systems.
How officials have responded
Faced with public questions about the outages, US officials have emphasised they have found no evidence that the recent incidents are part of a coordinated attack.
President Donald Trump himself has tried to allay fears in his recent media appearances.
“Tell them to relax. Everything is good. These are individual events,” Trump told Fox News on Thursday when asked about the outages and whether the public should be preparing for emergencies.
Local officials have also addressed the outages by highlighting government emergency planning. New York Governor Kathy Hochul and New York City Mayor Zohran Mamdani, for example, addressed the disruptions on November 17.
Hochul said she had been receiving daily briefings from state intelligence and cybersecurity teams since the first Microsoft Outlook problems. The state, she explained, had also taken steps to strengthen critical infrastructure.

Chelsea must sign centre-back or will achieve nothing with Levi Colwill and Wesley Fofana, says Jamie Carragher
Sky Sports' Jamie Carragher analysed Chelsea's leaky defence on Monday Night Football, highlighting the partnership of Levi Colwill and Wesley Fofana as a major concern; watch Nott'm Forest vs Chelsea on Friday, live on Sky Sports; kick-off 8pm
Monday 23 November 2026 20:07, UK
Jamie Carragher believes Chelsea must sign a dominant centre-back or they will have "no chance of achieving anything".
Chelsea have conceded 20 goals in 11 Premier League games this season and were thrashed 4-1 at home to Leeds on Saturday, which has put pressure on new manager Xabi Alonso, with his side sitting eighth and already 12 points behind leaders Arsenal.
Leeds overpowered Chelsea with their physicality, as Dominic Calvert-Lewin bullied centre-backs Levi Colwill and Wesley Fofana, exposing their weak defence the same way Sunderland's Brian Brobbey did in their 1-0 win before the international break.

Chelsea are five points behind fourth-placed Liverpool and are already without European football this season - but Carragher feels qualifying for the Champions League will be a difficult task with their current centre-back pairing.
"Chelsea have got a massive problem at centre-back and if they don't change it in January, they're going to have a big problem in terms of where they feel they should be this season with the Champions League," he said on Monday Night Football.
"Colwill at Sunderland against Brobbey gave the penalty away, and the manager took him off at half-time. Fofana's performance against Man United, especially in the first half, was one of the worst you'll see from a centre-back this season.
"As a partnership, this will never work because they're not physical enough and there's no real leader there.
"It almost feels like you've got two novices playing, but one cost £75m, and Colwill has been talked up a lot not just at Chelsea but at international level as well."
Chelsea signed centre-back Maxence Lacroix from Crystal Palace for £51m in the summer, but he has missed the last three matches with a hamstring injury.
"Those two (Colwill and Fofana) can't play in a back four as a two, but it reminds me of myself at Liverpool," said Carragher. "We didn't fix it defensively and we were seen as weak, conceding from set pieces and long throws. It wasn't until we signed Sami Hyypia, 6ft 4in, dominant centre-back, leader, great player, that it changed for us.
"This is not going to change with what they have. Lacroix is a decent player, that's a sticking plaster until the next transfer window in January or the end of the season. Until they sign that dominant centre-back and leader, they've got absolutely no chance of achieving anything."
Chelsea have kept the fourth fewest clean sheets in Europe this calendar year, which largely predates Alonso's tenure, although Carragher has been surprised by the former Bayer Leverkusen and Real Madrid head coach's style.
"There's a lot of talk now about Xabi Alonso and I think watching Chelsea this season, they haven't been that impressive even when they've won games in terms of how I think we all felt they would play," he added.
"Everybody had this idea, myself included, who had watched Leverkusen play, you think of the player Xabi Alonso would play, the Spanish influence and managed by Pep Guardiola. You're expecting Chelsea to be more of a possession-based team and when you watch them the football isn't amazing and they rely on the front three a lot.
"Cole Palmer has dropped off in the last few weeks and Joao Pedro has been injured as well. When they've all been there, it always felt like there was an overreliance on that front three. The goal on the weekend was a direct play; you can get goals in different ways, but there hasn't been that intricate football that we were expecting."
Merson: My worry is that Liverpool thought Alonso wasn't good enough
In his latest Sky Sports column, Paul Merson has raised doubts about whether Alonso is good enough as Chelsea manager after Saturday's home loss to Leeds.
Merson believes Liverpool may have snubbed Alonso for the head coach role - eventually taken by Andoni Iraola - due to concerns about his pedigree.
He told Sky Sports: "My biggest worry is that Liverpool could have had Xabi Alonso and they chose not to. Obviously, Liverpool didn't think he was good enough.
"Alonso took the Chelsea job, and Liverpool sacked Arne Slot two weeks later. You can't tell me that Liverpool couldn't have spoken to Alonso and say: 'Don't take the Chelsea job, we're going to take you'.
"He was out of a job as well, Liverpool could have had him and he'd have gone there all day long. So why didn't they take him? Did they know something that we're seeing now?
"It just always sits in my mind. That was my worry - and now it's playing out.
"If this was Liam Rosenior in charge at Chelsea and getting these results, he'd be in major trouble. One hundred per cent, he'd be in trouble. And remember, Rosenior didn't have Morgan Rogers in his Chelsea team, bought for £116m.
"But it's because of the unbelievable job he did at Bayer Leverkusen that everybody is thinking: it will be alright."

items.text:
Russia threatens ‘hostile’ Estonia with ‘open war’
Moscow accuses Tallinn of ‘hostile actions’ including border closure, allowing Ukraine to launch attacks from its territory, and discrimination against Estonia’s ethnic Russian population.
Russia has accused Estonia of carrying out numerous “hostile actions” and threatened “open war” against the neighbouring Baltic state.
Russia’s Ministry of Foreign Affairs on Monday accused Tallinn of a range of hostile actions, asserting that the NATO and European Union member state is “on the verge of triggering open war”.
The outburst comes after Estonia announced the planned closure of its border with Russia, and a Ukrainian attack on a Russian ship in the Baltic Sea.
The ministry set out its accusations in a statement after summoning Estonia’s charge d’affaires in Moscow, Marek Uhtegi, to issue a formal protest over Tallinn’s decision to close the border.
“The Estonian diplomat was once again told that such provocative and extremely dangerous actions are on the verge of triggering open war with Russia,” it said, adding that Estonia is displaying “Russophobic” tendencies.
Among a list of additional accusations, the ministry said Estonia had “tacitly allow[ed] its airspace to be used by Ukrainian drones for attacks on northwestern Russia”. Tallinn was swift to deny the claim.
It also accused Estonia of trying to obstruct the movement of Russian cargo ships in the Baltic Sea, banning the transit of Russian and Belarusian grain, seeking a ban on the Russian language and threatening to close the Russian Orthodox Church.
“The Russian side reserves the right to take comprehensive political and diplomatic measures aimed at protecting Russia’s national interests and the legitimate rights of its citizens,” the ministry said.
Estonia is host to a sizeable ethnic Russian population, which Moscow has often claimed is subject to discrimination.
Russia’s incursions into eastern Ukraine in 2014 were based on claims of suppression of Russian speakers’ rights in the region.
Earlier this month, Estonia said it would close border crossings with Russia from December 1 for at least six months, having accused the Kremlin’s security services of staging an attempted arson attack on an Estonian defence company.
This marked a sharp escalation in tensions between Estonia and Russia, which Tallinn – Kyiv’s ally – sees as part of a broader campaign of hostile activity linked to Moscow’s war in Ukraine.
Russia has denied any involvement in the attack. Closing the border, the ministry said, “will inevitably backfire – not only on Tallinn itself but also on its allies within the EU and NATO”.
In a statement, the Ministry of Foreign Affairs of Estonia did not respond to all of the allegations but denied that it allows its territory to be used for Ukrainian military operations.
“While we generally do not comment on or engage with Russian propaganda narratives, in this case we can reiterate that Estonia has never allowed, and will never allow, its territory to be used for military operations by another country,” it said.
“Other countries in our region have also made this position clear,” it added.
Russia has long accused Estonia and other NATO states in the Baltic region of allowing Ukrainian drones to use their airspace. Ukrainian drones have frequently entered NATO airspace, but Kyiv says this is a result of Russian signal jamming.
NATO countries have repeatedly denied intentionally allowing drones to use their airspace, and blamed Russia for the incursions.
NATO Secretary-General Mark Rutte, speaking in Berlin, said the alliance was monitoring the situation in Estonia, along with an incursion last week by Russian missiles into Poland, adding that NATO had options available to respond.
“We see situations in Poland and Estonia, etc ,” Rutte said. “When it comes to the military domain, we will always make assessments of our deterrence and defence and make updates where necessary.”

items.title: Google Search’s AI Mode can now tap into Drive and Wallet for more personalized responses
items.summary: Google announced on Monday that it’s expanding Personal Intelligence in Search’s AI Mode with integrations for Google Drive, Google Wallet, and the Gemini app. Personal Intelligence is designed to offer users more personalized, context-aware answers by connecting to their Google apps and drawing on
items.text:
Google announced on Monday that it’s expanding Personal Intelligence in Search’s AI Mode with integrations for Google Drive, Google Wallet, and the Gemini app. Personal Intelligence is designed to offer users more personalized, context-aware answers by connecting to their Google apps and drawing on information from their digital lives. The feature can already connect to apps like Gmail, Google Calendar, and Google Photos.
By bringing Personal Intelligence in AI Mode to Drive, Wallet, and the Gemini app, Google is leveraging the wealth of user data that’s already within its ecosystem. Since users rely on these services, the tech giant can deliver more personalized experiences that rivals aren’t able to match. Of course, not everyone wants AI looking at their Wallet and Drive, so connecting the apps is optional, and you can turn Personal Intelligence on or off at any time.
Google says that connecting Google Wallet to Personal Intelligence lets users track their financial goals, cut everyday spending, and make better use of credit card rewards. The tech giant notes that if users choose to connect their Wallet, AI Mode can only read information from accounts and isn’t able to move or manage their money.
As for Drive, the company says important information related to a project or major decision is often scattered across documents and spreadsheets. By connecting Google Drive to Personal Intelligence, AI can draw on those files to provide more relevant, personalized answers, such as creating a tailored plan for tax season.
Users will also be able to share context between their Gemini app and AI Mode in Search, which means that if they explore an idea in the Gemini app, they won’t have to start over with AI Mode because it will already have the information, and vice versa.
Additionally, Google says users will soon be able to view the context that AI Mode uses via a new “Personalization” icon that will appear below responses.
The company also announced on Monday that users will start to see more personally relevant responses in AI Overviews and AI Mode that will be tailored to users’ recent search context.

items.title: Nothing’s upcoming Ear Note is a pair of earbuds with AI transcription
items.summary: Nothing’s new AI device is the Ear Note, a set of earbuds and their microphone-equipped charging case that can record and transcribe conversations, with a connected app to manage the recordings, transcriptions and AI-generated summaries, similar to Apple’s new Watch feature and devices like Amazon’s
items.text:
Nothing’s new AI device is the Ear Note, a set of earbuds and their microphone-equipped charging case that can record and transcribe conversations, with a connected app to manage the recordings, transcriptions and AI-generated summaries, similar to Apple’s new Watch feature and devices like Amazon’s Bee wearable. Nothing CEO Carl Pei demonstrated the new device to Bloomberg, but said the company hasn’t yet settled on a price ahead of a planned launch on December 8th.
Nothing’s upcoming Ear Note is a pair of earbuds with AI transcription
The new AI device from Nothing can record and transcribe audio with AI from the earbuds or via microphones on their charging case.
The report also says Nothing’s rumored plans for an AI smartwatch and smart glasses are delayed, while it will be “pursuing a more aggressive smartphone release schedule next year than it did in 2026.” In a post on X, Pei said this is “the first of many products building a hardware context layer for AI. Rather than ask you to carry a new product, we took something you already wear and trust and made it intelligent.”
According to Bloomberg, the earbuds will “support interactions with various AI agents, including a more basic voice-control system developed by Nothing, letting users engage in back-and-forth conversations.” Users will also be able to record themselves with a “Talk” button on the case, like Nothing previously included on the Ear 3, which also has recording capabilities. Earlier this year, Nothing introduced an Audio Snapshot recording feature in the Ear 3A. Anker’s Soundcore Liberty 5 Pro Max can also record directly to the earbuds’ case and generate AI transcripts and summaries in an app.

On his team, he says the missing Igor Thiago presses superbly from the fron
items.text:
Key events
Before we dig into the teams, here’s Keith Andrews, who acknowledges Brentford’s best start to a Premier League season, but is also frustrated they’ve not got more points – especially after a brilliant pre-season.
On his team, he says the missing Igor Thiago presses superbly from the front, but Callum Wilson wasn’t just signed as a sub and has added a lot to the dressing room. Brentford will tweak their method to account for the change, but won’t alter their essentials.
Back to pre-season, he says he hit on an XI towards the end of it, which is why Mikel Damsgaard hasn’t played much, but he’s a talented player and gets his chance tonight.
Brentford (4-3-3): Kelleher; Kayode, Ajer, Van den Berg, Lewis-Potter; Yarmoliuk, Janelt, Damsgaard; Outtara, Wilson, Anthony. Subs: Valdimarsson, Schade, Jensen, Carvalho, Sangare, Diouf, Nunes, Schuster, Fredrick.
Everton (4-2-3-1): Pickford; O’Brien, Tarkowski, Branthwaite, Mykolenko; Garner, Armstrong, Rohl, Dewsbury-Hall, George; Barry. Subs: Travers, Maitland-Niles, Keane, Grealish, Dibling, Johnson, Norgaard, Alcaraz, Hackney.
Referee: Craig Pawson (Sheffield)
Though the standard at the top of the Premier League reflects neither its spending or self-mythologising, the level below that is perhaps higher than in any league, ever. Every team is organised, physical and athletic, with technical players in pretty much every position and various able to settle a game. As such, only seven points separate Bournemouth, in fifth place, from Ipswich Town, in 16th, results dependent not just on which side is better but who plays whom when, with final positions a reflection of what happens to be happening when the music stops.
Tonight’s match is emblematic of this condition. Only one side in that top 16 – 15th placed Fulham – have scored fewer than Everton’s 12 goals in 10 games yet, somehow, David Moyes’ men are seventh in the table. Brentford, meanwhile, are two points behind in 10th and, outside of the top four, only sixth-placed Leeds have conceded fewer than their 11 goals.
Which is one way of saying tonight’s encounter is unlikely to deliver a goal-fest. But, on the other hand, it will give us two focused, settled, confident sides, fuelled by intensity, skill and just a little bit of magic.
Kick-off: 8pm GMT

items.text:
Tajikistan withdraws from ICC, follows US call
November 23, 2026
Tajikistan has now become the fourth country to announce its formal withdrawal from the International Criminal Court (ICC) in the Hague, Netherlands since the US announced its intention to "dismantle" the body — joining Chad, Naoero [formerly Nauru] and Venezuela.
US President Donald Trump and Secretary of State Marco Rubio have railed against the court as abusing its jurisdiction, with Trump publicly attacking the ICC during remarks at a trilateral meeting with Chinese President Xi Jinping and Russian President Vladimir Putin — who is wanted by the court for war crimes committed during the course of Russia's full-scale invasion of neighboring Ukraine.
Trump's public attacks on the world's permanent war crimes tribunal prompted an amused smirk from Putin during their meeting in Shenzhen, China.
Why is the ICC important?
The ICC prosecutes individuals accused of genocide, crimes against humanity, crimes of aggression and war crimes in instances when national cannot or will not act.
The ICC issued an international arrest warrant for Putin in March 2023.
Tajikistan's government said it made the decision to initiate the one-year withdrawal process on Friday, when Putin made a stopover visit after leaving his trilateral meeting with Trump and Xi.
The ICC said it "regrets" Tajikistan's decision, adding that the move undermines "the collective pursuit of justice" and weakens "global efforts to end impunity."
"The ICC stands at the heart of the international system of accountability, and its effectiveness depends on sustained and unequivocal support from the international community," an ICC statement continued.
Tajikistan signed the Rome Statute that established the ICC back in 1998 and ratified it in 2000.
Burkina Faso, Mali and Niger have also announced their withdrawal from the court, blasting it as a tool of "neocolonial repression."

The feud between George Russell and Max Verstappen reignited in spectacular style in Las Vegas following a clash between the pair in practice; watch the Qatar Grand Prix live on Sky Sports this weekend, with qualifying at 6pm on Saturday and the race at 4pm on Sunday
Monday 23 November 2026 18:44, UK
The reignition of the long-running feud between George Russell and Max Verstappen has added an entertaining twist to the end of the 2026 Formula 1 season, but it may not be what the Mercedes driver needed at this moment.
Russell and Verstappen clashed during final practice at the Las Vegas Grand Prix when the Red Bull driver, slightly cheekily, snatched track position from his Mercedes rival as they both prepared for push laps.
Irked by Verstappen's actions, which he later said he felt breached a gentleman's agreement the drivers share, Russell attempted to reclaim track position from the weaving Red Bull, with the pair making slight contact.

The stewards summoned the two drivers following the session as they conducted an investigation, before handing Verstappen a warning.
The incident came less than a month on from Verstappen being involved a similar incident with Racing Bulls driver Liam Lawson during practice at the Mexico City Grand Prix, which resulted in both drivers being given one-place grid penalties.
Speaking to Sky Italy later that evening, Russell said: "There's nothing in the rules to say you cannot overtake someone who is starting a lap but when you do this, you are screwing this person over and he does this week in, week out with many drivers and everybody accepts it.
"I'm not just going to accept somebody to screw me over like this and walk around like they're bigger and better than everyone else. Somebody's got to stand up to that guy."
Russell's comments came after the result of qualifying in Las Vegas dictated that the pair would start together on the front row, with Verstappen ahead in pole position.
That setup a Saturday night showdown, in which the pair engaged in a thrilling battle for the lead for much of the race, before Russell dropped behind Kimi Antonelli in the latter stages and then drove into a barrier attempting to pass his Mercedes team-mate.
Verstappen reacted on team radio with apparent glee having seen Russell's error in his mirrors, and then, after closing out a superb victory, further stuck the boot into the British driver during the post-race press conference for the top three.
The four-time world champion said: "The thing is, he speaks a lot next to the track. And honestly, for me, it doesn't really bother me because he's so far below my level that it doesn't really make any sense for me anyway to try and challenge that. So, it doesn't bother me.
"And today, karma is a b****. It was honestly fantastic when I looked in my mirror and I saw what was happening [when Russell crashed]. I was like, 'fantastic, my day is only getting better.' And of course, when I then crossed the line in first, my day was complete."
A history of the Russell-Verstappen feud
With less than five months separating them in age, Russell and Verstappen have been racing each other in karting since they were children.
While Mercedes team principal Toto Wolff reflected in Las Vegas that the feud may have stretched back to those days, the first notable F1 flashpoint between the pair came in the 2023 Azerbaijan Sprint when they made contact through several corners on the opening lap.
In a post-race exchange broadcast to the world, Verstappen barked at Russell to "expect next time the same" and swore at the Mercedes driver as he walked away. He would later refer to Russell as "princess George" in an interview with the Dutch media.
A spectacular fall out between the pair then occurred towards the end of the 2024 season, after Verstappen felt Russell had played an unreasonably key role in the Red Bull driver being given a grid penalty that cost him pole for the Qatar Grand Prix.
Verstappen said in Qatar that he had "lost all respect" for Russell, who then responded with a remarkable explosive verbal attack on the Dutchman the following week at the season-ending Abu Dhabi Grand Prix.
Russell said Verstappen had threatened to put him "in the wall" in Qatar, and said that "people have been bullied by Max for years". Verstappen questioned the accuracy of Russell's claims and labelled him a "loser" and "backstabber".
The pair clashed once more on track at the 2025 Spanish Grand Prix when Verstappen, enraged at his own team for instructing him to let Russell through to avoid receiving a penalty, appeared to wave the Mercedes past before lunging into the side of it.
Verstappen was penalised by the stewards, later admitted the move was "not right" and apologised to his team, but did not personally address Russell.
Less talked about than the pair's clashes is a potential further tension added by Russell's boss Wolff having very publicly tried to sign Verstappen from Red Bull. Russell told Sky Sports F1 in June 2025 that his own contract extension was being delayed by Mercedes' attempts to sign Verstappen.
More 2026 pain for Russell?
The previous clashes between the pair came when Russell was in a position of strength at Mercedes, given he had performed hugely impressively during his first four seasons with the team from 2022 to 2025.
Russell had expressed belief on many occasions over the years that if Mercedes delivered a title-winning car, he was ready to grab the opportunity, and few doubted him.

items.text:
India pledges $1.6bn in flood relief for Nepal as Balendra Shah visits Modi
Nepal’s PM Balendra Shah is in New Delhi for a two-day visit – his first since coming to power in March.
India will provide Nepal with a $1.62bn economic package in the wake of August’s devastating floods in the country, which led to the deaths and disappearances of thousands of people.
The sum announced on Monday is one of its largest-ever relief commitments, and comes as New Delhi boosts ties with its Himalayan neighbour, where it competes with China for influence.
The announcement followed talks between India’s Prime Minister Narendra Modi and his Nepali counterpart Balendra Shah, who is in New Delhi for a two-day visit – his first bilateral trip abroad since coming to power in March.
“We express our deep condolences for the loss of lives caused by the devastating floods in Nepal in August,” Modi said, standing alongside Shah in New Delhi. “To support Nepal’s reconstruction, and give fresh momentum to its long-term development, we announce a development cooperation package worth 240 billion Nepali rupees [$1.6bn].”
August’s floods, which scientists say were caused by the effects of climate change, were triggered when part of a mountain glacier collapsed and a torrent of water and mud flooded down into Nepal’s Rasuwa and Nuwakot regions, as well as into China’s Tibet region on August 26. More than 1,300 people have been confirmed dead, and more than 5,000 remain missing.
In October, the United Nations’ climate loss and damage fund set aside a sum of $20m for aid to Nepal.
India’s package will include a $377m grant for post-disaster reconstruction and new infrastructure projects, and a $1.24bn line of credit for energy projects, the countries said in a joint statement.
India is Nepal’s largest trading partner, accounting for more than 60 percent of its imports, worth $8.6bn, while China accounts for 13 percent, or $1.8bn, according to World Bank figures.
Besides the flood relief package, the pair agreed on further cooperation in education and research, satellite communications, and sustainable urban development. The two leaders also jointly opened a train link connecting the countries.
“May the friendship between Nepal and India be one where trust stands as tall as the Himalayas,” said Shah.

items.text:
Iranian authorities flog singer who performed without hijab, lawyers say
- Published
A prominent singer who performed without the mandatory hijab and four members of her band and production team have been flogged by Iranian authorities, lawyers say.
Parastoo Ahmadi, three musicians and a producer were each given 74 lashes in the city of Qom, a member of their defence team told the BBC.
Ahmadi, 29, wore a sleeveless dress during a concert that was livestreamed in December 2024. Iran's laws ban public performances by women and require them to wear headscarves and modest clothing.
This June, a criminal court in Qom convicted Ahmadi and eight others of "offending public decency" through the publication of "obscene and indecent material", which they had denied.
In addition to being sentenced to 74 lashes, they were banned from audiovisual activities and from leaving the country for two years.
At the end of September, an appeals court in Qom rejected the defendants' appeal and confirmed the sentence, her lawyers said.
There was widespread condemnation of the sentences from other Iranian artists and human rights activists, who warned that flogging constituted cruel, inhuman and degrading punishment, and violated the international prohibition on torture.
On Monday, one of the defendants' lawyers told the BBC that Ahmadi and four of her male co-defendants had been flogged at the third branch of the Criminal Sentence Enforcement Office in Qom.
"We did everything in our power to have the verdict overturned, or at least to secure a reduction in the sentence or a suspension, but it didn't work out," he said.
"The other lawyers and I even tried to get the enforcement of the sentence postponed, but the enforcement branch insisted on carrying it out immediately."
Pro-reform daily Etemad cited another defence lawyer, Mostafa Nili, as identifying the four men flogged alongside Ahmadi as Soheil Faghih-Nasiri, Amin Taheri, Amirali Pirnia and Mohsen Lashkari.
"Parastoo Ahmadi's flogging for singing and dressing as she chooses is a flagrant violation of her fundamental rights and a chilling demonstration of the Iranian authorities' determination to suppress women's freedoms and to violently punish anyone who dares to challenge their discriminatory laws and policies," said Bahar Ghandehari, director of advocacy at the US-based Center for Human Rights in Iran (CHRI).
Under Iranian law, which is based on the country's interpretation of Sharia, women and girls above the age of puberty must cover their hair with a hijab and wear long, loose-fitting clothing to disguise their figures.
In 2022, protests swept across the Islamic Republic following the death in custody of Mahsa Amini, a 22-year-old Kurdish woman who was detained by morality police in Tehran in September that year for allegedly wearing her hijab "improperly".
Women burnt their headscarves or waved them in the air at the nationwide demonstrations against the clerical establishment, during which hundreds of people were killed in a crackdown by security forces.
Since then, many women and girls have stopped covering their hair in public altogether in open defiance of the dress code. Authorities have responded with periodic waves of arrests, warnings, business closures and other measures.
In January this year, thousands of people were killed and tens of thousands were arrested when security forces crushed another wave of mass anti-establishment protests, this time sparked by the country's economic crisis.
Since the start of Iran's war with the US and Israel in late February, authorities have intensified their use of the death penalty against protesters.
According to the Norway-based group Iran Human Rights, at least 39 men convicted over January's protests and two convicted over the 2022 unrest have been executed, along with 16 people allegedly affiliated with banned opposition groups and 17 others convicted of espionage or collaborating with foreign states.
Another 121 protesters detained in January, including six women and five juvenile offenders, have been sentenced to death and are at imminent risk of execution, it says.

items.text:
Danish top court’s ‘ghetto law’ ruling supports hardline immigration policy
The country’s top court said eviction of ‘non-Western’ families did not constitute discrimination.
Denmark’s top court has ruled that the eviction of “non-Western” tenants from a social housing estate under the country’s “ghetto law” was not discriminatory.
The Supreme Court on Monday rejected an appeal by seven families, after lower courts had dismissed their legal suits against the termination of their leases by landlord Boliggarden in 2022 on the basis that they had been discriminated against based on ethnic origin. The ruling backs Denmark’s tough stance on immigration.
The country’s “ghetto law” housing legislation, adopted in 2018, allows for the relocation of residents from areas in which more than half of residents are “non-Western”.
It requires social housing estates to change the social mix by renting at least 60 percent of homes at market rates by 2030. The government has described the legislation as a bid to promote integration.
The seven families were among 91 that had their leases terminated in Helsingor, north of Copenhagen, most of them “non-Western”.
A lower court found in 2022 that the law’s criterion of “immigrants and descendants from non-Western countries” is neutral and not a measure of ethnic origin.
The Supreme Court on Monday upheld that, ruling “that applying the criterion of the law involves dividing people into two groups (people who are immigrants and descendants from non-Western countries, and all other persons)”.
“Both groups include a very large majority of different ethnic origins, and there will simultaneously be persons with the same ethnic origin in both groups.”
The judges also noted that there had been “no information about the ethnic background of the residents who have been evicted”.
It therefore concluded that “the category ‘immigrants and descendants from non-Western countries’ provided for in the social housing law must be regarded as a neutral criterion and not as a criterion relating to ethnic origin”.
“We’re obviously disappointed,” one of the plaintiffs, Riad, told AFP.
Eddie Khawaja, the families’ lawyer, told Al Jazeera earlier this month that in his view, “non-Western” is “a proxy for ethnic origin”.
‘Parallel societies’
Denmark has pursued a tough line on immigration for more than three decades.
The 2018 “ghetto law” is aimed at combatting segregation and “parallel societies” in disadvantaged neighbourhoods, according to the government. It has been widely criticised by tenants and tenants’ associations but has broad political support.
“Non-Western” is one criterion the Danish government uses to define “transformation areas”, which it previously termed “hard ghettos”.
According to Statistics Denmark’s definition, “non-Western” countries include every country in the world except the 27 member states of the European Union, as well as Andorra, Britain, Iceland, Liechtenstein, Monaco, Norway, Northern Ireland, San Marino, Switzerland, the Vatican, Canada, the United States, Australia and New Zealand.
Housing Minister Jacob Mark said in a statement that he was satisfied with the Supreme Court decision, reiterating the assertion that the law “strengthens security, social cohesion, and integration”.
Nonprofit housing accommodates more than one million people in Denmark and is open to all. Under the 2018 legislation, however, some 11,000 people will be forced to leave their apartments to be rehoused elsewhere by 2030, according to tenants’ associations.
The European Union’s top court ruled last year that the law could amount to ethnic discrimination.

items.title: Madness erupts as Sevilla deny Betis in wild end to Spain’s ‘derby of derbies’
items.summary: “If we didn’t celebrate a goal, especially in this game, that would be madness,” Kike Salas said. items.text:
“If we didn’t celebrate a goal, especially in this game, that would be madness,” Kike Salas said. Instead, this was madness, the kind of moment a derby is meant to have, even if it has nothing else. It was late, it was lucky, and there wasn’t even a winner but right there, right then, at 24 minutes past 8pm on Saturday evening in the Ramón Sánchez-Pizjuán Stadium, it felt like there was. Frankly it was a bit rubbish, as bad a goal as you’ll see, but it was also the best, practically Pelé against the Nazis. Suddenly there were arms and legs everywhere, tears too. Cameras confirmed it. Zoom in and there they are: actual, real life tears.
In the 91st minute of the 146th meeting between Sevilla Fútbol Club and Real Betis Balompié – “derby of derbies” according to Luis García, the Sevilla coach for whom it was the first – Salas’s shot from 18 yards went through Marc Bartra’s legs and Álvaro Valles’s hands. The ball dribbled into the Betis net so apologetically it barely touched the net at all and hadn’t got there before Sevilla’s vice-captain was gone. Raised in Morón de la Frontera, to the south of a city divided, Salas joined Sevilla at 11; now, having levelled the game at 1-1, he went tearing towards the terraces, absolutely losing it like they were.
In the six-yard box, Robbie Ure, the Scottish striker who had watched the ball pass and whose own shot barely 100 seconds before was the eighth Betis blocked, resigned to the fact that it just wasn’t going to happen, reacted to the fact that it actually had with his right arm pumping like Animal on the drums. Screaming as he went, Salas thumped at his chest as hard. Around the Sánchez Pizjuán, 42,983 went wild except the 600 Béticos high in the corner. They couldn’t believe this and nor could their players: of all the ways to let go. From the Sevilla bench, everyone ran towards the team.
García went the other way through the crowd in his blue suit, like the final scene of a romcom: a man fighting against the rush-hour tide, bundling into a busy subway station desperate to reach the train before it leaves with her on board. He was in the middle of the pitch when he put the brakes on and returned, alone. He had been through the emotions; frustration, relief, joy, vindication and frustration again. A colleague awaited with a high five that was hard too. They could have won. But they also could have lost – Sevilla had trailed to Antony’s goal, which wasn’t great either, and Odysseas Vlachodimos’s superb save had prevented the Brazilian from getting Betis’s second and ending it – but at least they had salvaged a point.
At the final whistle, the Betis midfielder Dani Ceballos came to console Valles. “You’ve been our best player this season,” he told the goalkeeper, which was true. No one in La Liga has made more saves and none have been more significant either. Valles’s xG avoided is 8.3; the next best is 4.1. At the same time, Salas tried to do the post-game interview but couldn’t hear over the noise. Behind him, his family were waiting for a hug. As Betis’s players made their way, Sevilla’s players stood before supporters at the north end, applauding and applauded back.
“When you go to your greatest rivals’ ground, you deserve to win but they get a draw and on top of that they celebrate it, you know you’re doing things right,” said the Betis captain Bartra, who also claimed that Salas shouldn’t have been on the pitch to score the equaliser after he had trodden on Isco’s ankle. “A bad game from us only allows them to draw at home,” said the Betis president, Ángel Haro. “Fortunately, we’re in a period when a draw feels like sadness to us and a triumph for them.”
And so the debate was served, so the accusations came, the usual nonsense. In Spain? In Seville? Surely not?! Etc and so on. But if the words of Betis’s captain and president prompted that, if those words were a little pointed in a city where they pride themselves on being wind-up merchants and the derby is the most passionate in the country, there is an obvious response: well, yeah. Not least precisely because it’s about putting one over on each other. Every goal is an explosion and Sevilla got theirs in the 91st minute. Against Betis. From the centre-back who’s been at the club half his life. Of course they celebrated it.
If it might have seemed a little odd for Sevilla to stand there before their fans celebrating when they hadn’t won and a run of one win in seven in the league had been confirmed, that too was part of it. Because Bartra and Haro were right, to their credit and to Sevilla’s too. At the start of this derby, a huge banner came down over the north stand; a supporters’ work of art made by hand as ever, it lauded a history of greatness, but maybe history is the word, and that’s the real greatness: it is three years since Sevilla won a trophy or qualified for Europe, those days not just fading fast but long gone, yet here they are anyway, more than 35,000 of them every week.
Sevilla are a club in crisis, where the former president José María del Nido is at war with the former president José María del Nido – and, yes, they are father and son. Where the debt is almost €200m (£167.2m) and the solution, a sale to a consortium led by Sergio Ramos, fell through. Where they have the lowest salary limit in the whole of primera, at €20m (£16.7m), and four second division teams were allowed to spend more. Where this summer they had a net spend of minus €25m (£20.9m). And where they qualified for the Champions League three years running under Julen Lopetegui, sacked him, went through seven managers in three years and finished 12th, 14th and 17th, closer to relegation every season.
In May they finished 13th yet only escaped relegation in the penultimate week, and that was a miracle. The day that García had been presented as coach, arriving on a rescue mission that seemed impossible, the sporting director was overheard saying: “It’s like a funeral in here”.

items.text:
DK Metcalf denies poking Cooper DeJean in the eyes after ejection from Pittsburgh Steelers-Philadelphia Eagles game
DK Metcalf was ejected from the Pittsburgh Steelers' 19-16 loss to the Philadelphia Eagles on Sunday after two unsportsmanlike conduct penalties 10 offensive plays apart; the second of those appeared to see the receiver reach into Cooper DeJean's facemask and poke him in the eyes
Monday 23 November 2026 18:38, UK
Pittsburgh Steelers wide receiver DK Metcalf has denied intentionally poking Philadelphia Eagles defensive back Cooper DeJean in the eyes after being ejected from the game during the second half of their 19-16 loss on Sunday.
Metcalf was tossed for the third time in his career after being flagged twice for personal fouls following a couple of confrontations with DeJean, the second of which included Metcalf appearing to stick his fingers in between the Eagles defender's facemask.
Asked on Monday if he could go into detail about his exchanges with DeJean, Metcalf initially responded that he "couldn't remember" before backtracking and saying that he was trying to send a message to DeJean to "stop pushing me".
Metcalf had caught only one pass for two yards before being sent to the locker room.
The 28-year-old was suspended for two games last season for swiping at a fan in Detroit and was shown the door twice earlier in his career while playing for the Seattle Seahawks.
Asked why this keeps happening, Metcalf told reporters: "I think you got to ask the people that seem to do that to me".
Metcalf noted that opponents trying to get under his skin is nothing new, saying that San Francisco 49ers players attempted to do that regularly during the Seahawks' frequent meetings with their NFC West rivals.
The two-time Pro Bowler, who is on pace for career lows in receptions and yards receiving this season, declined to blame the heated interaction on frustration, pointing out that the Steelers are "winning", though Pittsburgh (6-4) has dropped two straight after losing in Philadelphia.
Steelers coach Mike McCarthy called Metcalf's actions "unacceptable" but said he needed more information before deciding whether to take any action.
Metcalf did not appear to be worried about being disciplined by the Steelers or the NFL. "You've got to ask [Pittsburgh general manager] Omar [Khan] that, or anybody else other than DeKaylin," Metcalf said, using his given name.
The highest-paid wide receiver in team history also added that the Steelers need to "score points when we get the ball and not stall on third down or get a turnover on downs, stay on the field so our defense can stay off the field".
Pittsburgh remain firmly in playoff position as Thanksgiving looms but face a daunting stretch over the next three weeks that includes a pair of meeting with first-placed teams in their division - the Denver Broncos (8-2) and Jacksonville Jaguars (7-3), as well as a key clash with fellow AFC wildcard contenders the Houston Texans (4-6).

items.text:
Tajikistan moves to leave ICC amid US push against court
The ICC had found that Tajikistan failed to comply with its request to arrest Russian President Vladimir Putin.
The governing body of the International Criminal Court (ICC) has expressed concern after Tajikistan formally notified the United Nations of its decision to withdraw from the tribunal.
Tajikistan is the fourth country to begin the withdrawal process since the United States urged countries in July to leave the court. It follows Venezuela, Chad and Naoero, the Pacific island nation formerly known as Nauru.
Tajikistan’s withdrawal from the Rome Statute, the treaty that established the court, is due to take effect on November 20, 2027.
The ICC prosecutes individuals for genocide, crimes against humanity, war crimes and the crime of aggression when national courts are unwilling or unable to act. Its 2024 arrest warrants for Israel’s Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu and former Defence Minister Yoav Gallant over alleged war crimes and crimes against humanity in Gaza remain outstanding.
The administration of US President Donald Trump has sanctioned ICC judges and prosecutors as part of its pushback against the warrants for Israeli officials and an earlier investigation into the conduct of US forces in Afghanistan.
In July, the US State Department said it would seek to disable the court’s operations, portraying it as an enforcement arm of a “globalist bureaucracy” and accusing it of threatening US sovereignty.
In March, the ICC found that Tajikistan had failed to comply with its request to arrest Russian President Vladimir Putin during his visit in 2025. Putin is wanted by the court over alleged war crimes in Ukraine.
Burkina Faso, Mali and Niger also announced their intention to leave in 2025, denouncing the court as an instrument of “neocolonial repression”. They formally notified the UN in June, before Washington launched its campaign. Withdrawal from the ICC was part of their joint announcement.
The ICC’s 125 member states still include all seven countries whose withdrawals are pending. The United States, Russia, China, Israel and India are among the nations that are not ICC member states.

items.text:
What failure of COP31 reveals about a divided world
- Published
Some may have found it ironic that the world's biggest conference on climate change should collapse over the very mention of fossil fuels - the main cause of global warming.
Yet that is what happened in Antalya, Turkey, on Sunday.
The failure tells us something about the state of climate diplomacy. But it may tell us even more about the increasingly divided world in which the negotiations take place.
Chris Bowen, the Australian minister who led the negotiations, spoke of a backdrop constituting "the most complicated and fraught geopolitical environment in living memory". The competing demands, he said, had become "unbridgeable red lines".
Murat Kurum, Turkey's environment minister and the summit's president, was blunter. Governments should not disappoint people desperate for climate action, he suggested, by getting "hung up on one word or phrase".
And Kurum had a point. Three years ago, at COP28 in Dubai, there was agreement to transition away from fossil fuels. The proposed Antalya Pact failed to mention them at all.
Was it really worth sacrificing the agreement over two words, then?
The countries that rejected it said the distinction was fundamental. They argued that there was a world of difference between promising to reduce greenhouse gas emissions and committing to move away from the fuels responsible for most of them. Without that explicit commitment, they feared the new agreement would weaken the one made in Dubai.
Normally, it is difficult to establish exactly who has said what at these conferences. Much of the bargaining takes place behind closed doors, and governments are often reluctant to admit which proposals they have opposed.
This time, some of the opposition was public - mostly from oil-producing nations.
Mohammad Ayoub, a Saudi negotiator speaking on behalf of the 22 Arab League countries, argued that Arab nations had contributed less than 2% of historical greenhouse gas emissions. It was wealthy industrialised nations, he said, that bore the overwhelming responsibility for the problem.
He defended the Arab countries' right to choose how to tackle climate change according to their national circumstances.
Russia's delegate Sergei Kononuchenko went further. Cutting oil and gas supplies before demand fell, he warned, would cause shortages, higher prices and energy poverty.
"For that reason, we cannot agree to any formulation on fossil fuel," he said.
The wider political backdrop was still more revealing.
The US, which in previous rounds of talks had helped broker compromises - sometimes working alongside China - had no official delegation in Antalya. President Donald Trump has rejected the entire international climate process.
And while delegates argued over fossil fuels in Turkey, Trump, China's President Xi Jinping and Russia's Vladimir Putin issued a joint declaration in Shenzhen that included a pledge to increase production and supply of refined petroleum products.
The priorities of some of the world's most powerful governments appeared very different from those being discussed in the negotiating rooms.
A majority that may yet offer hope
Yet, perhaps, the picture is more optimistic than it first appears. About 130 governments backed a demand for explicit language on moving away from fossil fuels - roughly two-thirds of the countries represented in Antalya.
Christiana Figueres, who led the UN negotiations that delivered the Paris Agreement, argued that countries were right to walk away rather than endorse a weaker political commitment that might undermine the progress already made.
Looked at this way, the collapse is not evidence that the world has lost its appetite for climate action. Quite the opposite - a substantial majority of governments were demanding more ambitious action.
So why not simply find a way for them to move ahead without waiting for the countries determined to block them?
The difficulty becomes clearer when you look beyond the dispute over fossil fuels.
Kononuchenko had another target in his sights: climate finance. Much of the money wealthy countries provide to poorer nations, he complained, comes as loans rather than grants. He said that developing countries ended up repaying more than they received.
"This is an old colonial distribution of labour under a new banner," he declared.
Then, in a striking moment, he leaned towards the microphone and switched from Russian into English to address his criticism directly to the Europeans: "First of all distinguished representatives of the EU."
Russia has its own reasons for attacking Europe, but the complaint about finance is one that many developing countries share. They argue that they are being asked to pay for damage they did little to cause while receiving too little help to adapt to climate change or build cleaner economies.
The EU had ruled out significant new funding before the negotiations began. Mohamed Adow, the Kenyan campaigner who heads Power Shift Africa, accused Europe of rejecting a flawed deal while refusing to acknowledge its own responsibility for the failure on finance.
So is it possible for a majority of countries to outvote those blocking progress?
The UN climate chief, Simon Stiell, has acknowledged the need to "improve, modernise and reform" the process. Some governments have proposed introducing voting when consensus proves impossible. Others want countries prepared to move faster to make their own agreements outside the formal talks.
But there is a reason the UN climate process depends on consensus. International climate co-operation is largely voluntary.
Voting might produce more ambitious agreements on paper, but would it persuade the governments that had been outvoted to act? Consensus also offers some protection to smaller and poorer nations that might otherwise find themselves overruled by the most powerful countries.

items.text:
Amazon has agreed to acquire a good chunk of Israeli startup Decart.
The e-commerce and cloud giant is paying $7.5 billion for the startup, according to Bloomberg.
Decart has made a name for itself building interactive real-time world models — most recently Oasis 3 — and AI video generation tools. But under the hood, the company stands out for its Decart Optimization Stack (DOS), software that helps AI models to run efficiently on Nvidia, Amazon, and Google’s hardware.
As part of the deal, Amazon will acquire the technology behind DOS, as well as Decart’s founding team and team of AI researchers and engineers, Amazon said in a blog post.
“Every leap forward in AI starts with getting more out of every chip,” said Peter DeSantis, SVP of foundational AI models, custom silicon, quantum computing, at Amazon. “More efficient compute means better training, better reinforcement learning, faster inference, and better models for customers at a lower cost.”
Amazon, which has been so far been using its Trainium chips at its own data centers, is preparing to start selling them to customers as a competitor to Nvidia. Decart’s technology could make it easier for customers to run their workloads on Amazon chips, rather than Nvidia’s, which has been the gold standard so far.
Decart and Amazon did not immediately return requests for comment.
