items.text:
Carlos Alcaraz: Spaniard is 'toughest player to play against' right now with Jannik Sinner out of the equation, says Tim Henman
Carlos Alcaraz will head into the 2027 season as the player to beat with Italian Jannik Sinner currently missing from the ATP Tour due to a knee injury; You can watch the Next Gen ATP Finals from 9-13 December in Reggio Calabria, Italy live on Sky Sports Tennis
Monday 23 November 2026 15:20, UK
Carlos Alcaraz is the "toughest player to play against" right now with Jannik Sinner out of the equation, says Tim Henman.
Alcaraz began the year facing questions over his split with long-time coach Juan Carlos Ferrero, but the Spaniard has answered them emphatically by completing the career Grand Slam and adding the elusive ATP Finals title to his collection.
Since returning at the US Open in late August, the 23-year-old has made up for lost time in a superb late-season charge that culminated in Sunday's triumph in Turin, where he beat top-ranked Alexander Zverev in the final.
- Keep track of the full tennis schedule live on Sky Sports
- Download Sky Sports app for analysis, news and video 📺
- Not got Sky? Latest Sky Sports deals or stream with no contract on NOW📱
By winning the ATP Tour's season-ender, Alcaraz joined Andre Agassi, Roger Federer and Novak Djokovic as the only men to secure the career Grand Slam and ATP Finals title.
With former world No 1 Jannik Sinner set to undergo surgery on a persistent knee injury in Finland this week, casting doubt over his participation in the Australian Open, Alcaraz looks set to dominate tennis in 2027.
Speaking at the ATP Finals in Turin, former British No 1 Henman told Sky Sports Tennis: "We can obviously have a deep dive into the five matches here, but I think in the context of being out of the game for four and a half months, that is not easy then to come back into a Grand Slam.
"He played well in New York, getting through to the quarter-finals, but then we just have to look at this last third of the season.
"For him to not lose a match, play a couple of matches at Laver Cup, and then he's gone on this tear where every aspect of his game has been so impressive. The physical side of things, the wrist has obviously been perfect.
"Yes, he had a challenge with the hamstring, but mentally and technically his game has been so good. In Paris, he didn't have it all his own way, and I think that was such a good sign that he can play and win with this sort of B or C game.
"He's now come into the Tour-ending championships, the best against the best, an event that he's never won, and he's taken the title."
Henman: A completely different level
Four of the Spaniard's six titles this year have come since he returned from injury, with triumphs in Tokyo and Vienna followed by victories at the Paris Masters and the ATP Finals - all under the guidance of head coach Samuel Lopez and brother Alvaro.
"He started the year off with a bang down in Australia, that was the one Grand Slam that he was missing from his CV," Henman said.
"To be able to achieve the career Grand Slam at such a young age was incredible.
"Then obviously on to the clay, getting injured in Barcelona, missing a big chunk, missing two slams at Roland-Garros and Wimbledon, coming back in New York.
"Zverev's got a better serve than Alcaraz, and he hadn't lost his serve. This is the skill set and the challenge of playing Alcaraz, and I think he's in Zverev's head, obviously, because it was just a completely different level.
"Zverev couldn't find the spots, and then his serve has been unbreakable by everyone else in the tournament, and Alcaraz has dismantled him."
Alcaraz is 'the best'
Former doubles No 1 Jamie Murray said: "He [Alcaraz] is amazing. He is the best. He plays in a completely different way to anything that we see these days on the ATP Tour.
"He obviously came back at the US Open, it's not an easy thing to do. I'm sure he was disappointed losing to [Ben] Shelton, the way that he went out there, but it definitely helped him after that for the rest of the year.
"He was up to speed, he had his rhythm. It's not a huge surprise, because he is one of the two best players in the world, and his level is so much better than everybody else when he's in full flow.
"It's an amazing run that he's won these last three tournaments, but it's not out of the realm of possibility for Carlos Alcaraz to do that."

items.title: Emery insists no change of plan for Aston Villa despite fears over Galatasaray surface
items.summary: Unai Emery has insisted he will not alter his plans for Aston Villa’s Champions Leaguegame at Galatasaray on Tuesday night on account of concerns about the state of the pitch. The Turkish champions hastily moved Saturday’s home fixture from Rams Park after starting emergency repairs to the surface t
items.text:
Unai Emery has insisted he will not alter his plans for Aston Villa’s Champions Leaguegame at Galatasaray on Tuesday night on account of concerns about the state of the pitch. The Turkish champions hastily moved Saturday’s home fixture from Rams Park after starting emergency repairs to the surface this month. The Villa defender Ian Maatsen said he and his teammates were aware the pitch was in a “bad condition”.
Villa were informed by Uefa last week that they would be unable to train at the venue the day before the Champions League game in order to give the pitch maximum time to recover after heavy maintenance work. Galatasaray played Saturday’s victory over Samsunspor at Basaksehir Fatih Terim stadium, a significantly smaller ground named after the former Turkey manager, who played for and managed Galatasaray.
Galatasaray’s manager, Okan Buruk, acknowledged the pitch would pose problems despite round-the-clock efforts to improve the hybrid surface, where sand remains present. “We are not expecting a perfect pitch, but we are at least expecting a pitch that will be playable and will not get any worse or deteriorate during the game,” he said.
Villa instead trained at Bodymoor Heath, their Warwickshire base, on Monday before flying to Istanbul. Villa typically choose to train there before flying to games overseas, though they trained at Fenerbahce on the eve of their Europa League visit in January, and at Besiktas Park 24 hours before their Europa League triumph in Istanbul in May.
“If we could have trained in the stadium of Galatasaray, maybe we would have decided for the same situation, but it’s not changing our routine,” Emery said. “How the pitch is going to be tomorrow is important, but it’s not an excuse because it’s [the same] for both teams. Hopefully the pitch will be as best as possible.”
The Villa manager added: “If the pitch was not available or a risk for the players, for some injuries, we are not playing there. I think it’s going to be [good] enough, well enough to play the match. We are thinking only to face them [Galatasaray] and thinking only to play how we are, not changing our idea or our plan for the pitch.”
Victor Osimhen is sidelined for Galatasaray with a knee injury, but the record 26-time Turkish champions expect to welcome back the former Tottenham defender Davinson Sánchez. The former Arsenal midfielder Lucas Torreira and Yunus Akgun, who spent 2023-24 on loan at Leicester, scored in the 2-1 win over Samsunspor, which maintained their three-point lead in the Super Lig.
Buruk was sent off after full-time, after receiving a second yellow card for failing to shake hands with the referee, Ali Sansalan, but his touchline ban does not apply to the Champions League. Galatasaray have appealed to the Turkish Football Federation against the dismissal.
“You can shake hands if you want, or not,” Buruk said. “As long as you don’t show disrespect or use abusive language, no one can punish anyone. The referee made a mistake. I expect that mistake to be reversed.”

items.summary:
Mexican soldiers attacked in wake of drug lord's arrest
- Published
Mexican soldiers have detained eight alleged members of a drug cartel whose leader was arrested on Friday, sparking a wave of violence in northern Sinaloa state.
The Mexican defence ministry said the soldiers were shot by the suspec
items.text:
Mexican soldiers attacked in wake of drug lord's arrest
- Published
Mexican soldiers have detained eight alleged members of a drug cartel whose leader was arrested on Friday, sparking a wave of violence in northern Sinaloa state.
The Mexican defence ministry said the soldiers were shot by the suspects on Sunday while on patrol in the town of Sinaloa de Leyva, trying to re-establish order in the wake of the arrest of Fausto Isidro Meza Flores.
Meza Flores, also known as "Chapo Isidro", was on the FBI's 10 most wanted list and had managed to evade capture for years.
The ministry said the eight had also been involved in the retaliatory violence unleashed by Meza Flores's cartel in the hours after his arrest on Friday.
In a statement published on social media, external, the ministry of defence said that one of the detainees was under age.
It added that its special forces had seized six vehicles as part of their operation, two of which had been fitted with bullet-proof armour and gun turrets.
The US Department of Justice described Friday's arrest of Meza Flores as "a spectacular military operation" and congratulated Mexico's military and special forces on his capture.
It said that the US Homeland Security Task Force had supported the Mexican military and praised the "bilateral effort".
Mexico's defence ministry said its special forces had used stealth and surprise to reach the home of the wanted man.
They also established a security perimeter to prevent Meza Flores from escaping and cartel reinforcements from arriving.
Nevertheless, a bloody firefight ensued, in which four soldiers and 16 "members of organised crime" were killed, according to the latest figure released by the defence minister on Monday.
Along with Meza Flores, his second-in-command, known as "Serafín", and his financial operator, were also arrested and quickly transferred by air to Mexico City.
As news of their arrest spread, members of their cartel erected barricades on major roads and set cars and some shops alight.
There were also reports of shoot-outs between the security forces and cartel members.
Who is 'Chapo Isidro'?
US Assistant Attorney General A Tysen Duva has described Meza Flores as "the most dangerous man in Mexico".
"For decades Meza Flores has promoted the terrorist objectives of the Sinaloa cartel," Duva said, accusing him of "flooding the United States with deadly substances".
The 44-year-old is believed to have started his criminal career with the Juárez cartel decades ago.
He later moved on to become the right-hand man of the leader of the Beltrán Leyva Organisation, a drug gang once allied to the Sinaloa cartel before the two groups split and became bitter enemies.
As early as 2013, the US Treasury identified Meza Flores as the leader of his own drug-trafficking organisation, named after him.
The US Treasury said at the time, that the Meza Flores drug trafficking organisation was responsible for "the distribution of large quantities of methamphetamine, heroin, marijuana, and cocaine to the United States".
It added that the turf war between the Meza Flores cartel and the Sinaloa cartel had "resulted in the quadrupling of drug-war killings" in between 2009 and 2013.
According to think tank Insight Crime, external, Meza Flores himself kept a low profile over the last decade while continuing to run his cartel out of Guasave, in Sinaloa state.
The head of the US Drug Enforcement Administration said that his capture was a "significant blow to a ruthless criminal organisation that has used extreme violence to traffic deadly drugs, including fentanyl, a designated weapon of mass destruction, into American communities".
His arrest, and the co-operation between US and Mexican officials which led to it, will be seen as a win for the government of Mexican President Claudia Sheinbaum.
Sheinbaum has stressed that she is keen to work with the US authorities to capture high-profile target as long as Mexican's sovereignty is respected.

items.summary:
Nvidia's board of directors brings Jensen Huang back as CEO
Nvidia says it is bringing back co-founder Jensen Huang to be its CEO, president and board director. In a statement, the company says the board voted unanimously in favor of reinstating Huang after a series of conversations and meetings, as
items.text:
Nvidia's board of directors brings Jensen Huang back as CEO
Nvidia says it is bringing back co-founder Jensen Huang to be its CEO, president and board director. In a statement, the company says the board voted unanimously in favor of reinstating Huang after a series of conversations and meetings, as well as input from people at "senior levels of the United States government."
"I am honored to return to NVIDIA and lead one of the most consequential technology companies in the world at the beginning of a new industrial revolution," Huang said in the statement. "I take this responsibility with the greatest humility and renewed commitment."
President Trump endorsed the move, calling it the "correct and proper decision." He said Huang's leadership was needed "in order to ensure the Success and Prosperity of not only the Company, but the American Economy."
Nvidia shares jumped sharply on the news Monday morning, as did the broader stock market.
Trump added that the government has "no reason to believe that Jensen's return to NVIDIA poses any risk to National Security," and that Attorney General Todd Blanche says the U.S. "does not possess evidence that he has engaged in any unlawful conduct."
Huang resigned from Nvidia less than two weeks ago, following reports that he had an affair with a woman suspected of being a Chinese spy. The board said as recently as Nov. 17 that it did not intend to reinstate Huang, though Huang publicly said he would return if the board allowed it.
The company's internal investigation into Huang continues, but the board says the turnaround followed a series of meetings with Huang that left them satisfied with his candor and ability to lead the company. Trump said Nvidia should continue looking to its own compliance with U.S. export controls as well.
Huang is expected to testify before congressional committees next week.

items.title: Nepal's new PM eyes closer ties with India amid lingering disputes
items.summary:
Nepal's new PM eyes closer ties with India amid lingering disputes
November 23, 2026
For years, Nepal's relationship with India was shaped by familiar faces, as leaders of the Himalayan country's erstwhile three major parties took turns in the prime minister's office through revolving coalition gove
items.text:
Nepal's new PM eyes closer ties with India amid lingering disputes
November 23, 2026
For years, Nepal's relationship with India was shaped by familiar faces, as leaders of the Himalayan country's erstwhile three major parties took turns in the prime minister's office through revolving coalition governments.
This week's state visit to India by Balendra Shah, a 36-year-old rapper-turned-politician, marked a clear break from that pattern.
As a young, first-time prime minister with a strong electoral mandate , Shah represents a new political force in Kathmandu.
But long-standing economic strain, along with August's devastating flash floods and the Nepalese public's high hopes for more jobs, investment and better governance at home, have made Shah's first bilateral visit abroad more than a mere diplomatic box-ticking exercise.
To safeguard Nepal's flood recovery and development, Shah needs to get off on the right foot with his country's southern neighbor and largest trading partner and its long-standing prime minister, Narendra Modi.
While Nepal and India share an open border, as well as deep cultural and historical ties, their relationship has also been marked by territorial disputes and a desire in Nepal to be seen as an equal by its much larger and more powerful neighbor.
Constantino Xavier, a senior fellow at the Center for Social and Economic Progress in New Delhi, however, cautioned against expecting too much from a single visit.
"We need a big, long-term ambition coupled with small, short-term steps," he told DW, arguing that economic cooperation should remain the central focus of relations because it directly contributes to the socioeconomic development of both countries.
Economic cooperation takes center stage
The young prime minister's test is to turn a strong domestic electoral mandate and political goodwill with New Delhi into tangible economic gain, as well as to address longstanding border disputes and a massive trade imbalance.
Shah's administration sees diplomacy as key to addressing the country's development aspirations, which was reflected in bilateral talks with Modi on Monday.
Economic cooperation featured prominently during the talks as both sides sought engagements in trade, investment, connectivity and infrastructure development.
Kathmandu's priority was securing Indian financial support for reconstruction following the August disaster that claimed the lives of more than 1,450 people, while 5,745 are missing or unaccounted for.
The floods swept away roads, bridges, hydropower projects and settlements, with reconstruction bills estimated at around $4.8 billion (about €4.4 bln)
At a joint press briefing after their talks in New Delhi, Modi announced a package of $1.63 billion to help rebuild flood-hit areas and upgrade other infrastructure projects — around $380 million as a grant, with the rest as a concessional loan.
The South Asian neighbors also agreed to deepen cooperation across a wide range of areas, including trade, investment, connectivity and people-to-people ties, and launched a new long-term vision aimed at strengthening economic integration and development.
The talks also yielded commitments to broaden educational and innovation partnerships, boost energy and infrastructure cooperation, improve market access and trade links, and enhance landlocked Nepal's connectivity through additional air and port access via India.
Bilateral trust and unresolved differences
Shah's visit offered an opportunity to break the ice in a high-level exchange visit and improve a relationship periodically strained by political mistrust, territorial disputes and differing strategic interests.
Nepal and India both have competing territorial claims over Kalapani, Lipulekh and Limpiyadhura, a strategic Himalayan territory in northwestern Nepal.
As mayor of Kathmandu, Shah raised the border disputes with India, which helped boost his nationalist image and set his broader political agenda. However, his India visit steered clear of such contentious issues.
Bimala Rai Paudyal, a former Foreign Minister of Nepal, said Shah avoided tricky bilateral issues to focus on his administration's economic agenda.
"This visit could be a good starting point towards resolving the border issues that have been the key strain in our relations," she told DW. "But the new government didn't show interest or the guts to address this."
Yet, economic pragmatism should not mean indefinitely sidelining political differences.
Ashok Swain, head of the Department of Peace and Conflict Research at Sweden's Uppsala University, said the visit's success should be measured by whether the two countries can establish a predictable and mutually beneficial relationship.
"Nepal's territorial disputes, concerns over the 1950 Treaty of Peace and Friendship and its economic and transit dependence on India need to be addressed," Swain told DW.
"Shah's biggest opportunity is to transform Nepal's geographical location between India and China from a strategic vulnerability into an economic and diplomatic asset," he added, arguing that Nepal should not be forced to choose between its two neighbors.
Whether the visit marks a tangible reset on the economic front will ultimately depend not on the number of agreements announced, but on how they are implemented and whether the two governments are willing to address the disputes that have long strained ties.

The new raise comes within six months of its previous round, which valued the co
items.text:
Enterprise customer experience company Sierra, co-founded by former Salesforce co-CEO Bret Taylor, said on Monday that it has raised $1.75 billion in a Series F round that doubles the company’s valuation to $30 billion. The new raise comes within six months of its previous round, which valued the company at $15 billion.
The new round was led by Greenoaks and Lightspeed Venture Partners, with participation from existing investors who have led previous rounds, including Benchmark, Sequoia, Greenoaks, GV, and Tiger Global.
Enterprise automation is among the few areas where AI has seen rapid adoption. Sierra said that it currently serves almost 50% of Fortune 50 companies, and its clients include BNY, HSBC, Singtel, Wells Fargo, JPMorganChase, Pearson, Next, and Cox Automotive. The company late last month said its outcome-based pricing model has helped it double its run-rate revenue to $400 million within five months.
That said, Sierra is working along similar lines as other customer experience players in the market, which is creating a platform to build agents and partner with model developers to provide choices to enterprises. As personal and work agents interact with enterprise systems, Sierra is also working on creating protocol definitions for agents with companies like Meta, Stripe, and Walmart.
Sierra will use the fresh cash build to its technology stack to layer agents for servicing, and hire more sales folks to sign and maintain enterprise contracts faster than its rivals.
Startups operating in the CX space have seen multi-million-dollar rounds come their way with soaring valuations. Voice AI company ElevenLabs is now valued at $22 billion; Decagon is valued at $4.5 billion; Wonderful is valued at $5 billion; and Parloa is valued at $3 billion. Multiple other startups have scored investments of more than $100 million.
During the HumanX conference in Amsterdam in September, Sierra co-founder Clay Bavor argued that despite the popular belief that AI-powered CX companies are replacing humans in contact centers, a majority of its customers are reassigning roles to existing employees.

items.text:
Nvidia board reinstates Jensen Huang as CEO
Huang stepped down as CEO earlier this month after revelations of at least two affairs, including with a suspected spy.
Jensen Huang is returning to Nvidia as chief executive, a little more than a week after he resigned amid extramarital affairs, including one with an alleged Chinese spy.
On Monday, Nvidia board reinstated Jensen Huang as president, CEO and as a member of the board.
“I am honored to return to NVIDIA and lead one of the most consequential technology companies in the world at the beginning of a new industrial revolution,” said Huang in a statement as the company announced his return.
“I take this responsibility with the greatest humility and renewed commitment. I want to thank the NVIDIA Board for its confidence and deliberation through this process.”
United States President Donald Trump welcomed the decision in a post on social media.
“The NVIDIA Board of Directors has made the correct and proper decision to return Jensen Huang to the position of CEO,” Trump said in a social media post. “The United States Government has no reason to believe that Jensen’s return to NVIDIA poses any risk to National Security,” Trump said.
Wall street responds
Nvidia shares jumped up by nearly 30 percent on the news as US markets opened on Monday.
Analysts also praised the decision with Michael Monaghan, portfolio manager of Founders 100 ETF telling Al Jazeera that it is a “huge positive”.
“Founders like Jensen are irreplaceable. They bring unparalleled vision, execution and grit. Hard to overstate how important this is for America winning the SI race, Nvidia, and innovation in general,” Monaghan said.
“At the end of the day despite this Jensen saga the Board knew it had no choice but to bring him back and for the US technology sector this was the move it had to make,” Dan Ives, senior managing director at Yorkville Ives, said in a note on Monday.
Ives previously said that Nvidia could lose as much as 30 percent of its value without Huang.
More to come soon.

items.title: Nvidia reverses course and brings Jensen Huang back as CEO
items.summary: In a stunning reversal, Nvidia’s board said on Monday that it had reinstated Jensen Huang as the company’s CEO and president, less than two weeks after he resigned following his admission of at least two extramarital affairs, one of which was with a woman whom the U.S. government suspects to be a Ch
items.text:
In a stunning reversal, Nvidia’s board said on Monday that it had reinstated Jensen Huang as the company’s CEO and president, less than two weeks after he resigned following his admission of at least two extramarital affairs, one of which was with a woman whom the U.S. government suspects to be a Chinese spy.
The decision marks an extraordinary comeback for one of the tech industry’s most influential executives, whose abrupt departure raised questions about national security and the future of the world’s most valuable chipmaker. Notably, the U.S. government itself played a role in his return: Nvidia’s board said it consulted senior government officials before determining that Huang posed no national security risk.
Nvidia shares, which had already shot up in premarket trading, opened 30% higher. Nvidia shares were priced at $159.95 a share, up 27%, at 9:51 am ET.
In the days since Huang resigned, President Donald Trump has repeatedly expressed his support for the ousted executive, who is now back at the helm of the AI chip giant. Trump said in a post on Truth Social that the board “made the correct and proper decision to return” Huang to the position, noting that the U.S. government has no reason to believe that Nvidia poses any risk to national security.
Trump also said the U.S. Attorney General confirmed that the U.S. government doesn’t have any evidence that Huang engaged in any illegal activity.
A long list of high-profile tech executives were pushing the board — in social media posts and publicly aired interviews — to bring Huang back, including SpaceX and Tesla CEO Elon Musk, Replit CEO Amjad Masad, Epic Games CEO Tim Sweeney, Atoms founder Travis Kalanick, and Y Combinator CEO Garry Tan — all of whom signed a petition pushing for reinstatement.
The company said the board’s unanimous decision followed a series of discussions and meetings with Huang, after which they were “satisfied with respect to Mr. Huang’s candor and ability to lead Nvidia.”
Just a few days ago, the board had seemed immovable in its choice to push Huang out. During the company’s third-quarter earnings call, Nvidia board chair Harvey C. Jones said they didn’t intend reinstate Huang. Nvidia had even retained executive search firm Heidrick & Struggles to find a permanent replacement.
Jones, along with the rest of the board, now has a different view. In a prepared statement, Jones said the board believes Jensen is the right person to lead Nvidia, and that his reinstatement is in the best interests of our stockholders, employees, partners and customers.
“We have every confidence in Jensen and look forward to working with him as he resumes his leadership of the company,” Jones said. “We are grateful to Colette Kress for her outstanding service as interim CEO, in addition to her continuing responsibilities as Nvidia’s Chief Financial Officer.”
In a statement, Huang said he was honored to return to his role as the head of the company he co-founded in 1993.
“I take this responsibility with the greatest humility and renewed commitment,” Huang said. “I want to thank the Nvidia Board for its confidence and deliberation through this process. I am especially grateful to Harvey Jones for his leadership as Chair, and to Colette Kress and our executive staff for leading Nvidia during this period. I am also deeply thankful to our employees, shareholders, leaders across the industry and partners around the world for their extraordinary support. Above all, I am grateful for the love and support of my family. I can’t wait to get back to work.”
This story is developing...

items.title: PSG had the best attack in Europe but Doué and Kvaratskhelia injuries will test Luis Enrique
items.summary: Luis Enrique is in uncharted territory, even if he insists that “it isn’t a first”. Since arriving at Paris Saint-Germain in 2023, only three players have spent more than 100 days on the sideline – Nuno Mendes, Lucas Hernandez and Presnel Kimpembe – and only Mendes is an important first-team player.
items.text:
Luis Enrique is in uncharted territory, even if he insists that “it isn’t a first”. Since arriving at Paris Saint-Germain in 2023, only three players have spent more than 100 days on the sideline – Nuno Mendes, Lucas Hernandez and Presnel Kimpembe – and only Mendes is an important first-team player. But for the remainder of the season, or at least the vast majority of it, Luis Enrique must do without two of his stars: Désiré Doué and Khvicha Kvaratskhelia.
Doué arrived in Nice on Saturday evening already bearing scars. The PSG forward wore a mouth guard after Davide Frattesi had dislodged one of his front teeth with a stray arm during France’s defeat by Italy during the international break.
He showed it off to the crowd when he tapped home an Achraf Hakimi cross to give PSG a 2-1 lead a mere 24 seconds after Senny Mayulu had levelled the score from the spot for PSG. Just six minutes later, without making any contact with the oncoming Sofiane Diop, Doué was left screaming on the floor, clutching his right knee.
The Nice players Alidu Seidu and Youssouf Ndayishimiye, both of whom have sustained ACL injuries in recent times, quickly grasped the severity of the injury, the nature of which was confirmed on Sunday. Tests revealed an ACL tear that will probably rule Doué out until the end of the season; Kvaratskhelia suffered the same fate last month.
“We have other players in our squad. We will overcome it as a team,” said Luis Enrique, who added that they are “open” to dipping into the market. Eli Junior Kroupi is being linked with a move from Bournemouth to the Parc des Princes, but should the two-time European champions opt against recruiting this winter, it will be a test of the club’s continued assertion that “the star is the collective”. That mantra belies a continued level of spending at PSG that far outstrips their domestic competitors and an accumulation of talent that led Nice’s manager, Olivier Pantaloni, to describe them as a “club apart” in Ligue 1.
Pantaloni noted PSG’s capacity to turn on “at the press of a button”, which left him in no doubt that PSG would “steamroll” the domestic competition once again this year. His side’s 3-2 defeat at their hands, although valiant, reasserts a hierarchy that no one questions, injuries or no injuries.
Ligue 1 may not challenge PSG but, shorn of two of their most technically gifted players, top European sides will. Even in domestic games, wins have oftentimes relied on call-in-the-cavalry hour, with Ousmane Dembélé, Kvaratskhelia, Vitinha and the like unleashed against already exhausted defences to seal the win. Their victories over Le Mans and Strasbourg, notably, were obtained in this manner.
The serious injuries sustained by Doué and Kvaratskhelia mean there is no longer a cavalry to call upon. PSG will also have to change their contentious policy of resting key players in domestic competition. Will Dembélé have to play more, and can his body sustain it? That is one question among many.
Mika Godts has said he has time on his side to establish himself at PSG. Not any more. Will he step up? Will Ferran Torres, who scored PSG’s third in their 3-2 win against Nice, rediscover his early-season form? Is Mayulu, fresh from making his France debut, ready? Is Nuno Mendes a viable option on the left wing? And can Maghnes Akliouche, who has so quickly curried favour with Luis Enrique, add goals and assists to his impressive performances?
The answers to these questions will determine PSG’s ability to challenge for a third consecutive Champions League title. Diminished in quantity and quality, PSG’s forward line no longer looks the best in Europe.
It was the abject failure of the Neymar-Kylian Mbappé-Lionel Messi frontline that forged the concept of the modern-day PSG. Star quality was not a guarantor of success; the system, it was decided, would be king. In the absence of Doué and Kvaratskhelia, the limits of this accepted truth will be tested this season.
 
Talking points
Several French clubs used the international break to correct their course. Lens called time on the failed Yannick Cahuzac experiment and brought in Didier Digard, fresh from his sacking at bottom side Le Havre. Strasbourg pulled the plug on Hugo Oliveira after 10 games and hired Vítor Matos from Swansea City to become their fourth manager of 2026. Valérien Ismaël has replaced Digard at Le Havre. And Lyon, whose hand was forced by Paulo Fonseca’s wish to manage boyhood club Sporting, welcomed Carlos Vicens, formerly part of Pep Guardiola’s backroom staff.
Vicens was the only manager to secure all three points on his debut, winning 1-0 at Davide Ancelotti’s Lille. In doing so, the Spaniard became the first manager in Lyon’s history to arrive mid-season and beat a top-flight side in his first away match. Lens showed promise in their 1-1 draw against Toulouse but were denied three points by an inspired performance from goalkeeper Guillaume Restes. There are no signs of revival at Le Havre, who lost 3-1 to promoted side Troyes – or at Strasbourg, who were beaten 1-0 by Brest at the Meinau. Chelsea’s partner club currently occupy the relegation playoff spot.
Five consecutive wins in Ligue 1 had lifted spirits in Marseille, but Bruno Génésio had warned that the revival teetered on a “knife’s edge”. An excellent Le Mans exposed their fragility. Goals from Amine Gouiri and Igor Paixão gave Marseille a 2-0 lead only for Le Mans to run riot in the final quarter of the game and win 3-2.
Patrick Videira’s side secured all three points thanks to Jean Vercruysse’s dramatic 95th-minute winner. “There is a global phenomenon of fragility as soon as we concede a goal,” was Génésio’s explanation for Marseille’s collapse. For Videira, Marseille represent the biggest scalp of his managerial career, although draws against Nice, Lens, and Monaco had already shown the club’s ability to compete at this level.
This is an article by Get French Football News

items.text:
Nvidia reinstates Jensen Huang as CEO despite China scandal
November 23, 2026
US tech company Nvidia said on Monday that it had resinstated Jensen Huang as its CEO "effective immediately."
This follows just a matter of days after his resignation after admitting to extramarital affairs, reportedly including a dalliance with a woman who was a Chinese intelligence asset.
The board unanimously decided that his return was in the "best interests of the company," Nvidia said, adding that it was satisfied that Huang had demonstrated his "candor and ability to lead."
Trump hails Huang's return
US President Donald Trump rapidly commented on the development online, saying it was the "correct and proper decision" and referring to Huang by his first name as a "Great Patriot and National Treasure."
"The United States Government has no reason to believe that Jensen's return to Nvidia poses any risk to National Security," Trump wrote, adding that the US had no evidence of him engaging in unlawful conduct.
Huang liked to flaunt his personal relationship with Trump. He was reportedly influential in convincing the US president to allow the export of higher-quality Nvidia chips to China that are useful in AI development than other US officials and entrepreneurs endorsed.
Nvidia stock volatility continues, with spike after announcement
The decision was announced as trading started for the new week in New York.
The stock price of what investors deem the world's most valuable company has nosedived amid the scandal, with Nvidia's stock price falling from almost $220 (roughly €200) per share in late October to around $125 per share at the end of last week.
The announcement prompted a rapid early-morning rally on Wall Street, including Nvidia stocks rising back into a region between $160 and $170.

Fury vs Joshua undercard: Martin Bakole steps in for Jai Opetaia to fight former heavyweight world champion Deontay Wilder
Martin Bakole will replace Jai Opetaia and fight Deontay Wilder on the Tyson Fury vs Anthony Joshua undercard at the Principality Stadium in Cardiff on December 11; Bakole lost to Joseph Parker at short notice and has scored outstanding wins over Tony Yoka, Carlos Takam and Jared Anderson
Monday 23 November 2026 14:30, UK
Martin Bakole will fight Deontay Wilder on the undercard of Tyson Fury vs Anthony Joshua on December 11.
Fury and Joshua finally meet after a long-running rivalry in the main event at the Principality Stadium in Cardiff.
Wilder is a former WBC heavyweight world champion renowned as one of the hardest punchers in the sport.
He was due to box Australian cruiserweight star Jai Opetaia, who withdrew injured and will now remain in the 200lb division.

Prior to that Bakole scored outstanding wins over Tony Yoka, Carlos Takam and elite American hope Jared Anderson.
Opetaia's promoter Dana White said: "Jai Opetaia had to withdraw from his fight against Deontay Wilder next month. Stepping in is Martin Bakole, a six-foot-six, 300lb knockout artist who's ready to take on one of the hardest-hitting heavyweights in boxing.
"Wilder and Bakole have 66 wins and 59 knockouts, so you don't want to miss this fight."
Welsh heavyweight Moses Jolly also joins the card in a bout against Igor Adiel Macedo with more bouts still to be announced.

items.summary:

Nvidia on Monday said it was reinstating disgraced tech titan Jensen Huang as its chief executive, effective immediately, marking an extraordinary reversal under pressure from US President Donald Trump. Huang resigned less than two
items.text:
Nvidia board reinstates Huang as CEO, Trump hails 'correct' decision
Nvidia on Monday said it was reinstating disgraced tech titan Jensen Huang as its chief executive, effective immediately, marking an extraordinary reversal under pressure from US President Donald Trump. Huang resigned less than two weeks ago amid revelations of extramarital affairs, including with an alleged Chinese spy. Trump quickly applauded the move, saying it was a "correct and proper decision".
Nvidia on Monday reinstated Jensen Huang as chief executive after input from senior US government officials left its board confident he posed no national security risk, less than two weeks after the co-founder resigned following revelations of his extramarital affairs, including with an alleged Chinese spy.
President Donald Trump welcomed the move as a "correct and proper decision".
Read moreAlice Huang had contact with China spy agency during affair with Nvidia boss, New York Times reports
The board voted unanimously to bring Huang back as president, chief executive and board member, effective immediately, after a series of meetings left directors satisfied with his "candour and ability to lead", the company said in a statement.
Nvidia did not name the government officials it consulted or say what they told the board.
The decision came three days after Trump publicly urged Nvidia to take Huang back, calling him "one of the truly most brilliant minds in the world" and saying he would "love to see Jensen be given a second chance".
Trump described Huang as "a good man" who "made some bad decisions", and said the company should rehire him "if they were smart".
Watch moreXi welcomes Trump: Does Nvidia scandal upend US-China AI race?
Huang had offered to return, but the board initially refused.
Board chair Harvey Jones had said on an earnings call last week that directors had unanimously accepted his resignation and did "not intend to reinstate Jensen as CEO".
"I take this responsibility with the greatest humility and renewed commitment," Huang said, thanking the board, staff, shareholders and his family. "I can't wait to get back to work."
Huang, 63, stepped down on November 12 following reports that he had a relationship with Alice Huang – no relation – a former executive at Singapore-based Megaspeed, a company that bought billions of dollars worth of Nvidia chips.
Read moreAlice Huang had contact with China spy agency during affair with Nvidia boss, New York Times reports
US intelligence services reportedly concluded she passed information to Beijing, which has denied the allegations.
Board chair Harvey Jones said Monday that directors now believe Huang "is the right person to lead Nvidia" and that his return serves the interests of shareholders, employees, partners and customers.
Jones, a former Synopsys chief executive who was named Nvidia's first-ever board chair during the crisis, will stay in the role. Chief financial officer Colette Kress, who served as interim CEO, will continue as CFO.
Nvidia said a committee of independent directors set up earlier this month to investigate whether Huang was targeted by a foreign intelligence effort will see its probe through to the end. Huang supports the investigation and has committed to cooperating, the company said.
Nvidia shares went up almost 30 percent in pre-market trading upon Huang's return.
(FRANCE 24 with Reuters and AFP)

items.text:
Nvidia has reinstated Jensen Huang as its CEO. The company announced on Monday morning that the board “voted unanimously to reinstate Mr. Huang following a series of discussions and meetings with Mr. Huang, after which the Board was satisfied with respect to Mr. Huang’s candor and ability to lead NVIDIA.”
Jensen Huang is back as Nvidia’s CEO
The board voted unanimously to bring back Huang as CEO, President, and Board director.
In its statement, the board says that it received input “from senior levels of the United States government” and determined that “Huang’s reinstatement poses no national security risk.” Donald Trump responded to the board’s decision in a post on Truth Social, saying Nvidia “made the correct and proper decision to return Jensen Huang to the position of CEO… The United States Government has no reason to believe that Jensen’s return to NVIDIA poses any risk to National Security. The Attorney General of the United States has confirmed that the U.S. Government does not possess evidence that he has engaged in any unlawful conduct.”
The board’s statement says that its investigation into reports that Huang was the target of a Chinese spy plot will continue, with Huang’s support and cooperation, while interim CEO Colette Kress will continue as CFO, and Harvey Jones will remain as the recently appointed board chair.
“I am honored to return to NVIDIA and lead one of the most consequential technology companies in the world at the beginning of a new industrial revolution,” Huang said in a statement. “I take this responsibility with the greatest humility and renewed commitment. I want to thank the NVIDIA Board for its confidence and deliberation through this process.” This move comes after Jones said during an earnings call last week that the Nvidia board “does not intend” to return Huang as CEO.
Huang resigned as CEO earlier this month following reports of extramarital affairs with an alleged Chinese spy and two Nvidia employees, including an executive who reported to him. In the wake of his departure, more than 200,000 people, including Tesla CEO Elon Musk, Epic Games CEO Tim Sweeney, Y Combinator CEO Garry Tan, and Uber co-founder Travis Kalanick, signed a letter to Nvidia’s board, calling for his reinstatement.
Nvidia shares tumbled in Huang’s absence, while industry analysts raised concerns about an outsider replacing him at a time when Nvidia is so critical to the AI boom. Nonetheless, the board maintained as recently as last Tuesday that Huang wasn’t coming back.

items.title: Jensen Huang Reinstated as Nvidia CEO
items.summary: NVIDIA (NASDAQ: NVDA) today announced that effective immediately, Jensen Huang has been reinstated as President and Chief Executive Officer and as a member of the Board. The Board of Directors voted unanimously to reinstate Mr. Huang following a series of discussions and meetings with Mr. Huang, aft
items.text:
NVIDIA (NASDAQ: NVDA) today announced that effective immediately, Jensen Huang has been reinstated as President and Chief Executive Officer and as a member of the Board. The Board of Directors voted unanimously to reinstate Mr. Huang following a series of discussions and meetings with Mr. Huang, after which the Board was satisfied with respect to Mr. Huang’s candor and ability to lead NVIDIA. In the process of reaching its decision, the Board received input from senior levels of the United States government, and based on that input, the Board is confident that Mr. Huang’s reinstatement poses no national security risk.
“The Board believes Jensen is the right person to lead NVIDIA, and that his reinstatement is in the best interests of our stockholders, employees, partners and customers,” said Harvey C. Jones, Chair of the Board. “We have every confidence in Jensen and look forward to working with him as he resumes his leadership of the Company. We are grateful to Colette Kress for her outstanding service as interim CEO, in addition to her continuing responsibilities as NVIDIA’s Chief Financial Officer.” Harvey Jones will remain as Board chair.
“I am honored to return to NVIDIA and lead one of the most consequential technology companies in the world at the beginning of a new industrial revolution,” said Jensen Huang. “I take this responsibility with the greatest humility and renewed commitment. I want to thank the NVIDIA Board for its confidence and deliberation through this process. I am especially grateful to Harvey Jones for his leadership as Chair, and to Colette Kress and our executive staff for leading NVIDIA during this period. I am also deeply thankful to our employees, shareholders, leaders across the industry and partners around the world for their extraordinary support. Above all, I am grateful for the love and support of my family. I can’t wait to get back to work.”
As previously announced, in light of recent reporting that Mr. Huang has been the target of a foreign intelligence effort, the Board formed a committee comprised solely of independent directors to investigate, and the committee retained independent counsel to assist it in that investigation. The Board reiterated that the committee’s investigation will proceed to conclusion. Mr. Huang fully supports the investigation and is committed to cooperating with it.
The Board also recently formed a National Security and Export Control Committee comprised solely of independent directors to oversee trade compliance and national security risks. The committee is engaging counsel with experience in national security matters, and such counsel will be retaining advisors with expertise in national security matters. NVIDIA is commencing a search to fill a new position, Chief Compliance Officer, to oversee compliance across NVIDIA and report to the Nominating and Corporate Governance Committee. NVIDIA will continue to cooperate with ongoing government investigations and inquiries.

items.title: Raya injury 'not too serious' says relieved Arteta
items.summary:
David Raya injury: Arsenal goalkeeper avoids surgery and blow is not as bad as first feared, says Mikel Arteta
David Raya came off injured during Arsenal's Premier League draw with Newcastle; the Spaniard is the Gunners' undisputed No 1 goalkeeper with Kepa Arrizabalaga and Illan Meslier as back-up
items.text:
David Raya injury: Arsenal goalkeeper avoids surgery and blow is not as bad as first feared, says Mikel Arteta
David Raya came off injured during Arsenal's Premier League draw with Newcastle; the Spaniard is the Gunners' undisputed No 1 goalkeeper with Kepa Arrizabalaga and Illan Meslier as back-up options; the 31-year-old got injured at a time where Arsenal have some big games coming up
Monday 23 November 2026 14:42, UK
Mikel Arteta has revealed that David Raya's shoulder injury is not as bad as first feared, but is unsure when the Arsenal goalkeeper will return to action.
Raya came off with a shoulder problem in Saturday's 2-2 draw against Newcastle and there were initial fears that the Spaniard could miss several months if he required surgery.
However, an MRI scan over the weekend has revealed that Raya does not require surgery and while he will miss Tuesday's match with Borussia Dortmund, more scans are needed on Tuesday to understand the full extent of the damage.
- Transfer Centre LIVE! | Arsenal news & transfers🔴⚪
- Arsenal fixtures & scores | FREE Arsenal highlights▶️
- Got Sky? Watch Premier League games LIVE on your phone📱
- Not got Sky? Latest Sky Sports deals or stream PL games with no contract📺
"He's not fit for [Dortmund] unfortunately, but it doesn't look too serious," said Arteta.
"We need some more tests tomorrow but it's quite encouraging with the pain he was showing. Immediately the action, we were quite worried but it's not as bad as we expected.
"We expected something much worse because he could almost not handle the amount of pain he had. The first tests we have done showed something much more encouraging. [On Tuesday] we need to ratify that to give you more specifics.
"There was no need for surgery. That was the main fear, because that would have ruled him out for months. Let's see."
Asked if he could return for Arsenal's big Premier League home game with Manchester City on Sunday, live on Sky Sports, Arteta replied: "Tomorrow we will have more tests. Then you will know."
So does Kepa or Meslier play against Dortmund?
Raya's injury means Kepa Arrizabalaga and Illan Meslier will compete for the goalkeeper spot at Arsenal until the Spain international returns from his injury.
Kepa was widely regarded as Arsenal's No 2 goalkeeper and replaced Raya at Newcastle off the bench.
However, Meslier started against Fleetwood Town in the Carabao Cup fourth round defeat - which was the last time Raya was rotated out the Arsenal starting line-up.
"I think it's clear for us who is going to play tomorrow," said Arteta about who starts out of Kepa and Meslier.
When asked why Meslier started against Fleetwood, Arteta replied: "Because I want everybody to be part of it and to feel part of it. You need to play, and Illan has been really good with us.
"We believe that it was the right thing to share those minutes, the competition. To give a player that every single day is so consistent, so reliable, so supportive, with the rest of the boys, to have the feeling that we trust him as well."
Merson on Raya: Arsenal's next five or six games are crucial
Sky Sports' Paul Merson:
"Raya's injury is a leveller for the other teams - not that much of a leveller because Arsenal still have some good players. When Chelsea miss a key player like that, that's it for them. But I don't think that's the case for Arsenal, they've got a very good squad.
"But that goalkeeper saves you points. That will be the problem for Arsenal.
"The next five or six games for Arsenal are decisive for them. If they come out of this run of games and they are five or six points clear of the pack, it's impossible for anybody to catch them. Every one of their next five or six games is a difficult football match.
"For me, Raya will be a miss. You'd be more comfortable going into those games with him in goal.
"He's the best goalkeeper in the world, by far, at making angles. He reads the game by always making the right angles.
"A lot of people don't see it. When the ball goes back to the goalkeeper, he'll always be on the right angle to get the ball - and then will always play it into the right player's foot.
"If Declan Rice comes short, he'll play it onto his right foot so the ball can go smoothly out to the right-back. All these little things help.
"And now it looks like Kepa is going to come in - and he's not played for a long time. And all these things have to work for him. That could be a worry for Arsenal."

items.title: North Macedonia remains stalled on its EU path after 21 years as a candidate while Montenegro and Albania move closer to membership
items.summary:

The European Union's enlargement drive has regained momentum: Montenegro could become the bloc's 28th member in 2028, while Albania is rapidly advancing through accession talks and could complete accession negotiations by the end o
items.text:
North Macedonia watches as EU enlargement moves on
November 23, 2026
The European Union's enlargement drive has regained momentum: Montenegro could become the bloc's 28th member in 2028, while Albania is rapidly advancing through accession talks and could complete accession negotiations by the end of 2027 if it maintains its current pace of reforms.
But North Macedonia, an EU candidate since 2005, remains stalled on the road to accession.
That contrast will be particularly evident at Wednesday's EU-Western Balkans summit in Brussels.
"The Western Balkans' future is in the European Union. Their accession is our priority, our shared ambition and a crucial geopolitical investment in these turbulent times," European Council President Antonio Costa said ahead of the meeting.
Prepared, but the handbrake is still on
North Macedonia formally opened accession talks with the EU in July 2022 but has yet to open the first of the EU's six negotiating clusters, the groups of policy areas through which candidates align their laws and institutions with EU standards.
But the lack of movement does not mean the country is unprepared for membership.
EU Enlargement Commissioner Marta Kos said in November that North Macedonia was "among the countries with the highest level of preparedness" in aligning with EU law and had recently accelerated reforms under the EU Growth Plan.
However, she added, "the handbrake on its accession negotiations is still on."
Kos said that to release this handbrake and open the first cluster, North Macedonia must adopt the constitutional amendment agreed with the EU in 2022.
What's blocking N. Macedonia's EU progress?
The stalemate has deep roots.
For years, a dispute with Greece over the country's name blocked North Macedonia's progress along the EU accession path.
Although the 2018 Prespa Agreement resolved the dispute, and the country changed its constitutional name, clearing the way for NATO membership, a breakthrough on EU accession did not follow.
Bulgaria later blocked the process amid disputes over history, language and identity. A compromise brokered during the French EU presidency in 2022 lifted the veto but made further progress conditional on North Macedonia amending its constitution to explicitly include Bulgarians among the country's recognized communities.
The amendment requires a two-thirds majority in parliament, which has so far proved unattainable.
'Not blocked by a member state'
From the EU's perspective, this is no longer a Bulgarian veto, but a condition North Macedonia accepted as part of its negotiating framework.
"It [North Macedonia] is not blocked by a member state. It is blocked because it doesn't want to date to do what it knows needs to be done," Gert Jan Koopman, the European Commission's director-general for Neighbourhood and Enlargement Negotiations, recently told an Atlantic Council podcast.
North Macedonia's government sees the problem differently.
EU membership remains its declared strategic goal, but Skopje wants guarantees that amending its constitution will not simply pave the way for further demands from Sofia.
Those concerns are rooted partly in long-running disputes over identity and history: Bulgarian governments have challenged North Macedonia's interpretation of a centuries-old distinct Macedonian identity, while some Bulgarian politicians have gone further, describing Macedonian as a regional variant of Bulgarian, and Macedonians and Bulgarians as one people.
President Gordana Siljanovska-Davkova says North Macedonia is ready for talks with Bulgaria and the EU but wants certainty that one constitutional change will not simply be followed by demands for another.
"We only want certainty. We only want this not to be yet another amendment for the sake of an amendment, followed by another one," she said.
Strong support for membership, little appetite for compromise
After more than two decades of waiting, the deadlock has also become a domestic political problem in North Macedonia.
A nationally representative survey by the Institute for Democracy "Societas Civilis" illustrates the contradiction: 71% of respondents support EU membership, but only 24% back the constitutional amendments needed to advance the process. Among ethnic Macedonians, support for the amendments falls to just 11%.
Skopje-based political analyst Petar Arsovski describes the public mood as "passive-aggressive:" Strong support for joining the EU coexists with weak support for making the concession currently required to move forward.
That, he says, helps preserve the status quo.
High domestic political stakes
The dispute is now deeply embedded in domestic politics in both North Macedonia and Bulgaria, where retreat from established positions could easily be portrayed as a national defeat.
The political cost is particularly high in Skopje, where the current government came to power in part on a platform of opposition to constitutional changes under the existing conditions.
For North Macedonia's government, accepting the amendments without further guarantees carries considerable domestic political risks.
The EU, meanwhile, is not offering to reopen the negotiating framework.
The uncertainty is compounded by debate over how future EU enlargement should work. German Chancellor Friedrich Merz and French President Emmanuel Macron have proposed allowing candidates to gradually gain some benefits of membership before formally joining, while stressing that full membership remains the ultimate goal.
According to Arsovski, uncertainty over the future course of enlargement gives ammunition to Eurosceptic narratives and reduces the political incentive for a difficult compromise.
"If these overall conditions remain unchanged, the most likely scenario is that EU summits come and go, while political actors remain dug in, with no real convergence of positions and no genuine commitment to a substantive compromise," Arsovski told DW.

Anti-austerity strike spurs transport chaos across Belgium
National action against planned austerity measures causes widespread disruption, with government’s fate hanging in the balance.
Transport services across Belgium have been disrupted, with hundreds of flights and trains cancelled, as trade un
items.text:
Anti-austerity strike spurs transport chaos across Belgium
National action against planned austerity measures causes widespread disruption, with government’s fate hanging in the balance.
Transport services across Belgium have been disrupted, with hundreds of flights and trains cancelled, as trade unions called a national strike to protest against the federal government’s austerity measures.
Monday’s walkout grounded planes across the country after air traffic controller Skeyes said it was unable to provide regular services at Belgian airports.
In a statement on its website, Brussels airport said that “unfortunately, all departing and arriving flights from 7am to 9pm local time (06:00-20:00 GMT) will have to be cancelled”.
Air traffic was also halted on Monday at Brussels’ Charleroi airport, which is used by low-cost airlines such as Ryanair.
The Board of Airline Representatives in Belgium, which represents about 25 carriers, said the strike would be the 11th affecting Belgian airspace in as many months.
The national strike has also caused disruption to buses, trains, schools, and other public services. Belgium has faced repeated cost-of-living protests and strikes in recent months, with much of the anger directed towards Prime Minister Bart De Wever and his attempts at cost-cutting.
The Belgian government is trying to save 10 billion euros ($10.9bn) in the coming years to reduce the country’s high deficit, but the issue is dividing the ruling coalition and threatens to collapse the government.
De Wever has already offered King Philippe his resignation, but the monarch refused to accept it, giving him more time to find a solution to the budget impasse. The prime minister has now set a new December 31   deadline for his government to reach an agreement on next year’s budget, after another week of talks ended without a result.
“Should we not have a budget agreement [before the end of the year], the government will effectively be unable to govern, thereby bringing its existence to an end”, De Wever’s office said in a statement.
The government is looking at spending cuts, notably in healthcare, and a VAT increase to bring down the deficit, but unions have been pushing for taxes on high earners to offset some of the cuts, as protests against rising living costs continue, not only in Belgium but across Europe.

items.title: India pledges $1.6bn to Nepal in reset of ties

India pledges $1.6bn to Nepal in reset of ties
- Published
Nepal's Prime Minister Balen Shah has repeatedly called for his country to be treated as an equal by its powerful neighbours. His first visit to the Indian capital, Delhi, put that approach to the test, as both sides sought to reset a relati
items.text:
India pledges $1.6bn to Nepal in reset of ties
- Published
Nepal's Prime Minister Balen Shah has repeatedly called for his country to be treated as an equal by its powerful neighbours. His first visit to the Indian capital, Delhi, put that approach to the test, as both sides sought to reset a relationship strained by years of friction.
The contrast between the two leaders was striking.
Shah, 36, wearing his trademark black suit and sunglasses, stood beside Prime Minister Narendra Modi, 76, dressed in white. Shah rose to power after a wave of Gen Z-led protests toppled his predecessor.
Modi, meanwhile, is serving a third term and has recently faced student-led protests in India.
Yet, the two leaders seemed determined to project warmer relations. They exchanged gifts, inspected a military guard of honour and jointly flagged off a new cross-border train service.
For Nepal, the stakes were about far more than repairing diplomatic ties.
The two countries announced a series of agreements covering trade, hydropower, transport and education for Nepali youths.
India, more crucially, unveiled a $1.6bn (£1.22bn) support package as Nepal recovers from devastating floods earlier this year.
The floods killed more than 1,400 people, with thousands still missing. Shah's government has faced criticism over support for families which lost homes and loved ones.
The country faces a huge reconstruction challenge. The government estimates rebuilding could cost as much as $4.8bn. Addressing the UN General Assembly in September, Shah warned that when climate disasters devastate poorer countries, "the answer cannot simply be another mega-loan".
Modi pledged nearly $1.6bn in Indian support. Most of it will come as a line of credit for energy projects, alongside about $400m in grants for reconstruction and infrastructure.
While Nepal would have preferred a larger package, former senior Nepali diplomat Vijay Kant Karna says it is still "a significant amount" and could help stabilise a relationship that has often been uneasy.
A Hindu-majority nation wedged between India and China, Nepal has long had to navigate competing interests from its two giant neighbours. Allegations of political interference and an unresolved border dispute have frequently complicated ties with India.
Nepal's former Prime Minister, KP Sharma Oli, who leads a communist party, was widely viewed as being closer to China. Shah, by contrast, emerged as a political outsider when he was elected earlier this year. The former rapper, then 35, led a party that was only four years old.
His new approach of dealing with India may explain why the border dispute was largely absent from the leaders' public remarks, although the joint statement acknowledged that outstanding issues remained.
According to Govind Pokharel, a former vice-chairman of Nepal's National Planning Commission, Shah's government may have chosen to set contentious issues aside in order to secure progress on more immediate development needs.
"Right now you can go home and convince the young Nepalis that it will be handled later," Pokhrel says, "but if they don't deal with these issues in the future, there will be criticism."
Veteran Indian diplomat Anil Trigunayat says both sides appear to have opted to leave the dispute to established mechanisms rather than engage in what he calls "cartographic aggressions".
There were other gains for Nepal as a result of the Delhi visit.
As a landlocked country heavily dependent on India for trade, Nepal secured access to two additional Indian ports, Kandla and Paradip. The two sides also agreed to improve road and rail connectivity.
The leaders jointly inaugurated a train service linking Ayodhya in India, revered by Hindus as the birthplace of Lord Ram, with Janakpur in Nepal, traditionally regarded as the birthplace of his wife Sita.
There was, however, disappointment on aviation.
Nepal has long sought greater access to Indian airspace in order to attract international traffic to its airports at Bhairahawa and Pokhara.
Some analysts believe the lack of an agreement reflects Indian concerns over Chinese involvement in the two airport projects.
"The airport in Pokhara can pose certain security challenges for India, so it is a more complicated issue to resolve," says Trigunayat.
India did, however, agree to make an existing air route linking Kathmandu, Bhairahawa and Lucknow bidirectional.
"Nepal invested a huge amount of money in those airports," says Pokharel. "It fell short of expectations, but the bidirectional route is a breakthrough."
Shah must now manage relations with China as he seeks to balance the interests of Nepal's two much larger neighbours.
For now he returns home with substantial financial commitments from India as Nepal continues the long task of rebuilding.

items.title: COP31 has failed. The climate system is working as designed
items.summary:
COP31 has failed. The climate system is working as designed
The collapse in Turkiye exposes a diplomacy that protects fossil-fuel power while leaving vulnerable countries to pay the price.
COP31 ended without an overarching agreement on Sunday in Antalya, Turkiye, after nearly 200 countries failed t
items.text:
COP31 has failed. The climate system is working as designed
The collapse in Turkiye exposes a diplomacy that protects fossil-fuel power while leaving vulnerable countries to pay the price.
COP31 ended without an overarching agreement on Sunday in Antalya, Turkiye, after nearly 200 countries failed to agree on a final climate pact. The proposed text could not even name the principal cause of global warming: fossil fuels. The European Union, several Pacific island states and other governments rejected it, while oil-producing countries resisted stronger language. After three decades of annual summits, this was the first such breakdown since 2009.
It is tempting to call this an extraordinary diplomatic failure. But the collapse reveals something more enduring. Climate negotiations have become remarkably effective at keeping governments at the table while avoiding the economic changes that meaningful climate action requires. The system is not designed literally to produce no agreements; it is designed to accommodate interests powerful enough to prevent decisive ones.
Consider what happened in Antalya. The EU objected that the final draft did not even mention fossil fuels. Yet the omission was not a clerical oversight. Earlier language on moving away from oil, gas and coal had been weakened as negotiations proceeded. The summit could not agree on how to implement the agreement reached at COP28 in Dubai in 2023 to transition away from fossil fuels in energy systems. What should have been the starting point for action became the point at which diplomacy broke down.
The contradiction is built into the negotiating process. Under the Paris Agreement, governments determine their own emissions commitments, with no enforcement mechanism to compel a country to stop expanding fossil-fuel production. COP decisions also depend on consensus, giving determined holdouts considerable leverage. The result is an international forum in which the most reluctant participants can limit what everyone else is allowed to say, let alone do.
That does not mean all countries are equally responsible. Nor does it mean that every COP has achieved nothing. The Paris framework helped establish common goals, and climate summits have encouraged investment and cooperation. Antalya itself adopted limited decisions on other matters, including one on a just transition. But these gains cannot substitute for a credible timetable to wind down fossil-fuel extraction. The distinction matters: diplomatic activity is not the same as structural change.
Indeed, fossil-fuel power operates well beyond the conference hall. Producing states defend revenues and geopolitical influence, while consuming states continue to rely on cheap energy and established infrastructure. Even governments that speak forcefully about climate ambition face incentives to protect their own industries and voters from immediate costs. The global energy transition is therefore not simply a technological problem. It is a struggle over who must relinquish assets, profits and power.
This helps explain the appeal of technological promises. The failed Antalya draft promoted carbon-removal technologies to deal with warming beyond 1.5C, while disagreements also centred on carbon capture and storage. Such approaches may have limited roles in reducing or counterbalancing emissions from difficult-to-abate sectors. But when presented as substitutes for reducing extraction, they allow governments and corporations to promise that future machines will repair the damage of continued emissions. The political benefit is immediate; the promised atmospheric benefit remains uncertain.
The same structural inequality shapes climate finance. Countries that contributed least to historical warming face mounting costs from droughts, floods, displacement and adaptation. Yet the proposed $120bn adaptation target disappeared from the revised text and disputes over financial commitments helped sink the talks. Wealthy governments can celebrate climate ambition while leaving poorer countries to borrow, divert public spending or simply absorb losses.
This is precisely why climate finance cannot be treated as discretionary charity. It concerns responsibility for harms produced through an unequal world economy. Grants, predictable funding and meaningful decision-making power for affected countries are not extras to be negotiated after emissions targets. They are conditions of a transition that poorer countries can undertake without sacrificing education, healthcare and basic development.
There is also a danger in allowing the EU to emerge from Antalya as the uncomplicated defender of climate justice. Its refusal to accept a pact silent on fossil fuels was justified. But wealthy countries cannot demand ambitious language abroad while resisting the financial obligations and domestic changes that would give it substance. Conversely, some developing countries depend on fossil-fuel income or need affordable energy. A just phaseout must distinguish their circumstances from those of rich, historically high-emitting economies.
What would a different climate politics look like? It would begin with enforceable plans for ending new fossil-fuel expansion and phasing down production, with richer countries moving first and fastest. It would fund adaptation and loss and damage through reliable, primarily grant-based transfers rather than debt-creating loans. And it would give countries most vulnerable to climate change greater influence over the decisions that determine their futures.
None of this requires abandoning multilateralism. It requires refusing to confuse its survival with success. When consensus rules repeatedly protect the interests most responsible for the crisis, governments must also pursue complementary agreements, domestic regulation and coalitions willing to move faster. Otherwise, the promise of universal participation becomes a mechanism for universal delay.

items.title: Flights and train services cancelled in Belgium due to strike
items.summary:
Flights and train services cancelled in Belgium due to strike
- Published
Hundreds of flights have been cancelled and public transport severely disrupted across Belgium as a result of a strike against planned austerity measures.
All air traffic has been halted at Brussels Airport in Zaventem as well
items.text:
Flights and train services cancelled in Belgium due to strike
- Published
Hundreds of flights have been cancelled and public transport severely disrupted across Belgium as a result of a strike against planned austerity measures.
All air traffic has been halted at Brussels Airport in Zaventem as well as at Charleroi, home to low-cost airlines such as Ryanair.
Underground services have also been halted in capital Brussels, where large numbers of people joined a protest march.
The protest comes as Prime Minister Bart De Wever continues talks with his coalition allies over a budget to cut borrowing costs. King Philippe declined his resignation earlier this month, giving De Wever more time to negotiate.
No flights are taking off or landing at Brussels Airport between 07:00 and 21:00 local time (06:00-20:00 GMT) as a result of the strike by air traffic controllers.
"In total, 404 flights today cannot be operated, which has an impact on more than 50,000 passengers," Brussels Airport spokesperson Jeffrey Franssens said.
Reuters news agency spoke to Florence Faure, a French passenger who had arrived in Brussels from China's capital, Beijing, only to find that her flight to Paris Charles de Gaulle airport had been cancelled.
"Since our luggage was supposed to go on to Paris Charles de Gaulle, we didn't even collect it," she said.
A similar situation has affected Charleroi, where all flights were shown as "scheduled", regardless of the time of departure or arrival.
One passenger told Belgian broadcaster RTBF that she had received no warning and only discovered there were no flights when she arrived at the airport.
Philippe Naime, a teacher, was one of the tens of thousands taking part in the protest march in Brussels.
"Quite simply, no more money is being invested in education, and people are left to fend for themselves. But people do not have the means to do that," he told Reuters.
Public transport, schools and other public services are also facing disruptions.
The Belgian prime minister leads a five-party coalition.
One of its members, the socialist Vooruit, has been refusing to endorse plans agreed by the other four. It wants to raise taxes on the rich and for there to be fewer cuts to pensions and the health sector.
De Wever met King Philippe on Monday for the third update since the impasse.
"While expressing regret over the lack of significant progress, the king encouraged the prime minister to persevere in order to reach an agreement as soon as possible," the royal palace said in a statement.
The leader of one of the country's main unions, FGTB, said the government had alternatives to "dismantling the social protection system".
Bert Engelaar, head of the union, called for "a genuine wealth tax, fair taxation, and the elimination of tax loopholes".
"Political responsibility is not about keeping a government afloat at all costs. It's about knowing when to stop," he added, praising the Vooruit party.
Another union leader, Ann Vermorgen of the CSC, criticised government plans to cut bank holidays when they fall on weekends.
