items.text:
After Japan's APEC snub, what's next for its China ties?
November 23, 2026
Japanese Prime Minister Sanae Takaichi received a cold shoulder from China during the recent Asia-Pacific Economic Cooperation (APEC) summit in the tech hub of Shenzhen.
After Takaichi arrived in Shenzhen on November 18 for the two-day summit, there was an immediate issue when the mobile stairs to the door of her aircraft were some way short of the threshold, requiring her to hold on to the door frame to step down around 40 centimeters (about 15 inches) to the top step.
It may have been completely inadvertent, but upon safely reaching the airport tarmac, her official welcome was decidedly low-key. There were no musical performances, no cheering crowds or traditional dances, which were laid on for many other APEC leaders as they arrived.
Japan's Yomiuri newspaper reported on November 20 that when Takaichi met Chinese leader Xi Jinping at the dinner reception, "his reaction was cold." And while many other regional leaders managed at least a brief one-on-one with Xi on the sidelines of the main event, the Japanese delegation was not granted such access.
Frosty China-Japan ties on full display
"The level of frostiness from the Chinese side was on full display from the moment Takaichi's plane landed," said William Yang, a Taiwan-based analyst for the International Crisis Group.
"I cannot think that the issue with the plane steps was anything other than deliberate and there was a huge contrast between the welcome she received and virtually everyone else," he told DW.
Yang added that the ice didn't break when Takaichi tried to speak to Xi at the dinner reception and the entire occasion "just reflects the state of bilateral relations."
China and Japan share a troubled history, marked by the Japanese invasion of China in the 1930s and the often brutal occupation of cities that were captured and subjugated.
Chinese schoolchildren learn about the horrors of the Nanjing Massacre and the use of chemical and biological weapons by Japanese forces.
Japan maintains that its repeated post-war apologies and massive economic aid that helped China to become the economic powerhouse it is today are overlooked amid the criticism.
Diplomatic relations were normalized in 1972 and Tokyo pursued a policy of engagement over the following decades, although that came to a halt in the mid-2000s, points out David Adebahr, a professor of international relations and Asia-Pacific security policy at Kobe University.
Japan's Taiwan comments open new rift with Beijing
"China's rising military spending, the breakdown of talks over the East China Sea in 2006, and a resurgence of nationalism raised concerns even among Japan's more China-friendly diplomats, while defence analysts noted an increase in Chinese submarine activity near Japanese waters," he told DW.
The nationalism on display during the 2008 Beijing Olympics, coupled with China's more assertive stance over the Senkaku Islands, which Japan has sovereignty over but which Beijing claims, accelerated this shift.
Ties took a sudden nosedive in November 2025 when Takaichi responded to a question in Japan's parliament, the Diet, by saying that any "contingency” involving Taiwan would also inevitably threaten the national security of Japan.
According to Adebahr, the Japanese leader was merely saying out loud what "had long been the internal logic of Japanese security planning." Nevertheless, Beijing has reacted with fury.
China has demanded that Takaichi retract the statement and raised pressure on Japan by restricting exports of rare earth minerals critical to Japanese industry, banning imports of Japanese seafood and telling tourists to take Japan off their destination list.
And while ruffled national feelings have been smoothed in the past with shows of reciprocal goodwill, China is standing firm on its demands this time.
"From Tokyo's perspective, it is clear that Beijing believes it holds more cards than in the past," said Adebahr.
"Today, Beijing has considerable leverage: Japan's dependence on Chinese rare earths; an increasingly visible military presence around Japan, sometimes in conjunction with Russia; and a US administration that has urged Tokyo to de-escalate rather than firmly backing it."
Adebahr added that this left China with little incentive to offer Takaichi a face-saving compromise. However, he pointed out that Beijing's reliance on coercion could backfire by prompting Japan to increase defence spending and seek closer ties with other partners.
Japan's leadership faces the China test
Still, the Japanese leader finds herself in a difficult position, said analyst Yang.
As a committed conservative who has talked tough on Beijing's rapid military buildup, its seizure of islands and atolls in the South China Sea and the inexorable pressure on Taiwan to capitulate and become one with mainland China, Takaichi cannot give in to Xi's demands for fear of losing face with her hardline base.
"This is a major test of her abilities and wisdom as the nation's leader," Yang said. "She is walking a political tightrope between reducing tensions with China but, at the same time, preparing the nation and its allies for a potential contingency over Taiwan."
"I foresee China maintaining its current approach, continuing to step up the pressure by limiting targeted exports and amplifying the assertion with Russia and North Korea that Japan is embracing remilitarization," he said.
Yang added that Japan was likely to seek opportunities to signal goodwill and improve relations "in return for small-scale compromises." However, he said that a reset in the dynamics would depend on how the Trump administration shaped its foreign policy for the remainder of his presidency.
Analyst Adebahr said that while he expects diplomatic relations to remain frosty, there are too many interdependencies for a full decoupling between China and Japan.

items.title: Manchester United to appeal against Leny Yoro red card in defeat by Liverpool
items.summary: Manchester United intend to appeal against the red card Leny Yoro received in the eighth minute of the 4-0 defeat at Liverpool on Sunday. The defender was dismissed after fouling Alexander Isak outside the penalty area but Mauricio Pochettino believes the striker would not have reached the ball to t
items.text:
Manchester United intend to appeal against the red card Leny Yoro received in the eighth minute of the 4-0 defeat at Liverpool on Sunday. The defender was dismissed after fouling Alexander Isak outside the penalty area but Mauricio Pochettino believes the striker would not have reached the ball to take him through on goal against Senne Lammens and therefore it was not worthy of a sending-off.
United’s head coach said: “I don’t agree because the ball wasn’t in Isak’s control. Leny was running with him and when Isak saw the control wasn’t good and the ball was going to the keeper it is normal you delay, you stop running, and you wait to feel the touch and you go down. It is never a foul.”
Dominik Szoboszlai scored from the resulting free-kick to give Liverpool the lead and Florian Wirtz doubled the lead three minutes later. Rio Ngumoha and Victor Muñoz completed the scoring as Pochettino lost his first game in charge of United, leaving them 19th in the Premier League.
“We’re at the lowest we’ve ever been and no one’s coming to save us,” the midfielder Kobbie Mainoo told MUTV. “There’s no helping hands coming so we’ve got to work together and lean on each other and keep working and hopefully it’ll come good.”
Yoro is due to serve a one-match ban at home to Brentford in the Premier League on Saturday. He is available for United’s Champions League match at Sporting on Wednesday.

items.title: Esposito emulates Vieri with Inter hat-trick but De Ketelaere haunts him again
items.summary:
This ought to have been a magic moment for Pio Esposito. He had just scored his first Serie A hat-trick, becoming only the third Italian to get one for Inter in the era of three points for a win. The last to do it was Christian Vieri, back in 2003. Two years before Esposito was born.

items.text:
This ought to have been a magic moment for Pio Esposito. He had just scored his first Serie A hat-trick, becoming only the third Italian to get one for Inter in the era of three points for a win. The last to do it was Christian Vieri, back in 2003. Two years before Esposito was born.
We will come back to that. Esposito has been drawing premature comparisons to Vieri for some time and especially now after a barnstorming November in which he has scored eight times in five games, including three in two for his country, and two of those as part of a man-of-the-match performance during an upset win against France.
He was the nation’s cover star after that win, variously punching the air, roaring or spreading arms open wide across the front pages of Italy’s sports newspapers. His body language on Sunday night was different. By the end of Inter’s 4-4 draw with Atalanta, Esposito carried the haunted look of a Dickensian protagonist who had just been visited by the ghost of Belgium past.
“I’m really struggling to give an explanation right now,” Esposito told the TV cameras when asked how his team had failed to win a game that they led 2-0, 3-1 and finally 4-2 as late as the 76th minute. “It’s a beautiful thing [to score the hat-trick] but I’m having a hard time enjoying it because we threw two points away.”
A sentiment that can only have been heightened by a sense of history repeating. Esposito’s goals against France had put Italy on course for the quarter-finals of the Nations League. All they needed to do was draw their final group game away to Belgium. Esposito struck again to give them an early lead at the King Baudouin Stadium. And then they collapsed to a 4-1 defeat.
These stories share another recurring character: Charles De Ketelaere. He provided the assists on Belgium’s first and third goals, turning that game on its head in the space of 10 minutes. On Sunday, he was at it again, scoring Atalanta’s second and third goals then winning the penalty from which his teammate Franck Kessié finally equalised in second-half stoppage time.
Even by the standards of this barmy Serie A season, on a weekend that gave us two 5-1 scorelines and a 4-0, this was a preposterous game of football. Inter looked completely in control heading into the final 20 minutes, leading 3-1 thanks to Esposito’s hat-trick.
He might have made it to three before half-time if Marco Sportiello had not denied him from point-blank range when the score was still 1-0. Instead, Esposito had to wait until just after the interval to bag his third, running on to a Marcus Thuram through ball and lifting it over the Atalanta keeper.
None of the three goals were spectacular, but together they illustrated what a menace Esposito has become. For the first, he simply held his spot in the middle of the penalty area after an initial cross was half-cleared, punishing Atalanta’s defence for losing its shape on the second ball. His second was a glancing header at a corner.
In moments like this, it is easy to see why people want to make that link to Vieri, another powerful Inter No 9 who could dominate in the air. But, leaving aside the obvious point that we are comparing a 21-year-old with 13 top-flight goals to a player who won both Serie A’s capocannoniere award and the Pichichi trophy for top scorer in La Liga, is that even the most apt former star to draw parallels with?
Vieri has said that anyone who thinks they are similar “doesn’t understand much about football”, noting that Esposito’s 6ft 3in height and broad-shouldered physique remind him more of Luca Toni.
Esposito’s brothers Salvatore and Sebastiano – both also professional footballers – have compared him to another former Inter player, Edin Dzeko, whom he looked up to while working his way through the club’s academy. There are certainly echoes of the Bosnian in the work he does as an attacking pivot, holding off defenders to make space for runners from midfield.
But Esposito will not be a carbon copy of any player who has gone before him. Part of the thrill of seeing him excel for club and country over the last month has been watching him start to define himself as confidence grows. He played 48 times for Inter last season, yet always was the understudy to Thuram and Lautaro Martínez. This campaign already feels different. He is becoming a main character in his own right.
If only his supporting casts could perform to the same level. Eljif Elmas’s first goal back for Atalanta had been fortuitous, the ball coming back to him after a first scuffed shot was blocked by Federico Dimarco. After Esposito’s third goal, there were 20 minutes in which Maurizio Sarri’s team barely fashioned a chance. Inter contrived to give them a way back in.
De Ketelaere’s first goal came out of the blue, a header from a corner. Was Esposito himself at fault for not being closer to the Belgian as he leapt in a failed attempt to intercept the cross? In any case, Inter responded immediately, Petar Sucic scoring from the penalty spot after Davide Zappacosta fell and handled the ball while trying to cut out a cross from Thuram.
That should have been the end of things, but it wasn’t. Atalanta’s English winger Jonathan Rowe was allowed to twinkle-toe along the byline and flick an outside-of-the-boot pass back to an entirely unmarked De Ketelaere, who smashed home from the middle of the box. Then, in the 90th minute, the Belgian headed the ball on to Alessandro Bastoni’s outstretched arm, earning the spot-kick that Kessié converted.
Had De Ketelaere also fouled Bastoni while challenging for the ball? Inter had a stronger claim that Zappacosta ought to have been shown a red card for his handball. It was the Zappacosta’s blocked cross that wound up falling to Rowe before Atalanta’s third goal.
But Inter’s manager, Cristian Chivu, is not one to indulge that sort of self-pity. His focus after the game was all on his own team’s mistakes, noting that none of the goals they conceded had come in transition but always “a dife

items.title: Uganda minister at COP31: 'We need a just transition'
items.summary:
Uganda minister at COP31: 'We need a just transition'
November 23, 2026
Ugandan Environment Minister Beatrice Atim Anywar has come to the UN climate talks in Antalya, Turkey, seeking to secure more funding for her country as it grapples with climate change.
"This is a thing we are living with," she
items.text:
Uganda minister at COP31: 'We need a just transition'
November 23, 2026
Ugandan Environment Minister Beatrice Atim Anywar has come to the UN climate talks in Antalya, Turkey, seeking to secure more funding for her country as it grapples with climate change.
"This is a thing we are living with," she told DW on the sidelines of the COP31 summit, where she's leading the Ugandan delegation. "People are displaced, people are dying of harm, hunger. It has implications on food security and livelihoods."
In recent years, the East African nation has been hit by a series of climate-related disasters, from deadly landslides and floods washing away villages, to droughts damaging harvests and hydroelectricity production.
"When we come to COP and we talk of what the reality is on the ground, we Ugandans have suffered it," Anywar said, referring to the effects of climate change.
"It has an implication for the health of our people, on national budgets," she added.
Climate financing for developing countries to deal with the impacts of a warming planet has become a major sticking point at this year's climate talks. The gathering of some 200 states is seeking to close gaps on how to scale up financing from developed states and whether support should be provided through grants or loans.
Africa contributes less than 4% of the global greenhouse emissions that drive rising temperatures globally, but the continent is among the most vulnerable to climate impacts.
Ramping up electricity production
As it deals with the affects of climate change, including extreme weather, Uganda is also rapidly expanding investment in electricity production from renewables such as hydropower and solar.
In the country of some 53 million people, more than 90% of Ugandan households still rely on wood and charcoal as the most affordable fuel for things like cooking. Biomass accounts for 90% of the country's final energy consumption.
While using wood and charcoal leads to deforestation, Ugandans have little choice. Only around 2% of the country's energy comes from electricity — which is largely derived from hydropower — and less than half of the population has access to electricity.
"Now we are deliberately going into scaling up the production of electricity — hydropower electricity — and making it cheaper for cooking," Anywar said. "We have other alternative energy sources... to mitigate this charcoal use. But the use needs to be phased out in a systematic manner by giving them alternatives."
Drilling for oil
At the same time, the country is seeking to boost economic development by becoming an oil producer. Due to open in 2027, a controversial 1,443-kilometer (897-mile) pipeline is nearly complete. It connects two oil sites in eastern Uganda with a port on the Tanzanian coast.
Environmentalists have criticized the East African Crude Oil Pipeline project, which can transport up to 246,000 barrels per day. Environmentalists say it runs counter to the goal of limiting global temperature rise and could damage fragile ecosystems.
The Climate Accountability Institute said it would release 379 million tons of climate-heating pollution over its 20-year lifetime.
Oil wells for the project, operated by French energy giant TotalEnergies, are also located in Uganda's largest and oldest national park, Murchison Falls.
"That has been also a sticky issue. And actually, that is one of the challenges we are facing at COPs," Anywar said. She stressed that measures have been taken to limit emissions, and that the project was progressing in a "very deliberate way."
The minister also urged developed countries to cut less wealthy nations some slack for using the resources they have to drive much-needed development, saying oil revenues could help fund the transition to cleaner energy.
"You cannot tell us to cut off the umbilical cord that feeds us, as much as it has to be cut off," Anywar said, criticizing the lack of financing from developed countries to deal with climate change. "We are here begging for funds that are not forthcoming."
Anywar added that developing countries "need a just transition," referring to an equitable shift away from fossil fuels that focuses on protecting workers and communities.
Carbon trading 'breakthrough?'
Another way Uganda is looking to finance climate change adaptation is through carbon credits, Anywar said, describing them as a potential "breakthrough."
Carbon credits are tradeable permits representing one ton of carbon dioxide that has been reduced or removed from the atmosphere through initiatives such as forest protection, renewable energy projects or tree planting schemes. Companies or governments can buy them to offset emissions they have not cut themselves.
"Our country is rich with biodiversity. And that is what we are looking forward to — attracting investors into our natural setup so that we earn some finances," Anywar said.
Carbon credits have been promoted as an important source of income for developing countries. But they have also faced criticism, for a lack of transparency and allowing polluting activities to continue.
"We need to have a bankable approach to all interventions. Otherwise… it's not going to work for us," Anywar said, adding that her country also wants to attract investment and build partnerships in smart agriculture and the energy transition.
"If we rely on begging for funds which are not forthcoming, we shall go back empty handed."
This interview also appeared as a video.

items.title: 'I want to destroy capitalism, not France': On the streets with the French ultra left
items.summary:
'I want to destroy capitalism, not France': On the streets with the French ultra left
- Published
France is in turmoil. Crippling public debt, a "lame-duck" president with six months left in office, and massive social unrest - sparked by student protests which have erupted into looting and violence.
items.text:
'I want to destroy capitalism, not France': On the streets with the French ultra left
- Published
France is in turmoil. Crippling public debt, a "lame-duck" president with six months left in office, and massive social unrest - sparked by student protests which have erupted into looting and violence.
This Saturday marked the sixth weekend in a row of demos against soaring prices, worsening public services and alleged police brutality. Violence by protesters is down on last month but still present.
President Emmanuel Macron has publicly blamed riots on "delinquents" and "ultra-left groups" whose aim, he says, is to bring down the French Republic.
That's quite a claim – and one that needs examining.
The unrest in France has become a political football ahead of key presidential and parliamentary elections next year. The left in France blames the centre and right for the cost-of-living crisis that's making French people so upset and angry. They blame the hard left for fomenting violence (which they deny). While the nationalist right pledges, if elected, it will return order and security to France's streets.
So, who exactly are these "ultra-left" groups Macron speaks of? And how organised and dangerous are they?
It's infamously hard to speak to members of the radical left. They don't much like what they call mainstream media. We're viewed as part of an establishment many of them despise.
My best bet was to head out into the protests and try to approach people dressed in all black and ski masks or balaclavas (worn, they say, to hide their identity from police). It's a quasi-uniform associated with left-wing rioters or disruptors, known as the Black Block.
You see them at demos all over Europe. In France, they tend to appear from city side streets, as daytime protests are dying down, dusk is falling and riot police begin to emerge in full force.
French intelligence drastically underestimated the outpouring of anger, looting and destruction following protests last month. More than 1,000 police officers were reportedly injured, young protesters had bones broken and two reportedly lost a hand in altercations with police armed with stun grenades. Le Monde newspaper has an article, external it is constantly updating to investigate a rising number of reports of protester injuries. The French Insurers Federation estimates damages to shops and private property on 17 October alone - the day of the biggest riots - came to around €207m (£175.5m).
Since then, the French authorities are trying to tightly manage demos. Police presence is heavy. Protesters say heavy handed.
Towards the end of one of the protests this month, we saw would-be rioters vastly outnumbered, glass bottles and homemade paint bombs at the ready to throw at police. They were no match for the batons, stun grenades and tear gas the officers had to hand.
As we were being forcefully kettled in by police, I tried to talk to would-be rioters. Few wanted to engage but I then met 18-year-old Nas (not his real name) and friends. They would only speak to me if they could hide their identity. This was to avoid police detection, they said.
Milling, you could say provocatively, by baton-at-the-ready police – they seemed to fit a radical-left rioter stereotype.
"How can you justify the violence?" I ask them.
"Without violence, you don't achieve anything," one of them tells me. "It's the only way to get our voices heard."
"We come from an area with a bad reputation. Our schools are a mess. Our teachers quit. You need qualifications to get a decent job. There is supposed to be equality in France. We won't give up our fight."
These young men, we discover, come from the sprawling housing estates common on French city outskirts - the banlieues - associated with deprivation, unrest and second or third generation immigrant families.
They weren't politicised or organised by the radical left, they insisted. Just angry.
Earlier, I had spotted two hard-left student activists, standing masked on top of a bus shelter, above the thronging crowd of protesters waving banners sporting the red anarchist sign and the symbol for the Antifa (anti-fascist) movement.
I put it to them that France has a proud tradition and respect for the right to protest but that the country has been horrified by the violence it's seen over the last weeks.
They were keen to downplay the rioting but - again – would only speak if they could remain anonymous.
"Violence ends up reflecting badly on our movements. We don't like it. But what's a smashed shop window compared to police using stun guns on protesting school kids? Also, people [in France] are regularly going cold and hungry. They're losing faith in this society."
How could they believe violence would bring about a juster society, I wondered?
They shrug off my question. In France, these days, the real violence is state violence, they say.
French intelligence estimates there are 5,000 "ultra-left" activists in the country.
Anticapitalist Starflix (that's his codename) counts himself as one of them. The 17-year-old is also a member of the violent Black Block movement. We'd arranged to meet on the edge of the protest, by a narrow canal.
Fearful about being apprehended by police, he asked to remain anonymous.
He showed me a couple of homemade paint-bombs - eggshells filled with paint and sealed with medical tape that he throws at police officers. He carries them in his rucksack, wrapped in a royal blue Italia football shirt.
"We throw the paint bombs at the visors on riot police helmets, so they have to lift them up in order to see and that makes them suffer their own tear gas that they've sprayed at us," he tells me.
"We pick up stones and rocks too. Anything we find on the streets of Paris, to throw."
I put it to him that he and others in the Black Block are causing a lot of problems on French streets: damaging businesses, hurting police officers, destroying the demos for peaceful protesters. What is he trying to achieve?

items.text:
Iran says it will use ‘all available means’ to counter US blockade
Ministry of Foreign Affairs says Iran will use all tools to confront the naval siege and defend itself.
Iran says it will use all means at its disposal to counter a United States naval blockade imposed during the nine-month US-Israel war on Iran.
The US blockade was imposed on April 13, lifted in June after Washington reached a draft understanding with Tehran, then restored on July 14 after the agreement collapsed.
“We will certainly not tolerate these actions and will use all available means to counter US aggression,” Iranian Ministry of Foreign Affairs spokesman Esmaeil Baghaei said at a news briefing on Monday.
“You should bear in mind that what the Americans have described as economic sanctions, an economic blockade and a naval blockade undoubtedly constitute an act of military aggression against Iran,” Baghaei said.
“Under these circumstances, Iran is entitled, pursuant to Article 51 of the UN Charter, to use any means at its disposal to defend itself.”
The war broke out on February 28 when the US and Israel carried out air strikes that killed Iranian Supreme Leader Ali Khamenei and other senior officials.
The conflict has since expanded after Iran launched missile and drone attacks across the region and with armed groups it backs in Lebanon, Yemen and Iraq also entering the fray.
The Strait of Hormuz has become the focus of the conflict with Iran continuing in its efforts to block the waterway, which is vital for oil and natural gas shipments.
In an attempt to force Iran to halt efforts to block the strait, the US imposed a blockade on Iranian ports and later announced a series of economic sanctions and launched a task force to disrupt land routes into Iran.
Iranian forces have made multiple announcements in recent weeks that ships have caught fire while trying to use routes that Tehran considers off-limits.
TankerTrackers.com said last week that a tanker was loading Iranian crude oil in the Gulf via ship-to-ship transfer and could become the first vessel to successfully export the country’s crude since the US reimposed the blockade in July.
Baghaei said on Monday that reports about Iranian ships loading oil are “speculation”.
Visible Iranian crude exports decreased to near zero in recent months due to the blockade.
Al Jazeera’s Resul Serdar Atas, reporting from Tehran, said the US blockade is hurting Iran economically.
“Iranians are aware of that and they are publicly admitting it because more than 80 percent of the country’s imports and exports happen through the Strait of Hormuz or southern ports of the country,” he said.
“Iranians are now looking increasingly for options to put an end to the US naval blockade,” our correspondent said, adding that military action against US military assets around Iran is being discussed.
“Escalation is now the main option on the table,” he said.
Diplomatic efforts to resolve the war remain stalled, especially since the collapse of a June agreement that laid out a path to a permanent settlement.
Iran has said Hormuz could be open within two days if Washington meets its conditions, including halting hostilities, lifting the blockade and waiving sanctions.
“If the American side fulfils its commitments, security can be restored to the Strait of Hormuz and the region in the shortest possible time,” Baghaei said.

items.text:
A reset for climate diplomacy?
November 23, 2026
The longest-running climate talks in history came to a disappointing conclusion on Sunday as negotiators failed to come to an agreement on a shared political direction on climate change.
After two days of extended talks, representatives from country after country, tiredness etched into each face, voiced their opposition to the so-called "Antalya Pact".
"I understand that there is no agreement on this text. For that reason, these decisions have not been adopted," said Murat Kurum, Turkish president of the COP31 climate summit.
'Fossil fuels' as one of main sticking points
One of the main sticking points: the words "fossil fuels". While some nations, including petrostates like Saudi Arabia and Russia, wanted them omitted from the text, others saw it as a "step backwards" not to include them.
Around 130 parties — including the vulnerable island nations, and other developing countries, richer states like the EU — called for the reintroduction of the two words into the text to no avail. And so many refused to support the adoption of the final COP agreement.
While it signals a failure for the UN process, that so many countries were willing to walk away from what they saw as a weak text was, arguably, a show of strength and one that had been long coming.
Three years after appearing in the closing decision of COP28 in Dubai with the promise of "transitioning away from fossil fuels in energy systems, in just, orderly and equitable manner", the words "fossil fuels" have been omitted from every decision since.
More extreme weather as climate change accelerates
But this year is different. This climate summit was the first to acknowledge that the world will breach the critical 1.5-degree Celsius (2.7-degree Fahrenheit) threshold that scientists said would avoid the worst impacts of planetary heating.
And so, the pressure was on for progress; to turn pledges from previous years into concrete action. But that progress didn't come.
"We don't celebrate the deep divisions exposed or the lack of a political signal from COP31 capable of driving climate action in line with science, equity, and the law," said Nikki Reisch, director of the climate and energy program at the Center for International Environmental Law, reiterating the value of multilateral space.
"But the rejected text would have done more harm than good," she added.
The lack of agreement was not just purely about "fossil fuels" but also about money.
Financing climate action in the Global South
Developing nations have long argued that they need additional financing, both as a means for them to move away from coal, oil and gas, but also to help them cope with the consequences of rising temperatures.
Countries all over the world are being battered by extreme weather events and catastrophes like flooding, drought, and wildfires fueled and worsened by rising global temperatures. Some of the worst hit are poorer countries that have contributed the least greenhouse gas emissions causing the problem.
And yet, richer states behind much of the historical emissions are increasingly unwilling to foot the bill. Dissatisfaction at home due to higher food and fuel prices has left many governments loathe to pay more to finance climate action abroad.
With the United States — the world's biggest historical emitter — now absent from negotiations and on the verge of leaving the United Nation's Framework Convention on Climate Change, the European Union was portrayed as this year's villain with some observers highlighting the EU's "hypocrisy."
"You can't demand action and then block the finance that makes this possible," Fanny Petitbon, policy analyst at 350.org, said in a statement.
As the world's largest provider of climate finance, the EU reportedly refused to negotiate on providing additional finance and has repeatedly called for other nations to step up.
Moving forward on climate action beyond climate summits
The failure to find an agreement is a particularly bitter turn of events for countries that face ever worsening impacts of climate change, like the island states that are being confronted by a reality that could see their countries wiped off the map as sea levels rise.
But things are not all bad.
Although the Turkey-led electrification agenda calling for an increase in global electricity consumption to 35% by 2035 was not formally adopted as it made up part of the rejected final agreement, more than 90 countries pledged to move forward regardless.
It's not a silver bullet. There was no agreement on ensuring the increase was forged only through clean, renewable energy. But it would still signal forward momentum — momentum that is also being driven by economic forces and a need for home-grown energy security.
And there are other hopes. The second conference on the Just Transition Away from Fossil Fuels will take place in Tuvalu in July 2027. Initiated at the COP30 conference last year in Belem, Brazil, it has seen increasing support from countries putting together concrete roadmaps for abandoning coal, oil and gas.
Who's responsible?
There has been much talk of blame and who is responsible for the breakdown and collapse of talks. What is clear is that the UN climate summits need reform. Progress, when it does happen, is slow. While currently based on consensus, with all countries having to agree on every measure, there have been many calls for majority-rule decision making. That could force the inclusion of language like "fossil fuels" into the text.
But ultimately, this is not the time to focus on fault. As the climate crisis accelerates, governments need to reflect — and quickly — on what can be done outside of these UN processes, within their nations, to speed up climate action.
"The take-home message from COP31 is clear: the world must do much more to confront the climate crisis — and it must do it now," said UN Secretary-General Antonio Guterres in a statement.

items.summary: NAIROBI, Kenya Nov 23 – Former Makueni Governor Kivutha Kibwana has clarified his remarks on the proposed meeting between Nairobi Senator Edwin Sifuna and New York City Mayor Zohran Mamdani, saying his comments were about Embakasi East MP Babu Owino and not a suggestion that Sifuna should meet the A
items.text:
NAIROBI, Kenya Nov 23 – Former Makueni Governor Kivutha Kibwana has clarified his remarks on the proposed meeting between Nairobi Senator Edwin Sifuna and New York City Mayor Zohran Mamdani, saying his comments were about Embakasi East MP Babu Owino and not a suggestion that Sifuna should meet the American mayor.
In a post on X, Kibwana said his earlier tweet had been misunderstood, insisting that he was referring to the possibility of Babu, a youthful Nairobi political leader, meeting Mamdani, who is of a similar age and serves as New York City mayor.
“My tweet was about Babu Owino, a Nairobi city chief meeting an agemate Mayor Zohran Mamdani of New York. It wasn’t a comment about whom you should meet,” Kibwana said.
Mamdani, who won the New York City mayoral election in November 2025, has attracted international attention for his youthful leadership and progressive political agenda.
He directly addressed Sifuna, expressing confidence in his leadership and warning him against allowing disagreements among supporters to distract him from his political objectives.
“Omwami Edwin Sifuna, we have faith in you. Don’t allow some supporters to detract you. We must keep our eyes on the ball,” he added.
The clarification comes amid debate over Sifuna’s ongoing US tour and suggestions that he should have sought an opportunity to meet Mamdani, who recently made history as New York City’s first Muslim and South Asian mayor.
Sifuna has maintained that his American visit is primarily intended to engage Kenyans living in the diaspora rather than pursue meetings with foreign political leaders.
Speaking during an engagement with Kenyans in Pennsylvania, Sifuna said he would meet Mamdani during a future visit to the United States for the United Nations General Assembly when he scales to presidency.
He explained that his immediate priority was connecting with Kenyans abroad, whom he considers an important constituency in the country’s political landscape.
Sifuna is currently undertaking a two-week tour of the United States, which began on November 21 and is expected to end on December 7, with engagements planned across New Jersey, Pennsylvania, Maryland, Washington DC, Texas, Washington State and California.
The tour features town hall meetings, church services, business forums, fundraising dinners and engagements with Kenyan professionals and community groups living in the US. He is accompanied by Vihiga Senator Godfrey Osotsi and former Meru Governor Kawira Mwangaza, among other members of his delegation.
Sifuna began the tour in New Jersey, where he opened the Linda Mwananchi Movement’s office in Hackettstown before proceeding to Pennsylvania for a church service and a town hall meeting with Kenyans in Allentown on November 22. His itinerary subsequently takes him to Maryland and Washington DC for meetings with business leaders, diaspora groups, women and youth organisations.
He is also scheduled to hold engagements in Dallas and Houston, Texas, before travelling to Washington State, where he will attend church services, a gala dinner and town hall meetings. The final leg of the tour will take him to California, with engagements in San Francisco, Oakland and Silicon Valley before the visit concludes on December 7.
The visit is aimed at popularising the Linda Mwananchi Movement, strengthening its diaspora networks and mobilising financial and political support ahead of the 2027 General Election. It also provides Sifuna with an opportunity to engage Kenyans abroad on governance, the economy and the challenges they face while living outside the country.

Good morning. You're reading the Up First newsletter. Subscribe here to get it delivered to your inbox, and listen to the Up First podcast for all the news you need to start your day.
Today's top stories
Vote counts are concluding for the 2026 midterm elections, revealing a better picture of just how much Democrats dominated. Fifty-six percent of voters chose the Democrats in House races compared to 42% for Republicans. The 14-point gap is the largest margin won by Democrats in 50 years. The party has officially won the largest majority in Congress since the early 1990s. Take a look at NPR's breakdown of the U.S. House races, by the numbers.
Artificial intelligence is causing significant swings in the stock market as investors speculate about the future of the technology boom. While AI stocks have driven markets to record highs and bolstered the economy, concerns are growing about a potential bubble. Investors anticipated that AI giant Anthropic's stock market debut last week would lift markets, but instead Wall Street experienced one of its worst weeks in recent times.
- 🎧 The National Association for Business Economics released a survey asking firms about their AI experiences. NPR's Scott Horsley tells Up First that one in five reported measurable, widespread productivity gains, while about half said they saw some gains, but they weren't widespread. About 30% were either not using AI or felt it was too soon to assess its impact. Austan Goolsbee, head of the Federal Reserve Bank of Chicago, pointed out that the significant investment in AI is already affecting the economy, contributing to inflation by increasing demand for construction materials and electronic components. Although proponents believe AI could eventually help lower costs and limit inflation, Goolsbee tells Horsley that the Federal Reserve must address inflation challenges right now.
Poland has called an emergency NATO session for today after Russia fired three cruise missiles into its territory. The incident highlights the stakes for European countries in Russia's war on Ukraine, prompting nations along NATO's eastern border to seek enhanced air defense support. Poland plans to present proposals to increase surveillance capabilities and deploy more F-35s to intercept incoming missiles and drones.
- 🎧 Anti-missile systems and NATO flights were activated successfully, but Polish authorities say that poor weather prevented them from intercepting the incoming Russian missiles, according to reporter Teri Schultz. No injuries or damage were reported. More than a year ago, NATO established the Eastern Sentry to enhance air defense after a significant drone swarm from Russia entered Poland. Experts are now scrutinizing potential gaps in this defense. If this attack was deliberate by Moscow, Russia is risking severe consequences by endangering the lives of people on the ground in a NATO country, Schultz says.
Delegates at COP31 in Antalya, Turkey, couldn't agree on a plan over the weekend to address fossil fuels, the main cause of climate change. The event ran two days longer than expected, making it the longest in the history of these summits. Nearly 200 nations failed to finalize targets for electrification and financial aid for developing countries, or to address the impacts of climate change. The European Union rejected any conclusion that didn't advocate for a transition away from fossil fuels, while oil-producing countries like Saudi Arabia opposed this position. Fossil fuels contribute about 73% of global emissions.
- 🎧 Ultimately, the EU decided that no COP deal was better than a deal that didn't address fossil fuels, NPR's Rachel Waldholz says. She adds that money was another major issue. Developing nations sought increased support to tackle climate change, noting that they've contributed very little to climate change but often deal with the worst impacts. Wealthy nations agreed to provide funding under the Paris Climate Agreement. The U.S. was absent from the discussions due to the Trump administration's withdrawal from international climate negotiations. Many smaller and developing nations are strong defenders of these talks, viewing them as a vital platform to ensure their voices are heard alongside larger countries, Waldholz says.

This year's edition of Books We Love is dedicated to Rose Friedman, who edited a dozen editions and worked at NPR for 15 years before her death this year at age 38. Friedman was one of the original founders of Books We Love, formerly known as The Book Concierge. In her honor, start exploring and find something wonderful to read today.

items.text:
Watford set to appoint former Romania boss Iordanescu
- Published
Watford are set to appoint Edward Iordanescu as their new manager.
BBC Three Counties Radio report the Romanian is due to become the Hornets' sixth manager inside 18 months after they sacked head coach Alessio Dionisi following Saturday's 4-0 defeat at Sheffield United in his 18th game in charge.
The 48-year-old is understood to be arriving in the UK on Tuesday to sign his contract and plans to bring three members of staff with him and hopes to be in the dugout for Wednesday's Championship fixture at home to Blackburn Rovers (19:45 GMT).
Iordanescu guided Romania at Euro 2024 where they topped their group ahead of Belgium with all four sides ending level on four points from three games before a 3-0 defeat against the Netherlands in the Round of 16.
Iordanescu - whose father Anghel had three spells in charge of the Romanian national team, leading them in two World Cups and two European Championships - left his last role at Polish club Legia Warsaw in October 2025.
It was the 48-year-old's ninth club over a 15-year coaching career which has taken in Bulgarian club CSKA Sofia as well as Steaua Bucharest and Cluj among others in his homeland.
Dionisi, who departed with the Hornets in 21st, four points above the relegation zone, was only appointed in June after the departure of Ed Still, who himself lasted only three months at Vicarage Road.
Still, Javi Gracia and Paulo Pezzolano were all also given full-time contracts after Tom Cleverley left in May 2025.
The 46-year-old Italian was Watford's 12th head coach, not including interim bosses, since the end of the 2020-21 season, and leaves the Hornets searching for a 25th since the Pozzo family took over the club in 2012.
The club have had 57 permanent managers in their 145-year history.

items.summary:
How the US, China and Russia are competing for Africa’s mineral wealth
The US, China and Russia are vying for Africa’s mineral wealth, raising questions about who stands to benefit
From cobalt mines in the Democratic Republic of the Congo (DRC) to lithium deposits in Mali and uranium reserves in Nig
items.text:
How the US, China and Russia are competing for Africa’s mineral wealth
The US, China and Russia are vying for Africa’s mineral wealth, raising questions about who stands to benefit
From cobalt mines in the Democratic Republic of the Congo (DRC) to lithium deposits in Mali and uranium reserves in Niger, Africa’s mineral wealth is becoming an increasingly important arena of competition between the United States, China and Russia.
China dominates several critical mineral supply chains, while Russia has expanded its influence through security partnerships, particularly in the Sahel. The US, meanwhile, is seeking to secure access to strategic resources through diplomacy, investment and infrastructure projects.
The rivalry extends beyond mining to ports, railways and trade routes connecting Africa’s resources to global markets.
But as foreign powers compete for access, what do African countries stand to gain?
Why are global powers interested in Africa’s minerals?
Africa holds substantial deposits of cobalt, lithium, copper and uranium, resources vital to industries ranging from electric vehicles and renewable energy to advanced technology and defence.
For Washington, securing critical minerals has become a strategic priority amid concerns about dependence on China.
In February, President Donald Trump announced Project Vault, a $12bn initiative to establish a strategic mineral stockpile for US industries.
China has spent years investing in African mining, processing and infrastructure.
Trade between China and Africa reached a record $348bn last year, according to Chinese customs statistics, cementing Beijing’s position as the continent’s largest trading partner.
Russia’s economic footprint is considerably smaller. Moscow has instead relied heavily on military cooperation and security partnerships to expand its influence, particularly in countries that have distanced themselves from Western governments.
Its Africa Corps, established in 2023 under the Russian Ministry of Defence, has taken over much of the Wagner Group’s former operations on the continent.
Gold has also become strategically important to Moscow. A 2024 RAND Europe study commissioned by the United Kingdom’s Foreign Office identified the precious metal as a major feature of Russia’s engagement in Africa.
Why is the DRC central to the competition?
The DRC is the world’s largest producer of mined cobalt, accounting for an estimated 73 percent of global production in 2025, according to the US Geological Survey.
China has established a powerful position in the country’s mining industry, with Chinese companies owning or holding stakes in several major copper and cobalt operations.
Beijing also dominates global cobalt refining, giving it considerable influence over supply chains even when minerals are extracted elsewhere.
Washington is seeking to challenge that position.
Last December, the US and DRC signed a strategic partnership agreement aimed at expanding US access to critical minerals and supporting investment in infrastructure and processing.
Under the agreement, Kinshasa is to identify strategic mining assets and exploration areas, giving American and eligible partner investors rights of first offer on designated projects.
But securing agreements is different from developing mines and processing facilities.
This month, DRC Economy Minister Daniel Mukoko Samba urged Washington to translate the partnership into tangible investments, saying its success should be measured by completed projects rather than signed agreements.
Kinshasa wants investment to support domestic mineral processing, electricity access and economic development, rather than simply increasing raw material exports.
Why are transport corridors part of the rivalry?
Control over mineral supply chains depends not only on mines but also on the infrastructure needed to move resources to international markets.
China has made infrastructure investment central to its engagement with Africa through the Belt and Road Initiative, under which dozens of African countries have signed cooperation agreements.
The US, alongside European and African partners, is backing the Lobito Corridor, a transport network linking Angola’s Atlantic coast to the copper and cobalt-producing regions of the DRC, with a planned railway extension into Zambia.
The corridor is intended to provide a more efficient route for mineral exports while strengthening regional trade.
For Washington, it also offers an opportunity to diversify supply chains and reduce dependence on Chinese-dominated networks.
For African countries, the project could lower transport costs and attract investment. But its wider benefits will depend on whether it also supports local industries and communities.
Why is the Sahel another focus?
Mali and Niger possess significant deposits of lithium, gold and uranium, but political upheaval and armed group activity have complicated foreign investment.
Following military coups and deteriorating relations with Western governments, both countries strengthened security ties with Moscow, as did neighbouring Burkina Faso.
Russia deployed Africa Corps personnel across the region, consolidating its position as a security partner to military-led governments.
Washington is now seeking to rebuild relations.
In February, senior US State Department official Nick Checker visited Mali, signalling a desire to reset ties and reaffirming Washington’s respect for the country’s sovereignty.
The diplomatic outreach comes as foreign companies pursue opportunities in the region’s mining sector.
Mali produced an estimated 9,400 tonnes of lithium last year, according to the US Geological Survey, making it one of Africa’s leading producers.
Chinese interests are involved in the Goulamina lithium mine, while a subsidiary of Russia’s state nuclear corporation Rosatom secured an exploration licence for the Bougoula lithium project two years ago.

He said he was shaving last week when the wat
items.text:
Presidential villa suffers water and power cuts, Nigerian leader says
- Published
Nigeria's President Bola Tinubu says the presidential villa suffers from cuts in electricity and water - issues that are all too common for the country's ordinary citizens.
He said he was shaving last week when the water supply cut at the villa, known as Aso Rock, in Abuja.
He is seeking re-election next January and vowed to address these issues.
Tinubu made the disclosure on Sunday at a special prayer session organised in his honour by members of his family in Lagos.
He explained: "On the Wednesday of last week, I was shaving, and the water went off. In the villa, you won't know punishment dey dia too [there’s punishment there too in Nigerian pidgin].
"The water went off. So we will correct all this. No light, no water, no electricity, no development. We have just started. We can do it, and we will do it for Nigeria,” he said.
Aso Villa serves as both the office and official residence of the Nigerian president. It is situated at the base of Aso Rock in Abuja.
- Can Nigeria's president regain voters' trust after painful first term? 
  - Published12 November
- Search and rescue teams race against time after Nigeria boat tragedy 
  - Published41 minutes ago
Nigeria has long endured electricity shortages, but recent severe disruptions have been caused primarily by insufficient gas supplies and declining hydropower output, rather than the usual nationwide grid collapse.
Persistent blackouts in Lagos, Abuja and elsewhere have forced distribution companies to implement rotating power cuts, severely impacting households and businesses.
The country also suffers from chronic water shortages, the result of a structural crisis rooted in the gap between rapid urban population growth and decaying, inadequate public water infrastructure, leaving millions without reliable supplies, especially in Lagos.
Tinubu made a high-profile electricity promise during the 2023 election campaign, but the exact wording and how binding it is has become a major point of contention ahead of the election on 16 January 2027.
In 2022, months before the last presidential election, Tinubu said: "Whichever way, by all means necessary, you will have electricity, and you will not pay for estimated bills any more. A promise made will be a promise kept.
"If I don't keep the promise and I come for a second term, don't vote for me, unless I give you adequate reasons why I couldn't deliver,” he said.
Despite the continuing power cuts, some of his supporters point to improved electricity supplies in rural areas as well as a recently approved $2bn (£1.5bn) investment in a new East–West Super Grid, designed to expand electricity transmission capacity and strengthen the national grid, as evidence that he is doing his best to keep to his promise.
Tinubu defeated the country’s former Vice-President Atiku Abubakar as well as former Anambra state governor Peter Obi in 2023 and the three are seen as the strongest contenders once again.

items.title: Man Utd to appeal Yoro red card
items.summary:
Manchester United to appeal Leny Yoro's red card as ex-PL referee Dermot Gallagehr casts his verdict
Manchester United lost 4-0 to Liverpool in the Premier League on Sunday, with Leny Yoro sent off inside the first eight minutes for denying a clear goalscoring opportunity; the club have informed the
items.text:
Manchester United to appeal Leny Yoro's red card as ex-PL referee Dermot Gallagehr casts his verdict
Manchester United lost 4-0 to Liverpool in the Premier League on Sunday, with Leny Yoro sent off inside the first eight minutes for denying a clear goalscoring opportunity; the club have informed the FA of their plans to appeal decision; Dermot Gallagher agreed with the onfield decision
Monday 23 November 2026 12:51, UK
Manchester United have notified the FA of their intention to appeal Leny Yoro's red card against Liverpool.
Mauricio Pochettino's side lost 4-0 at Anfield in the Argentine's first game in charge, and his plans went up in smoke as Yoro was dismissed inside the first eight minutes for bundling over Alexander Isak as the striker ran through on goal.
There was some debate as to whether the foul was a clear denial of the goalscoring opportunity, as it was unclear whether Isak was in control of the ball as he made his way towards the penalty area.
Under the laws of the game, one of the considerations regarding a red card for Denying of an Obvious Goalscoring Opportunity (DOGS), is the likelihood of the attacking player "keeping or gaining control of the ball".
United boss Pochettino felt that not only did Isak lose control of the ball with his touch, but also that United should have been given a penalty for Jeremy Jacquet's challenge on Bryan Mbeumo at the opposite end just moments before.
However, former Premier League referee Dermot Gallagher backed the onfield decision in both instances.
- Transfer Centre LIVE! | Man Utd news & transfers🔴
- Man Utd fixtures & scores | FREE Man Utd highlights▶️
- Got Sky? Watch Premier League games LIVE on your phone📱
- No Sky? Latest Sky Sports deals or stream with no contract📺
"If you look at it from the referee's angle, is it a foul? That's the first step. Yes. Is he in possession of the ball? From that angle, yes.
"I think most people would have expected a red card. It would have been a surprise during the game if a red card hadn't been given.
"I don't know if he would have got to the ball before Lammens. You watch it play out. Do you think it's a red card? Gary Neville's immediate reaction was red card."
On Mbeumo's penalty appeal: "When players are side by side, you can do that. They are side by side. Jacquet was even in front of him."
Pochettino: 'The ball was for the goalkeeper'
Pochettino speaking on Yoro's red card:
"The ball was for the goalkeeper. In that situation, if you review the VAR you can see for sure, [Yoro] never had the intention to connect with Isak.
"When the control was long with the striker, the ball was going to the goalkeeper, he runs and goes down. In Leny's case, it wasn't intentional.
"If you look before, on the sixth minute. Jacquet on Mbeumo. Similar? No. If you compare the actions, that was a penalty."
'No chance' - Mainoo fumes at penalty decision
Manchester United midfielder Kobbie Mainoo on the red card:
"The game's been taken out of our hands by a red card that I don't think can be a red card," he said.
"No chance. The ball's already with the goalkeeper. They're both running full speed. What can we do? It is what it is.
"It's 10 vs 11, you come to a place like Anfield, it's a tough game anyway. Then you lose a man, it makes it hard. I can't fault the boys for their fight in the game. We take the pain and move on.
"I wouldn't say it all goes out the window. You can still take the things you did in training into the game, but it makes it 10 times harder with one less man in a situation like that."
Keane: Isak isn't getting to the ball
Sky Sports' Roy Keane speaking at half-time:
"Isak's not getting the ball. There's no way he's getting the ball.
"It's clumsy from United. Obviously it's one straight ball over the top. You shouldn't be in so much trouble.
"But there's no way he's getting that ball. Absolutely not. I know Isak is quick and he's sharp, but we've looked at it again.
"It's really poor defending. Players not smelling danger. But Isak is not getting that ball. Absolutely not."

items.summary:
England: Lewis Moody says he 'felt ready to play' after former captain joined England to face New Zealand's Haka
Former England captain Lewis Moody joined England to receive the Haka ahead of their 37-12 victory over the All Blacks on Saturday; Moody fronted England's arrow-head formation for the pr
items.text:
England: Lewis Moody says he 'felt ready to play' after former captain joined England to face New Zealand's Haka
Former England captain Lewis Moody joined England to receive the Haka ahead of their 37-12 victory over the All Blacks on Saturday; Moody fronted England's arrow-head formation for the pre-match tradition
Monday 23 November 2026 12:58, UK
Lewis Moody says he "felt ready to play" after he joined England to receive New Zealand's Haka, ahead of Maro Itoje's side's 37-12 victory over the All Blacks on Saturday.
Emotional scenes unfolded at Allianz Stadium, as Moody, who was diagnosed with motor neurone disease (MND) in 2025, walked arm-in-arm with Itoje onto the field.
New Zealand's players clapped as the former England captain took up position at the front of England's arrow-head formation - between Itoje and Ellis Genge - to accept the challenge of the Haka.
- Itoje: Moody gave England 'lift' facing Haka
- England produce complete performance to beat All Blacks
- Nations Championship: Schedule, results for rugby's inaugural tournament
Moody, who won 71 international caps during his career, had presented England's players with their matchday shirts at their Pennyhill Park base on Friday, and revealed Ollie Chessum had jokingly urged him to stay on the pitch and chase down the first kick.
"I honestly felt ready to play," Moody told BBC Breakfast.
"When the lads were hugging me after the Haka, I was like: 'Right, I'm ready to go'."
"The night before, Ollie Chessum told me where they were going for the first kick-off.
"He was like: 'Mate, if you're up for it, you can chase it!'
"I was almost ready to take him up on that."
In support of Moody's Front Up to Motor Neurone Disease campaign, England's players wore boots as well as special warm-up and arrival kit with the campaign's logo printed on them.
The players also signed warm-up tops and match shirts, which were donated to the My Name'5 Doddie Foundation, a charity founded by the late Scotland international Doddie Weir that provides funds for MND research.
"I was really aware that this was something that I would never get to feel again and hadn't felt for over 15 years," Moody said.
"So, I wanted to try and fully take in the moment.
"When I got out there, Maro [Itoje] brought me out there and positioned me.
"Ellis [Genge] embraced me, the bundle of physical energy that he is. That's inspiring in itself, to feel the power that's emanating through his body.
"The noise was almost overwhelming. And then [I tried] to recentre myself and focus on the Haka, through the peripheral vision of the England team that fanned out in front of me.
"It just brought a huge smile, and brought back a lot of wonderful memories of playing with all my former team-mates."
He added: "It was really unique and I feel humbled to have been a part of it."
Front Up to MND are organising a series of coastal walk fundraisers on June 12 2027 to raise money for the My Name'5 Doddie Foundation.
"To have the response that it did and to have the support that it has is only good for the cause that I was there for, which is the Front Up campaign supporting My Name'5 Doddie Foundation, to raise as much money as possible, to have a serious impact on this disease," Moody said.
"We need more drugs that have a significant impact for patients. They are the breakthroughs that we're looking for and this campaign will get us near, if not over the line with that.
"But we need thousands, if not tens of thousands, hundreds of thousands of people to support and get involved.
"And hopefully, if you're a little bit inspired or if you just loved watching the game at the weekend, and everything that represented, and you fancied taking on a challenge, come and join us on June 12, walking the coast."
Atkinson: It was special to be a part of
Asked whether Moody's presence motivated England, Seb Atkinson told Sky Sports News:
"Definitely, he came into the hotel last night and gave us some reflections on his career and some reflections on his diagnosis.
"It was really special to be a part of that. I think the lads really took it on board.
"Then to hear the noise of him coming out and taking part in our response to the Haka was really special.
"Also to see his family and his sons and speak to himself [Moody] in the changing rooms after, it just topped it off."

items.text:
Luke Littler: World No 1 faces nightmare route at World Championship with Luke Humphries a potential semi-final opponent
Luke Littler could face a nightmare draw at Alexandra Palace with a potential semi-final showdown against Luke Humphries; you can watch the World Darts Championship live on Sky Sports from December 11
Monday 23 November 2026 12:44, UK
World No 1 Luke Littler faces a potential nightmare route to World Championship glory with Gary Anderson, Michael van Gerwen, and Luke Humphries all in line to face him.
Littler crashed out of the Grand Slam of Darts after a shock last-16 defeat to Jermaine Wattimena in Wolverhampton last week.
His exit follows quarter-final losses at the World Series of Darts Finals and the European Championship and a first-round defeat at the World Grand Prix.
- Darts in 2026: Key dates, calendar, results 📅
- Got Sky? Watch on the Sky Sports app 📱
- Not got Sky? Get instant access with NOW 📺
Littler is now not due to play until the opening night of the World Championship on December 11, having failed to qualify for the Players Championships Finals in Minehead at the weekend.
'The Nuke' is projected to be the top seed for the 2027 PDC World Darts Championship, putting him on a potential semi-final collision course with Luke Humphries while keeping him apart from Gian van Veen and Grand Slam winner Gerwyn Price until the final.
Before that, the 19-year-old from Warrington could face a tricky third-round showdown against former semi-finalist Dave Chisnall, with two-time champion Gary Anderson a potential fourth-round opponent.
They famously met in the semi-finals of the Grand Slam in 2024, which Littler memorably won in a deciding leg thriller.
If Littler gets through that, he is likely to face three-time winner Michael van Gerwen or two-time semi-finalist, Nathan Aspinall.
Then it could be a repeat of the 2024 final against Humphries for a spot in the January 3 showpiece where Van Veen or Price may await.
Price, who took home the £200,000 jackpot in Wolverhampton, has overtaken Littler with the most ranking money earned this season and means he is provisionally up to world No 3, with Littler still No 1, Van Veen at No 2, and Humphries down to No 4 - potentially shaking up the draw heading to Alexandra Palace in December.
In the 128-player bracket at the Worlds, all players enter in the opening round.
The top 32 players on the Order of Merit are seeded and cannot meet until the third round. Assuming all higher-ranked seeds win their matches, Littler's projected opponents by round is as follows:
- Round 1 - Unseeded international or ProTour qualifier (ranks 65-128)
- Round 2 - Unseeded Order of Merit or ProTour qualifier (ranks 33-64)
- Round 3 - Dave Chisnall (World No 32)
- Last 16 - Gary Anderson (World No 16) or Luke Woodhouse (World No 17)
- Quarter-finals - Michael van Gerwen (World No 8) or Nathan Aspinall (World No 9)
- Semi-finals - Luke Humphries (World No 4) or Jonny Clayton (World No 5)
- Final - Gian van Veen (World No 2) or Gerwyn Price (World No 3)
Commentator Dan Dawson says Price's victory over Van Veen to claim his fourth Grand Slam title has "done him a favour".
He explained on Sky Sports: "Price has had to battle to win this Grand Slam more than he has in any other since his first, because we've seen him play unbelievable stuff to win Grand Slam titles.
"But I think that's what he's had to do to become a winner again, and seeing him smile and seeing that pressure lift, just hearing him talk, I think that is an enormous sign because he's already looking ahead. What can I win next?
"We know that at Ally Pally he is up into No 3 in the world, with Humphries and Littler on the same side of the draw provisionally.
"That game there between Gian and Price, that would provisionally be the semi-final in the other half of the draw.
"So that has done him a favour if he is looking to become a world champion again."

NAIROBI, Kenya, Nov 23 – The National Authority for the Campaign Against Alcohol and Drug Abuse (NACADA) has arrested two suspects following a multi-agency operation that uncovered a suspected counterfeit alcohol production and distribution hub in Ngong, Kajiado County.

items.text:
NAIROBI, Kenya, Nov 23 – The National Authority for the Campaign Against Alcohol and Drug Abuse (NACADA) has arrested two suspects following a multi-agency operation that uncovered a suspected counterfeit alcohol production and distribution hub in Ngong, Kajiado County.
The intelligence-led operation was conducted in the Kiserian area of Kajiado West Sub-County, targeting premises and a homestead linked to the suspected manufacture and sale of illicit alcohol.
According to NACADA, officers recovered 15 boxes containing assorted suspected counterfeit alcoholic drinks.
Other items seized included a roll of Kenya Revenue Authority (KRA) stamps, assorted empty bottles, rolls of stickers bearing different alcohol brand labels, 20 litres of liquid suspected to be ethanol and a distillation drum.
The two suspects were arrested and taken to Kibiko Police Station as investigations into the suspected counterfeiting operation continue.
NACADA said the recovered materials were documented as part of the ongoing investigations to establish the extent of the alleged production and distribution network.
NACADA Chief Executive Officer Dr Anthony Omerikwa thanked members of the community for providing information that helped security agencies conduct the operation.
“We are deeply grateful to the community for being at the forefront in volunteering information to the Authority. You are the key stakeholders in the fight against alcohol and drug abuse, and we commend you for the good work,” Omerikwa said.
He emphasised the importance of community vigilance and timely information sharing in disrupting illicit alcohol networks and protecting residents from potentially harmful products.
The Authority said investigations were ongoing, with the multi-agency team pursuing additional leads linked to the suspected operation.
NACADA urged members of the public to continue reporting suspicious activities associated with illicit alcohol production, distribution and drug abuse.
It reiterated that sustained cooperation between residents, security agencies, local administrators and other stakeholders remains critical in the fight against alcohol and drug abuse.

items.title: Jamal Musiala controversy the nadir of Bayern Munich’s turbulent week
items.summary: It was, on paper, a perfect Friday evening for Bayern to flex their muscles once again, in the chill of their intimidating Allianz Arena against struggling opponents who had won just twice all season in the league.
