items.text:
It was, on paper, a perfect Friday evening for Bayern to flex their muscles once again, in the chill of their intimidating Allianz Arena against struggling opponents who had won just twice all season in the league. In the end, though, the best news of the night was that Saïd El Mala, the star of the visitors, Köln, who had scored a jaw-dropping consolation goal at the same stadium in spring, fluffed a far easier chance in the closing stages that would have condemned the champions to defeat.
The word crisis is rampantly overused in sport, but this was the weekend Bayern’s injury troubles reached critical mass. With Luis Díaz, Serge Gnabry and Ismaël Saibari already missing, their talisman Harry Kane had his game curtailed after 20 minutes and by the time the second half had begun, they’d lost Michael Olise too.
Olise inspired perhaps the greatest trepidation, leaving the stadium on crutches, though it looked worse than it was. The Frenchman could even be available for the midweek trip to Lille in the Champions League, though, given the current shortages in the front part of the squad especially, it feels like he might be better off being kept at home with his valuable feet up. Losing Kane, however, will have to be coped with. He has already had an operation to fix torn ankle ligaments. The England captain is not expected back for three months. “We now have seven games [until the winter break] with the squad we have,” said Bayern’s sporting director, Max Eberl, acknowledging that the loss of Kane was “a huge blow for all of us”. He hinted that Bayern will be ready to compensate for those losses in the transfer window.
Yet remarkably none of these – the sporting slip-up nor the growing injury headaches – were the headline. Just as this should have been a procession for Bayern, this should have been a happy return for Jamal Musiala, back as a substitute after more than two months out. Yet a cloud had hung over the No 10 since a very public discussion was begun by – of course – Uli Hoeness about reviewing the player’s lucrative contract, running until 2030 at a reported €25m (£20.9m) annually, should his injury and illness issues prevent him returning to his best form.
Karl-Heinz Rummenigge added fuel to the fire at full-time by actually backing his longtime colleague Hoeness, calling the latter’s words “perfectly understandable”. Rummenigge continued, referring to Musiala’s neurological condition – managed with medication – which caused him to collapse in successive pre-season games in August. “You have to talk to the family, to the player, and especially to the agency, because these sums [Musiala’s wages] are – with all due respect – no longer justifiable.”
The mushrooming situation forced Fifpro to step in on Saturday afternoon, with the union stating they were “deeply concerned by the repeated public statements from FC Bayern’s leadership”. underlining the club’s duty to look after a player attempting to recover his best, rather than applying publicly pressure to him amid negotiations with Musiala’s representatives which have gone on since summer, according to Süddeutsche Zeitung. “Making Musiala’s health and future a matter of public debate adds to that pressure,” the statement continued. “Any concerns about his contract should be raised privately with him and his representatives.”
Hoeness and Rummenigge can be expected to speak their minds, two giants of the club’s history no longer in key decision-making positions but with names and voices still able to make waves in public. Arguably the real issue was the CEO, Jan-Christian Dreesen, who had fallen short in defusing the situation in midweek. He initially talked about not putting Musiala under pressure. “He needs time to come back. He has to get that time.” Yet Dreesen finished his comments by adding “and then we’ll see how things look at the beginning of next year,” again (unhelpfully) applying a time frame. For somebody at the head of a global giant to frame his point so clumsily is damaging.
This is the crux of the matter. Bayern’s public treatment of Musiala, as if he were somehow to blame for being injured (which has covered the bulk of his unavailability) and ill and continuing to get paid, is chipping away at their image as a superclub apart, more family-focused and in touch with their roots than their European peers. That has been felt among the fanbase which, in keeping with German supporter power, always makes clear any issues with the club’s hierarchy. One supporter, the neurologist Jonatan Hoffmann, took the stage at Saturday’s club AGM to chide the club for their handling of the situation, emphasising Musiala needed support to widespread applause.
Yet beyond the fans, there are more than ripples. Maik Franz, the vice-president of the German players’ union (VDV) called Bayern’s dealing with the situation “shabby and unprofessional” in a column for Kicker, while former Bayern stars including Lothar Matthäus and Steffen Effenberg were scathing of their old club in the media over the weekend. Effenberg told Sport 1’s Doppelpass on Sunday that the behaviour of the Bayern big wigs had been “catastrophic”.
All of this will be enormously frustrating for Vincent Kompany, the man who should have been the week’s story but ended up as a footnote. He was appearing on the touchline for the first time since his frightening collapse during an under-23s training session at the club’s Säbener Strasse headquarters. When Kompany appeared before the media for the first time since his hospitalisation on Thursday, he appeared with his left arm in a sling having landed on and dislocated his shoulder, which required surgery, when he fell.
Kompany thanked a packed press conference for their concern, and swiftly announced he was fine and there was nothing more to talk about. Typical Kompany; adroit, aware, and draining all the drama out of the situation. Much of the success in recent seasons has been built on the calm that Kompany has brought to Baye

items.title: Merson on Chelsea: My biggest worry is Liverpool knew Alonso wasn't good enough
items.summary:
Paul Merson believes Liverpool knew Xabi Alonso wasn't good enough - and we're seeing it play out as Chelsea manager
Chelsea have suffered back-to-back defeats in the Premier League and are slipping towards the middle of the table; the Blues have won just once in five games in all competitions; watc
items.text:
Paul Merson believes Liverpool knew Xabi Alonso wasn't good enough - and we're seeing it play out as Chelsea manager
Chelsea have suffered back-to-back defeats in the Premier League and are slipping towards the middle of the table; the Blues have won just once in five games in all competitions; watch Nottingham Forest vs Chelsea live on Sky Sports this Friday, kick-off 8pm
Monday 23 November 2026 12:10, UK
In his latest Sky Sports column, Paul Merson has raised doubts about whether Xabi Alonso is good enough as Chelsea manager - after another disappointing defeat in the Premier League.
The Blues were beaten 4-1 by arch-rivals Leeds at Stamford Bridge on Saturday, with the Blues now on a run of just one win in their last five matches in all competitions.
Chelsea have now slipped down to eighth place - and sit five points behind the top four. They do sit two points behind fifth, but Brentford could go ahead of the Blues if they win on Monday Night Football against Everton.
- Transfer Centre LIVE! | Chelsea news & transfers🔵
- Chelsea fixtures & scores | FREE Chelsea highlights▶️
- Got Sky? Watch Premier League games LIVE on your phone📱
- Not got Sky? Latest Sky Sports deals or stream PL games with no contract📺
Merson believes Liverpool may have snubbed Alonso for the head coach role - eventually taken by Andoni Iraola - due to concerns about his pedigree.
There was no vacancy at Liverpool by the time Alonso took the Chelsea role on May 17, with Liverpool not sacking Arne Slot until June 1.
Read below for the Magic Man's thoughts...
'Did Liverpool see something that we're seeing now?'
My biggest worry is that Liverpool could have had Xabi Alonso and they chose not to. Obviously, Liverpool didn't think he was good enough.
Alonso took the Chelsea job and Liverpool sacked Arne Slot two weeks later. You can't tell me that Liverpool couldn't have spoken to Alonso and say: 'Don't take the Chelsea job, we're going to take you'.
He was out of a job as well, Liverpool could have had him and he'd have gone there all day long. So why didn't they take him? Did they know something that we're seeing now?
It just always sits in my mind. That was my worry - and now it's playing out.
If this was Liam Rosenior in charge at Chelsea and getting these results, he'd be in major trouble. One hundred percent, he'd be in trouble. And remember, Rosenior didn't have Morgan Rogers in his Chelsea team, bought for £116m.
But it's because of the unbelievable job he did at Bayer Leverkusen that everybody is thinking: it will be alright.
'Chelsea's defending is mind-blowing'
Tottenham and Leeds at home are Chelsea's two biggest games of the season for the fans - and they've lost them both. But while they're big for the fans, I'm not sure the players think that way. Not at all.
They probably think their biggest games are Arsenal, Manchester United and Manchester City.
The Leeds game changed when Moises Caicedo came off. For all the money they've spent… take Caicedo and Joao Pedro out of that team and Chelsea aren't good enough. They're the two players you cannot afford to miss.
They're not dominating football matches. The other major problem is defending. The goals they give away, the way it happens - it's mind-blowing. It's poor defending. Inexperienced defending.
The first goal against Leeds, Josh Acheampong gets stuck under the ball. I know he's a young kid but he still can't make that mistake. Then the ball gets to Noah Okafor, and Levi Colwill just jockeys to the side of him. He has to do something to stop that shot happening. He just dangles his leg out.
It's not be-all-and-end-all defending. You look at players like Dan Burn and Lewis Dunk for Newcastle and Brighton. They would dive in front of the ball and let the ball be smashed against them.
Sol Campbell, Tony Adams, Rio Ferdinand and Nemanja Vidic all had that mentality. Their job was to make sure you didn't score - and if you did, you'd have to produce something special to beat them. I just don't see that with Chelsea's defenders. It all seems far too easy.
We're talking about two Chelsea centre-halves, who are meant to be top drawer. One of them is an England international, and a future England captain not long ago in Levi Colwill. And then Wesley Fofana cost Chelsea £70m at a time when £70m was a lot of money.
Maxence Lacroix hasn't pulled up trees at Chelsea either. When he went off injured, it wasn't as if everyone had their head in their hands like if Caicedo or Pedro went off like that.
'I can't see Chelsea beating Forest'
I expected Chelsea to get in the Champions League this season. Get in that competition and it's a great season. They're a million miles off winning the league.
The problem is there are a lot of teams above them. But now I don't see them beating Nottingham Forest on Friday, after what Forest did to Manchester City a few weeks ago.
That's a huge, huge, huge game at the City Ground. Every game you play for Chelsea is big, but if they win it - then I'd expect them to beat Crystal Palace after all and it's all looking rosy again.
They need Joao Pedro back. We go on about their front three. But if you had The Three Musketeers but took one of them out, you'd struggle to sell a film.

items.text:
Inside the talks between student protest leaders and Macron’s government
Al Jazeera interviews two French student leaders who have met with top government officials as protests continue.
Paris, France – High school student Marius Mensil has participated in several meetings with top officials, including President Emmanuel Macron, Prime Minister Sebastien Lecornu, and Education Minister Edouard Geffray, aimed at addressing the concerns of thousands of protesting students.
“They’re very good at listening to us. They welcome us, smile at us, tell us, ‘Yes, you’re right, your demands are legitimate’, and in the end, they do nothing,” the 17-year-old told co-leader of the French high-school students’ union, Union Syndicale Lyceenne (USL), told Al Jazeera.
Held in government offices in Paris, the meetings have, on occasion, lasted as long as two hours, he said.
“With Geffray, it was mainly an exchange of arguments. We’d present our demands to him, and then he’d try to explain why they weren’t feasible,” said Mensil. “He used very technical language to try to confuse us. Macron and Lecornu were much more attentive. They took notes, smiled and gave us winks – in short, they did everything they could to show us that our demands were being heard. All of this, of course, was just a way to avoid making any concrete commitments.”
The student movement first began at high schools in the overseas territory of Mayotte. Then it moved to mainland France, with a high school in Creteil, a suburb southeast of Paris in the Val-de-Marne region, on September 17. Protests quickly spread to neighbouring Saint-Denis and the rest of France, and were joined by groups with other grievances.
For two months, students have blocked their schools’ entrances and taken to the streets, demanding an overhaul of the education system.
“It’s been clear ever since Macron took office – and even before – that conditions have deteriorated year after year. With every budget, there are fewer teachers. There are cuts to local governments, who manage school facilities,” Mesnil told Al Jazeera. “We’re not asking for five-star restaurants, MacBooks, or castles… We’re asking for enough teachers, buildings where the ceilings aren’t falling on our heads and class schedules adapted to our biological rhythms.
“We’re asking that, once we’ve earned our high school diploma, we can study at university.”
In response to the protests, officials invited high school students to voice their concerns. Since late October, representatives have attended several meetings, but despite some concessions, students say their demands remain unmet.
A key demand is to entirely reconstruct Parcoursup, the university admissions programme. Students claim the system is discriminatory and lacks transparency, with rejected students saying they are unable to find out why they were not accepted. The system and some degree programmes also value the academic standing of an applicant’s high school, meaning top students in disadvantaged areas may be overlooked.
They are also calling for an emergency plan to renovate failing school infrastructure. Some student groups and unions also want more teachers on permanent contracts and an additional 10 billion euros ($11bn) devoted to education.
In response to the protests, the government recruited 920 substitute teachers in early October and plans to hire 3,000 more. Next year’s budget includes an increase to cover more substitute hours for each high school.
The government also agreed to commit 1 billion euros ($1.1bn) per year through 2030 to building renovations, and to offer more opportunities for high school representatives to participate in national education discussions.
When contacted by Al Jazeera, the Ministry of Education responded with a statement that Geffray and the minister of higher education, research and space, Philippe Baptiste, sent to students on October 26.
In that statement, the education minister promised to cap class sizes at 28 students at the start of the next academic year in 2027 at “the most disadvantaged schools”, and reduce specialised course sizes. Although some high school students are still calling for Parcoursup to be abolished, the government has agreed to update the controversial platform “to help you plan your academic path with greater peace of mind”.
“Some measures will be implemented very quickly, while others will be included in the 2027 budget bill, which will be introduced in the coming weeks,” Geffray said.
Mesnil called the measures “a few crumbs”, but believes the concessions show that the student movement is making waves.
“The government is starting to give in,” he said. “Gen Z, together with the workers, have forced Macron to back down on some initial points, and we’re very happy about that.”
Beyond meetings, the government opened “High school students, the floor is yours”, a consultation platform for students to submit their opinions and complaints. More than 100,000 submissions were sent in during the 18 days it was open, starting on October 6. About 70 percent said the current school system is “ill-suited to their needs”, citing days that are too long and intense, with poorly structured schedules.
Many French high school students are in class from 8am to 6pm, with few breaks and heavy homework on top of the course load.
More than half of respondents, 56.3 percent, said buildings were dilapidated, improperly insulated and poorly equipped. Participating students also cited absent teachers, class sizes, the Parscoursup platform and negative mental health effects.
Students in disadvantaged areas say conditions are even worse in their suburbs.
Bilal Narjissi, 17, from the Paul-Eluard school in Saint-Denis and a member of the Renouveau Lyceen student union, took part in recent meetings with government officials and said they do not include many students from less advantaged schools.

items.text:
Israeli attacks have turned Gaza into 'toxic wasteland', Oxfam says
- Published
Gaza has been turned into "a toxic wasteland", with more than 99% of the Palestinian territory showing indicators of environmental contamination from Israeli military attacks, a new report from the non-profit organisation Oxfam says, external.
Heavy metals, explosive residues, and asbestos from destroyed buildings, dioxins and biological contaminants in the air, soil and water supply are threats to Palestinians now and potentially for decades to come, it says.
Oxfam International's executive director, Amitabh Behar, accuses Israel of "environmental war crimes" as part of an "ongoing genocide in Gaza."
"The destruction and contamination of Gaza will have fundamentally degraded the environmental conditions necessary for human safety and survival," he says.
Israel's government has been asked for its response to the report.
It has rejected genocide accusations in an ongoing case at the International Court of Justice as baseless and distorted. Israel maintains that its military campaign in Gaza is an act of self-defence against Hamas in response to the group's deadly attack on Israel on 7 October 2023, and that it takes steps to mitigate civilian harm.
Oxfam and the UK-based Conflict and Environment Observatory (CEOBS) used satellite imagery, remote sensing, spatial analysis and other open-source data to draw their conclusions in the most comprehensive report to date on the severe environmental impacts caused by three years of intense war in Gaza.
The report details how munitions used in Israel's intense bombardment, as well as the debris from destroyed buildings and infrastructure, all have an impact on the environment. In February, a UN special rapporteur stated that more than 200,000 tonnes of explosives were dropped on Gaza in almost two years - "the equivalent of the total energy of approximately 13 Hiroshima-type nuclear bombs".
Last year, the UN Environment Programme (UNEP) estimated that Israel's military operations destroying homes and infrastructure had generated more than 61 million tonnes of debris across the territory, with about 15% potentially carrying a high risk of contamination from hazardous materials.
"There are going to be chronic health impacts that are long term because a lot of these contaminants are persistent in the environment," Oxfam report author Lama Abdul Samad told the BBC.
She says that now and in future Gazans are likely to suffer from increased respiratory diseases, cancers, organ damage and a rise in birth defects and stillbirths.
With all six wastewater treatment plants out of operation in Gaza, untreated sewage currently makes its way into groundwater and the Mediterranean Sea. The health impact has recently been exacerbated by heavy winter storms causing rainwater to mix with wastewater and flow through streets and tent sites housing displaced people.
Testing types and levels of contamination is often not possible because Gazan laboratories have been destroyed and there are Israeli restrictions on the entry of specialist testing equipment and scientists. The BBC has approached the Israeli military for comment.
UNEP said security concerns also prevented its expert staff from previously travelling to Gaza.
The Oxfam report calls for a full, independent environmental assessment to be carried out in Gaza to identify contamination risks ahead of a clean-up. It says special attention must be given to the protection of workers involved.
Already, Gazan doctors have been reporting increased acute respiratory infections caused by dust and pollution from destroyed buildings and displaced people burning plastic, rags and cardboard to keep warm and cook food. Gastrointestinal diseases are linked to unsafe water and poor sanitation.
A Palestinian dermatologist, Dr Alaa Abu Hajar, told the BBC he had seen a five-fold increase in chronic skin diseases since the start of the war, putting this down to environmental pollution and overcrowded, unhygienic living conditions in tents and displacement camps.
"There are rodents, rubbish and sewage that's spread through the streets," he says. "Unfortunately, the age group most affected is children."
Farmers and those working in fishing say that pollution of the soil and sea mean they are unable to produce food that is safe.
"Sewage and wastewater are discharged into the sea without treatment and this is a great disaster," complains fisherman Abu al-Abed Sultan. "There is also rubble from destroyed houses that's dumped into the sea. When we lower our nets, we catch rubble and garbage. This harms the marine environment; the fish are affected and so are the fishermen."
At least 74,746 Palestinians have been killed since the start of the war in Gaza, according to the Hamas-run health ministry, whose figures are considered reliable by the UN. The UN says that humanitarian conditions remain dire.
Israel has conditioned large-scale Gaza reconstruction on the full disarmament of Hamas and other Palestinian armed groups. In July, Hamas accepted a plan put forward by the US-led Board of Peace to give up its weapons in exchange for an Israeli troop withdrawal. However, the Israeli government said the proposal was insufficient.

items.title: Morocco and Senegal await Afcon final verdict after court case
items.summary:
Morocco and Senegal await Afcon final verdict after court case
- Published
Everyone knows a football match should take 90 minutes, but the final of the 2025 Africa Cup of Nations has been playing out for 10 months.
Now, finally, Morocco or Senegal will be crowned winners. However, that moment of glo
items.text:
Morocco and Senegal await Afcon final verdict after court case
- Published
Everyone knows a football match should take 90 minutes, but the final of the 2025 Africa Cup of Nations has been playing out for 10 months.
Now, finally, Morocco or Senegal will be crowned winners. However, that moment of glory will come in a courtroom, not on the pitch.
On Tuesday afternoon sport's highest legal authority, the Court of Arbitration for Sport (Cas), will render its judgement on Senegal's appeal against the decision to strip them of the title they thought they won in January against the hosts in Rabat.
The case was heard in early October, and the wait is almost over.
So how did we get here?
What happened in the Afcon final?
With 66,000 fans creating an electric atmosphere in the Prince Moulay Abdellah Stadium, Morocco were chasing their first Afcon title since 1976.
But the final descended into chaos deep into second-half stoppage time.
With the match goalless, Senegal thought Ismaila Sarr had scored a dramatic winner, only to discover that referee Jean Jacques Ndala had blown for a Morocco free-kick.
The controversy deepened in the 98th minute when, after a video assistant referee (VAR) review, Ndala awarded Morocco a penalty.
Tempers boiled over on the touchline and in the stands. Senegal coach Pape Thiaw led some of his players and staff down the tunnel, while supporters clashed with security as order briefly collapsed.
Play eventually resumed and, in the 124th minute, Morocco missed a golden chance to end their 50-year wait for continental glory when Brahim Diaz failed to convert a penalty, chipping it 'Panenka' style into the arms of goalkeeper Edouard Mendy.
Pape Gueye's extra-time strike then secured a 1-0 win for Senegal, who lifted the trophy for a second time.
Or so they thought.
Why was the Afcon final result overturned?
The Royal Moroccan Football Federation (FMRF) quickly lodged a complaint with the Confederation of African Football (Caf), arguing that Senegal had breached competition regulations.
Article 82, contained within a chapter titled 'Withdrawals', states: "If, for any reason whatsoever, a team... refuses to play or leaves the ground before the regular end of the match without the authorisation of the referee", they shall be "considered [the loser] and shall be eliminated from the current competition".
In March a Caf appeals board agreed, ruling that Senegal had forfeited the match and awarding Morocco a 3-0 victory.
While there is precedent for Caf overturning results during Afcon and World Cup qualifying, some people, including one former senior Caf official, argued that only the referee has the authority to abandon a match if a walk-off occurs.
The FMRF said it was seeking the proper application of tournament regulations, but Senegal's federation (FSF) described the ruling as "unfair, unprecedented and unacceptable" and appealed to Cas.
What is the Court of Arbitration for Sport?
Founded in 1984 and based in the Swiss city of Lausanne, Cas was set up as an independent legal body designed to settle disputes as global sport became more lucrative and, as a result, more litigious.
For governing bodies which recognise Cas' authority, it is deemed to be the supreme arbiter, meaning its ruling is final unless, in rare cases, Switzerland's highest court decides to set it aside based on a limited number of technicalities.
More than 900 cases are filed every year, from more than 50 different sports, covering issues such as employment contracts and transfers, doping, corruption, TV rights and, in this case, the organisation of sporting events.
The FSF's appeal was heard in private on 8 October by a panel of three arbitrators chosen by Cas for their expertise in sports law.
The panel was led by Frenchman Gerald Simon, founder of the Sports Law Laboratory at the University of Burgundy and a Cas member for 23 years.
Italian international law professor Luigi Fumagalli and Hamburg-based attorney and professor of law at the University of Zurich Ulrich Haas completed the trio.
If the panel had failed to come to a consensus on the case, Cas president Simon will have made the final decision.
What could the long-term fallout be?
Although Caf's appeals board is independent, a reversal of its judgement would deliver another blow to the reputation of African football's governing body, which has been heavily criticised for the retrospective decision to hand Morocco the title.
Caf president Patrice Motsepe said in March that it will "adhere to" and "respect" whatever Cas decides, so, if things go in Senegal's favour, it could mean someone having to tinker with the Afcon rulebook.
The Senegal walk-off has, however, already brought about a change in football's rules.
"The referee may sanction with a red card any player who leaves the field of play in protest at a referee's decision," said Ifab, the game's lawmaking body, in April.
"This new rule will also apply to any team official who incites players to leave the field of play. A team that causes a match to be abandoned will, in principle, forfeit the match."
Thiaw lost his job following Senegal's last-32 World Cup exit this summer, while Walid Regragui, the man in the Morocco dugout in January, was dismissed in March.
Whatever the outcome of the case, animosity is likely to linger between the two federations.
The FMRF's senior hierarchy was furious with Senegal's behaviour, believing the pictures beamed around the world irrevocably tarnished the image of the first Afcon hosted by the kingdom since 1988 - a tournament into which a huge amount of time and money had been invested.
The FSF and the Senegalese government have leaned into a feeling prevalent across the continent that Morocco holds too much influence within African football.
Other incidents also irked Senegal, such as laser pens being directed into players' eyes and ball boys moving goalkeeper Mendy's towel, something which led to the barely believable sight of reserve keeper Yehvann Diouf b

items.title: Andreatta's masterplan to shock Sweden & take Scots to World Cup
items.summary:
Andreatta's masterplan to shock Sweden & take Scots to World Cup
- Published
Scotland intend to bring fancied Sweden's World Cup dream "crashing down - and do it in a truly Scottish way", according to women's head coach Melissa Andreatta.
Scotland face a two-legged World Cup qualifying play-off agai
items.text:
Andreatta's masterplan to shock Sweden & take Scots to World Cup
- Published
Scotland intend to bring fancied Sweden's World Cup dream "crashing down - and do it in a truly Scottish way", according to women's head coach Melissa Andreatta.
Scotland face a two-legged World Cup qualifying play-off against powerhouses Sweden, who are managed by Andreatta's former boss Tony Gustavsson.
The Swedes, who have been semi-finalists at the two previous Women's World Cups and are ranked eighth in the world, will be strong favourites to reach the tournament in Brazil next summer.
Andreatta, who has eight wins, two losses and four draws from her 14 games in charge of Scotland, was Gustavsson's deputy when he was Australia head coach from 2020 to 2024.
While the two have a connection from those years, the Australian is very much in business mode with next week's first leg at St Mirren Park looming.
"A few weeks ago Tony reached out, sent me a few messages and I took my time to respond," she told BBC Scotland.
"It wasn't much about football, just connecting on a personal level - which is probably a good thing, because I can be quite competitive. I just want to focus on business and not the personal level.
"I'm sure, like he is, all we're focused on is how we're going to win."
The Scots finished top of their qualifying group earlier this year after four wins from their six games before beating the Czech Republic 5-2 on aggregate in the play-off semi-final.
That set up the exacting play-off final against the Swedes, a team who narrowly missed out on a spot in the final at the previous two World Cups.
Scotland have made just one appearance at the tournament, in 2019, and Andreatta is excited by the prospect of getting one over her old boss for her new home.
"It's going to be a great occasion to face them at home first," she added.
"They are such a powerhouse nation that carries so much expectation to go to their next tournament. We want to bring that all crashing down and do that in a truly Scottish way. That's what we're going to focus on.
"I definitely won't be looking at their dug out, I'll be focused on us and what we need to do to get the result and go to another tournament.
"They are an exceptional team but we won't be swayed by a team's reputation or ranking.
"We firmly believe that anything is possible. Once that whistle goes, if you've done the work and you're prepared you're in the position to make anything happen. With this group of players and staff I know that's possible, we can take it to anyone on any given day.
"It is a massive challenge but we love those moments and that's why we're here. We've earned it."
Ayrshire beach helping Andreatta feel at home
There are more than 10,000 miles between Brisbane - where Andreatta grew up - and Ayr in Scotland, where she now calls home.
While the climate may be vastly different, there's one thing they do have in common - the beach.
"I love the coastal life. In Australia it's a big part of your lifestyle, being outdoors. I think there's something about the sea, being near it. Relaxing, calming, balancing," she said.
It has been 18 months since Andreatta was announced as Pedro Martinez Losa's successor as manager of the Scotland women's team and now, with her family alongside her - including two-year-old daughter Mackenzie - she feels at home.
"We've definitely settled in," she added. "We have the spots that we go to, our routine, we love it here. It's been a great landing spot for us on such a big move."
But what does her daughter make of her mum's job?
"She's got no idea," says Andreatta. "She just think's mum's on TV. Whenever she sees me she gets excited. Having her at the games is super special, being able to hold her on the pitch. She's such a joy.
"You do these things to make people proud and I want to make her proud."
- Scotland without captain Weir for World Cup play-off 
  - Published11 November
- New strategy launched to transform Scottish women's football over 10 years 
  - Published4 November
Andreatta was sitting in the pubs of Scotland over the summer as the Tartan Army headed over to the United States in their droves to watch the men's team compete at a first World Cup in almost 30 years.
The women won't have to wait that long if they can book a spot on the plane to Brazil next summer.
Andreatta is hoping to see just as many kilts on the Copacabana beach as there were in the bars of Boston.
"There is a strong desire among the group, not only players but also the staff, there is this desire to make their nation proud and show Scotland that the women's national team belongs here and deserves as much of the limelight as the men's," she added.
"Together we can make our nation proud and what better way to do it? To have our men at the World Cup and then the following summer our women.
"Watching from afar, what the fans did over there and in Boston, why can't we do that in Rio? That's what I'm envisaging but there's a lot to do and achieve before we get there."

items.title: Ukraine confirms it used naval drones to strike two Russian ships off Libya
items.summary:
Ukraine has confirmed it deployed naval drones in strikes on two Russian vessels off Libya on Sunday, including one that sank the corvette Merkury, one of Russia’s newest vessels.
Ukraine’s security service, the SBU, said seven domestically made naval drones were launched from a mothership in the op
items.text:
Ukraine has confirmed it deployed naval drones in strikes on two Russian vessels off Libya on Sunday, including one that sank the corvette Merkury, one of Russia’s newest vessels.
Ukraine’s security service, the SBU, said seven domestically made naval drones were launched from a mothership in the operation, which Volodymyr Zelenskyy described as “exemplary”.
“We continue our operations in designated waters. We are responding to Russia’s aggression. We are developing Ukrainian weapons,” the Ukrainian president added.
Zelenskyy released video footage, filmed by an approaching drone, showing the drones as they smashed into the side of the warship at its berth in the Benghazi naval base, triggering huge explosions that lit up the night sky.
In its own statement, the SBU said: “The defence forces of Ukraine have once again demonstrated that the Russian military fleet and its logistics networks have no safe routes, even far beyond the Black Sea.”
Zelenskyy said the other vessel hit on Sunday, the dry cargo ship MV Angara, was being used by Russia to transport weapons.
The operation, conducted 1,500 miles (2,400km) from the frontline in Ukraine, was the latest daring long-range assault by Kyiv’s forces. Last week Ukraine hitthe Kerch bridge - a key supply line to Russian-occupied Crimea – and the Russian Baltic sea port of Kaliningrad.
Residents in Benghazi heard loud explosions and saw flames at the naval base early on Sunday. Civil defence units rushed to the site and extinguished the fire, authorities in eastern Libya said.
The Merkury had docked to refuel and take on supplies as part of a cooperation agreement between Russia and the eastern-based government in Libya, the statement said without providing details about the vessel or its cargo.
Vladimir Putin had taken a personal interest in the ship. In 2019 he toured the St Petersburg yard where it was being built and backed naming it after a tsarist-era brig celebrated for fighting off two Turkish warships in the Black Sea in 1829.
At the 2023 Navy Day parade, the Russian president singled it out among 30 new vessels as evidence that Russia was “consistently building up the power of its fleet”. He hailed its St George flag as “a sign of the inviolability of our naval traditions” and said it was “gratifying” that the brig’s name had been revived.
Russian state media also talked up the ship. The news agency Tass called it the “newest missile corvette”, while the channel TV Tsentr claimed its stealth technology made it “invisible to radar”.
Divided Libya has emerged in recent years as a proxy battlefield. Moscow has long supported the breakaway government in Benghazi of Khalifa Haftar in its efforts use eastern Libya as a staging post for its military presence in north Africa and the Sahel.
More recently there have been reports of increasing Ukrainian operations. In April, the Associated Press reported that Ukrainian drone specialists had been operating at military sites in Misrata, Tripoli and Zawiya in Libya’s west. In September Libyan authorities denied reports by CNN that it allowed Ukraine to use a military base in the to launch drones against vessels from Russia’s “shadow fleet” in the Mediterranean.
The rival UN-recognised government in Tripoli said in a statement it was alarmed by “risks posed by involving civilian ports and facilities in activities linked to external conflicts”.
There was no immediate comment from Russia about the strikes. The UN mission in Libya (UNSMIL), however, expressed “serious concern” over the attacks, calling for “an immediate, independent and transparent investigation”. It said on X: “Libya cannot afford, and must not become a battleground for foreign conflicts.”
Ukraine prides itself on its military industry, particularly its progress in drone technology, which it has extensively developed since Russia invaded more than four and a half years ago. It has repeatedly touted the effectiveness of its domestically produced drones, including naval drones deployed throughout the war to hit Russian ships and infrastructure in the Black Sea.
In 2024, the Ukrainian general staff announced it had destroyed the Russian landing ship Cesar Kunikov with naval drones off the coast of Ukraine’s peninsula of Crimea, which was annexed by Russia in 2014.
Ukraine has also claimed to have attacked Moscow’s so-called shadow fleet – believed to carry Russian oil to circumvent sanctions – including in the Mediterranean last December. In March, a Russian liquefied natural gas carrier sank off the Libyan coast following an attack that Putin blamed on Ukraine.
Additional reporting by Pjotr Sauer

items.title: Erasmus set for France watch-along as SA coaches deny contact during Ireland loss
items.summary:
Nations Championship: Rassie Erasmus set to host France watch-along as South Africa coaches deny contact during Ireland loss
South Africa coaches have denied contact with suspended head coach Rassie Erasmus during their 20-17 Nations Championship defeat to Ireland in Dublin; Erasmus streamed a live
items.text:
Nations Championship: Rassie Erasmus set to host France watch-along as South Africa coaches deny contact during Ireland loss
South Africa coaches have denied contact with suspended head coach Rassie Erasmus during their 20-17 Nations Championship defeat to Ireland in Dublin; Erasmus streamed a live watch-along in which he could have breached team rules by communicating with staff or criticising officials
Monday 23 November 2026 12:27, UK
South Africa’s coaching staff denied suggestions they were receiving instructions from suspended head coach Rassie Erasmus during his online watch-along of Saturday’s 20-17 loss against Ireland in Dublin.
Erasmus was barred from having any involvement in matchday activity as part of a six-game ban from World Rugby for questioning whether "match-fixing" and "manipulation" was occurring in rugby after his side's thrilling defeat to France in Paris.
The 54-year-old nevertheless hosted the watch-along from the team's hotel, where he was muted for large spells of the event but could be seen speaking to an unknown party while wearing earbuds and covering his mouth.
The head coach has now announced that he will host another watch-along for South Africa's Nations Championship final clash against France at Twickenham on Sunday, two weeks after he received his ban for his comments on the officiating against the same opposition.
- Nations Championship: Latest fixtures, results and schedule for final week
- Itoje warns against win-at-all-costs culture amid Sandpapergate saga
- Nations Championship: Schedule, results for rugby's inaugural tournament
Asked if Erasmus was passing on messages during the Ireland game, Springboks assistant coach Felix Jones said: "I've no idea, we were busy with a Test match."
Fellow assistant coach Mzwandile Stick added: "Maybe he was communicating with his followers on that party that he was having, but with us we were just in the game."
Build-up to the heavyweight contest at the Aviva Stadium was dominated by Erasmus' sanction, with the watch-along representing a potential breach of World Rugby's rules should Erasmus have been recorded criticising any decisions or communicating with any members of the playing or coaching staff.
Jones continued by saying the situation was not a distraction as the Springboks slipped to a second successive loss, before questions on Erasmus were quickly shut down by the team's media officer.
"Thank you for everything this week. The messages, the photos and the support mean a great deal to me," Erasmus said in a post on X on Monday.
"Losing is never nice, but we are still number one in the world and we are in the final of the Nations Cup. So let's go again.
"I'd love to watch it with you. Put the final on your own TV on Sunday and join me."
'Big night for everyone who's Irish'
Ireland head coach Andy Farrell savoured a "big night for everyone who's Irish" and a major stepping stone in his side's journey towards next year's World Cup.
Robert Baloucoune claimed two first-half tries and Ronan Kelleher added another, with a long-range penalty from Sam Prendergast ultimately proving decisive amid a colossal defensive effort.
"It's something that we've been looking forward to and tried to challenge ourselves with about delivering when it matters against top-line sides," said Farrell.
"We knew that this fixture was coming, playing against the world's best - world's best by a stretch at this moment in time, I would have thought so.
"It was a game that we wanted to challenge ourselves and see how we went and obviously fronting up and showing the character that we did and coming out the right side of the win is a big night for everyone who's Irish."
South Africa ensured a pulsating encounter remained tantalisingly poised until the final whistle thanks to scores from Morne van den Berg and Malcolm Marx, plus seven points from the boot of Sacha Feinberg-Mngomezulu.
"I think we've taken a step forward and that was the aim," said Farrell.
"This game mattered to us in how we prepped for it. We didn't shy away from that and we took it on for what it was, which was a top of the tree game.
"We were able to perform. It wasn't perfect but we managed to come out with a win. The World Cup, it's all about stepping stones and this is a big one that's for sure."
Despite their defeat, South Africa progressed to the Nations Championship final at Twickenham after picking up a losing bonus point, with Ireland contesting the third-place final against Australia.
Asked about Erasmus, Farrell said: "Rassie is his own man and he's a smart guy. He does things for a reason.
"There's always going to be a plan or whatever. I don't know the ins and outs of it.
"The South African boys are in our dressing room having a beer and it's an unspoken rule that you just leave it alone, I would have thought. It is what it is."

items.title: Search and rescue teams race against time after Nigeria boat tragedy
items.summary:
Search and rescue teams race against time after Nigeria boat tragedy
- Published
Search and rescue operations are racing against time in Nigeria after a boat carrying mourners travelling to a funeral capsized on Friday.
Twenty-nine bodies have been recovered and 50 people rescued so far, a spokesper
items.text:
Search and rescue teams race against time after Nigeria boat tragedy
- Published
Search and rescue operations are racing against time in Nigeria after a boat carrying mourners travelling to a funeral capsized on Friday.
Twenty-nine bodies have been recovered and 50 people rescued so far, a spokesperson for the National Emergency Management Agency (Nema) told the BBC.
The government has responded by ordering stricter enforcement of safety standards on the country's inland waterways.
Overcrowding, poor maintenance and failure to observe safety regulations have contributed to previous deadly accidents on Nigeria's rivers.
The boat was travelling from Ayama community when it developed mechanical problems, according to police spokesperson Musa Mohammed.
Passengers asked the boat operator to steer towards land, but he allegedly declined, leading to the accident.
Survivors have described the panic that followed as passengers struggled to swim and stay afloat while waiting for emergency rescue services.
"As I swam, people were dragging me to the bottom, and I bit one woman and saved myself," Charity Ebikaboaere told local media outlet Arise News.
"Our things, our money, phones, everything lost, but me and my siblings are alive," said another survivor, Tari Samuel.
- Why do Nigeria's boat disaster keep happening? 
  - Published20 July
Nema spokesman Manzo Ezekiel raised concerns about the use of untrained boat operators and passengers travelling without life jackets.
"Some of them believe they're from river areas and they know how to swim," he said, warning that familiarity with waterways should not replace basic safety precautions.
The accident happened in a region where waterways are a key means of transport, especially for communities with limited road access.
"Overloading, speeding, recklessness and traveling without life jackets must stop. No journey is worth a life," Bayelsa Commissioner for Information Ebiuwou Koku-Obiyai said in a statement on Saturday.
Nigeria's President Bola Tinubu has relayed his condolences to the victims' families.
In a statement posted on X, Tinubu said he had directed relevant federal disaster response agencies to work together to ensure a successful rescue and recovery operation.
He also ordered that his election rally on Saturday, in Ibadan, Oyo State, be held without much fanfare in honour of those who lost their lives.
Boat accidents are a recurring problem in Nigeria, particularly in riverine communities where boats are a major means of transport.
In August, at least 50 people, mostly children, died after an overloaded boat capsized in the north-western Sokoto state. In January, at least 25 people died when a leaking boat capsized in Yobe state, in the north-east.

He is seeking re-election next January and vowed to a
items.text:
Nigeria’s President Bola Tinubu says the presidential villa suffers from cuts in electricity and water – failures that plague ordinary citizens.
He said he was shaving last week when the water supply at the villa, known as Aso Rock, in Abuja cut.
He is seeking re-election next January and vowed to address these issues..
Tinubu made the disclosure on Sunday at a special prayer session organised in his honour by members of his family in Lagos.
He explained: “On the Wednesday of last week, I was shaving, and the water went off. In the villa, you won’t know punishment dey dia too [there’s punishment there too in Nigerian pidgin].
“The water went off. So we will correct all this. No light, no water, no electricity, no development. We have just started. We can do it, and we will do it for Nigeria,” he said.
Aso Villa serves as both the office and official residence of the Nigerian president. It is situated at the base of Aso Rock in Abuja.
Nigeria has long endured electricity shortages, but recent severe disruptions have been caused primarily by insufficient gas supplies and declining hydropower output, rather than the usual nationwide grid collapse.
Persistent blackouts in Lagos, Abuja and elsewhere have forced distribution companies to implement rotating power cuts, severely impacting households and businesses.
The country also suffers from chronic water shortages, the result of a structural crisis rooted in the gap between rapid urban population growth and decaying, inadequate public water infrastructure.
Tinubu made a high-profile electricity promise during the 2023 election campaign, but the exact wording and how binding it is has become a major point of contention ahead of the 16 January election.
Tinubu defeated the country’s former Vice-President Atiku Abubakar as well as Peter Obi in 2023 and the three are seen as the strongest contenders once again.

Talk to Al Jazeera
Former Icelandic PM says world’s great powers are flexing their muscles
Iceland’s former prime minister warns climate change remains an existential threat as global power politics sidelines action.
Iceland’s former prime minister says that although climate change has fallen lower down on the international political agenda, it remains an existential crisis.
Katrin Jakobsdottir says our warming world is not just a catastrophe for nature, but a health and security emergency that cannot be ignored.
Her country is on the front lines of that emergency, with the Arctic warming at four times the rate of the rest of the world.
Almost all of Iceland’s glaciers are rapidly retreating – one was declared “dead” in 2019.
Jakobsdottir says it all comes at a time when the world’s biggest powers are flexing their muscles – and the politics of compromise are being squeezed out.

items.title: Infantino’s $20bn World Cup sell-off plan was to run for up to 96 years, documents show
items.summary:
Gianni Infantino’s failed Fifa Forward Enterprise plan could have locked football in for up to 96 years while paying its management up to 5% of the scheme’s multibillion-pound value, according to documents seen by the Guardian.
Previously undisclosed communications by Fifa and Thrive Capital, the le
items.text:
Gianni Infantino’s failed Fifa Forward Enterprise plan could have locked football in for up to 96 years while paying its management up to 5% of the scheme’s multibillion-pound value, according to documents seen by the Guardian.
Previously undisclosed communications by Fifa and Thrive Capital, the lead investor for the proposal, cast fresh light on the deal to sell off football’s crown jewels. They outline a plan, produced days before July’s final of the 2026 World Cup, to profit from the sport’s burgeoning commercial revenues for almost a century.
Infantino hopes to be re-elected for a fourth term as president in March and is the favourite to win that contest.
An internal Fifa risk assessment dated 17 July, designed as one of the final steps before concluding the FFE agreement, spells out the scheme’s extraordinary scope. “This deal provides for Fifa to create a for-profit subsidiary which would have all the commercial rights for Fifa events transferred to it for commercial exploitation for the next 96 years,” one section reads.
Another internal Fifa document written the following day, outlining the proposed agreement with Thrive, says the deal’s contract period “would be for rolling 12-year license periods to a sum maximum total of 96 years” and goes further in stating Fifa would assume 51% ownership “in perpetuity”.
The existence of a lucrative “management incentive plan” for unnamed individuals helming the scheme casts into stark light the extent to which its architects could have profited. The plan is first mentioned in a term sheet and “backstop letter” drawn up by Thrive on 17 July, which refers to FFE as “Project Box”, and sets aside up to 5% of FFE’s stock as a bonus pool for the new firm’s management. In theory it could have paid out up to $50m (£38.2m) for each $1bn added to the scheme’s value above $20bn, which was its initial valuation.
The term sheet says the plan “will permit the issuance of profits interests representing up to 5% of the fully diluted capitalisation of FFE, which will dilute all unitholders on a pro rata basis”. According to the Fifa memo the pool’s existence aimed to “ensure sufficient motivation to perform well”.
A further clause states that, if Fifa breached its agreement with Thrive or completed an agreement with a rival party, Thrive would have been entitled to a break fee totalling 1.25% – $250m – of FFE’s worth. Fifa would not have been permitted to engage in talks with other potential lead buyers for a year, or until the FFE deal closed.
Fifa’s memo of 18 July confirms there was no tender process “owing to the specific and unique nature of the proposed investment”. The risk assessment document confirms its own finance department was “not directly privy to the terms of the transaction”, casting further doubt about the processes followed in pursuing the deal.
Fifa declined to comment when contacted by the Guardian. The world governing body has consistently denied that Infantino stood to profit personally from FFE, which will raise questions as to who would have benefited from the management incentive plan.
The documents make clear that the issuance of so-called MIP units would be managed by the board of FFE, which Infantino was due to chair.

items.text:
COP31: What next after UN climate talks collapse
UN member states fail to agree on how to fast-track action to reverse global warming in blow to climate agenda.
United Nations climate talks have ended in collapse after countries deadlocked over the phasing out of planet-warming fossil fuels, aiding energy transition for developing countries and the response to natural disasters.
Known as COP31, the conference in Antalya, Turkiye, ended on Sunday as the European Union and others rejected a final deal they said was too weak to advance the fight against global warming.
The longest UN climate summit on record brought to the fore the divide between major polluters driving climate change and smaller nations bearing the brunt of its impact, after a year of climate-linked disasters from Europe to Asia.
It also laid bare the world’s inability to keep the Paris Agreement pledge to limit global warming to the 1.5C (2.7F) mark, which scientists expect to overshoot in a few years.
So what’s next for the fraught UN process and what else can nations do to deliver promises that have too often missed their target?
Why did COP31 collapse?
The 11-day-long negotiations that began on November 9 were stalled after oil-producing states blocked any mention of phasing out fossil fuels in the final deal put forward by the president of COP31, Turkiye, and main negotiator Australia.
Saudi Arabia and fellow members of the Organization of the Petroleum Exporting Countries (OPEC) opposed any mention of a fossil fuel phase-out, while insisting instead on carbon capture, the technology criticised as costly and ineffective.
Cosima Cassel, programme lead in Climate Diplomacy and Geopolitics at environmental think tank E3G, said petrostates attempted to slow momentum on the energy transition “following the disruption of the Strait of Hormuz and the projected decline in their incomes as global demand for fossil fuels falls”.
The European Union and several nations particularly vulnerable to climate change said they could not accept a text that failed to mention the main driver of global warming.
The revised text of a deal that emerged early on Sunday was angrily rejected after some 130 nations sent a letter to the presidency stating that a deal would have to mention a path for transitioning away from fossil fuels.
On the contrary, the text made no mention of fossil fuels while promoting carbon capture.
“A small group of blockers set the outcome against the clear position of a large majority,” Cassel told Al Jazeera. “These dynamics raise questions about the role of oil and gas exporters in undermining the only forum where vulnerable countries get to advance their concerns.”
Crucially for developing countries, there was also no progress on the funds needed to help them transition their energy systems and respond to natural disasters.
Under the 2015 Paris Agreement, developed countries are required to provide financial support to developing nations. However, the US-Israeli war on Iran and Russia’s war on Ukraine strained national budgets, leaving wealthy nations unwilling to commit trillions of dollars in climate finance.
Sebastien Duyck, senior attorney at the Center for International Environmental Law (CIEL), said wealthy developed countries, which denounced the obstruction by fossil fuel-producing nations, showed “considerable hypocrisy”.
“You cannot demand a just transition from others while failing to pay your fair share of its costs,” Duyck told Al Jazeera. “We need less finger-pointing and political theatre and more accountability. All major economies, particularly the wealthiest, must deliver on their existing legal obligations and climate finance commitments ahead of COP32.”
What’s next for the UN process – and for the planet?
The collapse of the climate talks in Turkiye has renewed questions about reform of its consensus-based process, centred around the principle that all countries must agree to the reforms.
The commitment to moving away from fossil fuels – including natural gas, coal and crude oil – was considered a landmark achievement of COP28 in Dubai, United Arab Emirates. But even then, the deal stopped short of calling for a “phase-out”, amid fierce lobbying from oil-producing countries.
Amid concern that fossil fuel producers wield more power than those who want to accelerate the transition to a low-carbon world, many believe the COP process remains important as a platform that brings together virtually every country in the world.
“The UN process remains the only forum where every country has a voice and a chance to shape outcomes and it is worth protecting and fighting for,” said E3G’s Cassel.
However, calls for reform are multiplying and a second tier of COPs – the Global Climate Action Agenda – is rising in prominence. Often called just the Action Agenda, the voluntary implementation pillar of the UN Climate Change process is bringing in real-world actors such as financial institutions, cities, regions, businesses and civil society on a voluntary basis.
“That spirit of collaboration stands in stark contrast to the adversarial dynamics that too often dominate the formal negotiations,” Cassel said.
Other routes are also being pursued. An International Court of Justice advisory opinion last year confirmed that states have a binding legal obligation to combat climate change. In April, the Santa Marta initiative convened 57 countries to promote non-binding cooperation around fossil fuel phase-out.
Duyck, at CIEL, said “the failure of governments to agree at this conference does not make the science any less clear or their legal obligations any less binding.” “A fair and orderly transition away from fossil fuels remains both an imperative and a collective responsibility,” he added.
The UN Environment Programme last year said the world would exceed the 1.5C (2.7F) mark – the internationally agreed-upon target set under the Paris Agreement – “very likely” within the next decade.

items.title: WSL talking points: Captain Spence inspires Spurs shock win at City and Lionesses impress
items.summary: Drew Spence rolled back the years with a vintage performance as her Tottenham side produced a shock 3-1 victory away against the defending champions, Manchester City. The 34-year-old marshalled the midfield and then had the vision to thread an outstanding through ball that split the City defence and
items.text:
Drew Spence rolled back the years with a vintage performance as her Tottenham side produced a shock 3-1 victory away against the defending champions, Manchester City. The 34-year-old marshalled the midfield and then had the vision to thread an outstanding through ball that split the City defence and found the run of Matilda Vinberg, who put Spurs 2-1 up. “She’s unbelievable. There are so many more gears in Drew and I wish I’d been able to work with her a bit earlier [in my career] because her leadership is second to none,” the Tottenham head coach, Martin Ho, said of the club captain. “Her performance levels, since I’ve been here, week on week have grown. She is covering every blade of grass and leads by example. For me, she’s one of the best midfielders in the league.” Tom Garry
London City Lionesses head into the international break with a spring in their step, their 6-2 defeat of Crystal Palace helping them to move to within two points of City and four of league leaders Chelsea, who both dropped points at the weekend. There was a resilience to Eder Maestre’s team in their last game before the international break and the full impact of their squad depth was on show against Palace. The visitors cancelled out Daniëlle van de Donk’s opener and pulled a goal back to make it 3-2 after 64 minutes but they ultimately could not cope with the fresh legs London City could turn to in the second half. Talk may be focused on the big-spending side being in the running for Champions League football next season, but on the basis of recent form, and with Chelsea up next in mid December, thoughts may turn to am unlikely title challenge. SW
After 10 straight defeats in the WSL, Charlton finally have something to show for their efforts, registering their first point of the season on Sunday. It has been a tough few months for the promoted side who have been statistically interesting for all the wrong reasons. In their 1-1 draw with Aston Villa, it was their bravery and work rate that shone through as they set about defending a 17th-minute lead. They had to spend significant periods without the ball but kept Villa to eight shots and matched their three on target. At the heart of it was the 21-year-old Keira Flannery who led the midfield with a performance that was beyond her years. She exemplified the character on show in stepping up to take Charlton’s early penalty despite having missed from the spot a fortnight previous. “I’m so proud of the girls,” she said. “We all dug deep and stuck it out to the end. A point is massive. It’s a stepping stone.” Sophie Downey
“You’re nothing special, we draw every week,” sang the Emirates faithful as an abject Arsenal were held to yet another stalemate by West Ham, becoming the first team in WSL history to draw their first six home games. This was probably the poorest performance of their disappointing season, the home side generating an xG of just 0.88. By half-time, they had registered one shot on target and failed to get out of their stupor until the final quarter. The full-time boos were reflected by high emotions on the pitch as the pressure on head coach, Renée Slegers, continues to mount. “I take my responsibilities because the results haven’t been good enough,” she said. “We’re not creating good enough chances to the final third, from all phases. It’s not the Arsenal standard and we need to do that better.” One positive of the afternoon was the news that Lisa Baum was stable after being carried off on a stretcher in the first half. The club confirmed that she was responding well having suffered from “shortness of breath”. SD
Chelsea had 47 touches in the Liverpool box and 19 shots but came away from St Helens with a scoreless draw. The Blues have scored just three goals in their last five games in all competitions, having found the net 30 times in the 11 matches prior to that. The goals have dried up. Getting their attack clicking without the injured duo of Melvine Malard and Lauren James will be critical if they are to find the balance between attack and defence that Sonia Bompastor says they need. “I’m really happy with a lot of things we are doing right now. When you have ambitions, when you want to win titles, you need to make sure to find the right balance between being strong defensively but also being able to score goals,” she said. Their defence is doing the heavy lifting, with the fewest goals conceded in the WSL – five, with Arsenal and Everton next best with 11 conceded – and none in Europe, and they need their attack to share the load. Suzanne Wrack
Failing to defend a set-piece cost Birmingham badly for the second week in a row as they conceded a 94th-minute winner against Manchester United, undoing much of the promoted side’s good work in a close contest. Second-from-bottom Birmingham, who were beaten 1-0 after conceding from a back-post header from a free-kick last time out away at Aston Villa, were again caught out with a far-post delivery, this time with Simi Awujo nodding in to give Manchester United victory. Eva Olid’s visitors are now unbeaten in nine WSL matches, winning six of those, and are enjoying a club-record 14-match unbeaten streak in all competitions, while Birmingham have lost four WSL games on the bounce. TG
Scott Phelan said Everton need to be more consistent in attack after their 1-0 defeat to Brighton. Phelan’s side have scored just eight goals in 11 league games this season – only 14th-placed Charlton have scored fewer. Everton had 12 shots on goal in the game, six of which were blocked. The result leaves them 11th in the league and they will have to find their shooting boots soon to avoid falling down further, especially with fixtures against Arsenal and Manchester City coming before the Christmas break. “We’ve been OK defensively,” Phelan said. “Those attacking phases of play need to be more consistent. items.text:
Ukraine claims drone strikes on Russian ships off Libya: What do we know?
A series of drone strikes on Russian vessels in Libyan and Finnish territories fuels fears that the war in Ukraine is spreading.
Ukraine has claimed responsibility for sinking a Russian warship and striking a cargo vessel off Libya’s coast, raising concerns about the Russia-Ukraine war widening geographically.
“It all took place off the coast of Libya. Our warriors deployed seven Ukrainian-made naval drones,” Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy said in a post on X on Monday.
The attack targeted the Russian corvette Merkury and the cargo vessel MV Angara, which Zelenskyy said was used to transport weapons.
The attacks come amid an intensifying Ukrainian campaign targeting Russian naval assets, energy infrastructure and vessels linked to Moscow’s so-called shadow fleet, which helps Russia circumvent Western sanctions.
The developments have also raised questions about the involvement of foreign powers in a divided Libya, and the risk of drawing other nations into the conflict, nearly five years after Russia launched its full-scale invasion of Ukraine.
Here is what we know about the attacks, who may be behind them and what they mean for the expanding reach of the war.
What do we know about the attacks?
The Russian Navy’s Merkury was struck at the Benghazi naval base in eastern Libya on Sunday, triggering an explosion and fire.
Satellite imagery showed most of the corvette had capsized and sunk, with only its bow visible above water.
Zelenskyy confirmed the sinking on Monday, saying a Russian Kamov Ka-27 military helicopter was also destroyed.
“Our second target was the Russian dry cargo vessel MV ANGARA, which the enemy used to transport weapons. Result: target hit,” he added.
A day earlier, the Russian cargo ship Sparta II was struck by drones in the Gulf of Finland. The vessel caught fire and drifted into Finnish waters. All 16 crew members were evacuated, with one slightly injured.
In Finland, the military assessed the vessel was likely struck by Ukraine. Russian authorities said two drones hit the Sparta II in international waters. Kyiv has not publicly claimed responsibility for Sunday’s attack.
Zelenskyy said his country would continue to launch operations in designated maritime areas in response to Russia’s aggression.
Kyiv’s attacks come as Russia has intensified its air attacks across Ukraine, using ballistic missiles, drones and guided bombs. Energy facilities, bridges, Black Sea ports and other civilian infrastructure have been targeted in Ukraine, which has countered with attacks on Russian energy sites and other targets.
What have Libya and Russia said?
Libya’s eastern administration condemned the attack as a violation of its sovereignty and said it had requested an international investigation through the United Nations.
“The Libyan government will not allow Libyan ports, territory or territorial waters to be turned into an arena for settling scores or exporting international conflicts,” it said.
Saddam Haftar, son of renegade military commander Khalifa Haftar, said Libya’s security and sovereignty are a “national responsibility that cannot tolerate political posturing or the exploitation of incidents to promote accusations and stir up fears”.
“Rather, it requires prioritising the national interest and dealing responsibly with everything that affects our country’s security and stability,” he said in a statement on Facebook.
The rival UN-recognised government in Tripoli also commented on the incident, saying it was concerned by “risks posed by involving civilian ports and facilities in activities linked to external conflicts”.
Meanwhile, the UN has called for an independent investigation into Sunday’s drone attacks.
On Monday, the UN Support Mission in Libya (UNSMIL) expressed “serious concern” over the attacks, calling for “an immediate, independent and transparent investigation”.
“Libya cannot afford and must not become a battleground for foreign conflicts,” UNSMIL wrote in a post on X.
The oil-rich nation has been divided between the government in Tripoli and a rival administration in the east since the overthrow of longtime ruler Muammar Gaddafi in 2011.
In September, Libya denied reports by CNN that it allowed Ukraine to use a military base in the northwest of the country to launch drones against vessels from Russia’s “shadow fleet” in the Mediterranean.
The origin of Sunday’s attack is still not confirmed.
How many Russian vessels have been attacked in recent weeks?
At least four Russian vessels have reportedly been targeted in November, including the Merkury, MV Angara and Sparta II.
The Finnish military also reported detecting a strike on a Russian warship in the Gulf of Finland during Ukrainian drone attacks the previous week.
In March, a Russian LNG tanker sank off Libya’s coast following an attack Moscow blamed on Ukraine.
In December 2025, Ukraine claimed responsibility for striking a Russian-linked oil tanker in the Mediterranean.
Is the Ukraine-Russia war expanding geographically?
Academic Alexey D Muraviev says the conflict has already expanded beyond Ukraine.
“The Mediterranean has firmly become an external theatre of operations, particularly maritime operations,” Muraviev, senior research fellow in defence and strategic studies at Edith Cowan University, told Al Jazeera.
He said the vessels targeted in Libyan and Finnish territories were likely involved in transporting military equipment or other supplies to Africa, potentially supporting Russia’s Africa Corps, which operates alongside Moscow-aligned governments.
Muraviev said Ukrainian forces had previously confronted Russian security personnel in Africa, demonstrating that the conflict had already extended beyond its original battlefield.
“Even in this sense, there have been cases when the war in Ukraine effectively extended onto the African continent,” he said.

items.title: Inside Fifa and US Soccer’s plan for 2031 World Cup: ‘the largest women’s sporting event in history’
items.summary: The biggest and most lucrative event in the history of women’s sport will be confirmed at an Extraordinary Fifa Congress in Zurich on Monday, with a joint bid from the United States, Mexico, Costa Rica and Jamaica to host the 2031’s Women’s World Cup to be formally ratified by a vote of Fifa’s 211 m
items.text:
The biggest and most lucrative event in the history of women’s sport will be confirmed at an Extraordinary Fifa Congress in Zurich on Monday, with a joint bid from the United States, Mexico, Costa Rica and Jamaica to host the 2031’s Women’s World Cup to be formally ratified by a vote of Fifa’s 211 member associations.
In the bid book submitted to Fifa last year the prospective hosts pledged to generate total revenues of $4bn if awarded hosting rights, which would represent a staggering increase on the $570m earnings from the last World Cup held in Australia and New Zealand three years ago, the first women’s tournament to break even.
While Fifa is forecasting an almost doubling of tournament revenues to $1bn for next year’s competition in Brazil, achieving a further fourfold growth by 2031 would appear to be challenging.
The United Kingdom’s bid for the 2035 tournament, which will also be ratified on Monday, does not include a revenue target. So how do the US and their co-hosts plan to generate $4bn, and what will be the impact on fans?
The legacy of 2026
Fifa has yet to publish its financial accounts relating to last summer’s men’s World Cup, but it was undoubtedly a huge success. Gianni Infantino told the national associations on the eve of the final in New Jersey last July that Fifa’s revenue projection for the 2023-2026 cycle had increased from $11bn to $15bn, the majority of which was the product of the World Cup itself.
Emboldened by that success, the US Soccer Federation is confident $4bn is a realistic target for 2031, a projection largely based on bringing in $1.4bn from commercial deals, $1.25bn in matchday revenue and $1bn in broadcast income.
“It is a very significant increase from 2023, but I expect [the] 2027 [Women’s World Cup] to continue to be a step forward, and in 2031 to really blow this out of the park because of the maturity of our market here and the excitement that we see,” Emily Cosler, US Soccer’s vice-president of strategy who will present the bid to Fifa in Zurich, told the Guardian.
“The market here in the US is unlike anywhere else. The 2026 World Cup will be well north of $10bn in revenue, and we’re looking at a tournament with the same number of teams involved. We do have a high level of confidence in that revenue number. We expect and plan for the 2031 Women’s World Cup to be the largest women’s sporting event in history.”
Stadiums
The most likely driver of growth is the sheer size of the would-be hosts’ plans for the tournament, which will be the first women’s World Cup to feature 48 teams, increasing the number of matches from 64 to 104.
Just as significantly, most games will be played at large NFL stadiums, with the 13 of the provisional shortlist of 20 venues in the official bid – 14 in the US, four in Mexico and one each in Jamaica and Costa Rica – having capacities of more than 60,000.
To further illustrate the scale of the tournament’s ambitions, seven of these US-based stadiums hosted matches at the 2026 World Cup, with three others having staged games at the 2025 Fifa Club World Cup.
While some smaller stadiums will be used in the group stages, the hosts are targeting a total 4.5 million tickets sold, which would bring average crowds of 43,000 per match, enough to generate ticket revenue of $550m, more than 10 times the $43m made from ticket sales of 1.8 million in 2023.
The bid also projects hospitality sales of $300m, plus $400m in other match day income such as merchandising, parking and transport.
The bid actually contains 50 potential stadiums across 35 different cities, and the initial shortlist is largely theoretical at this stage, with the final decision on venues to be taken by Fifa by the end of 2028.
All of the US venues are in operation other than the proposed redevelopment of the Washington Commanders’ RFK Stadium, which is due to be completed in 2030 but is under consideration.
Mercedes-Benz Stadium (Atlanta), AT&T Stadium (Dallas), SoFi Stadium (Los Angeles) and MetLife Stadium (New Jersey) have been identified as the most likely candidates to host the final, although that decision will not be taken until 2030.
“We think every knockout round can be in a 60,000-plus seat stadium,” Cosler said. “We’ve got the infrastructure to do that, and I have a high level of confidence that every knockout round game can be a sellout. The success of our women’s national team and the NWSL has proven that we’ve got the demand for that.”
Ticket prices
Fifa’s Evaluation Report published earlier this month is even more bullish than the bid in terms of the potential value of ticket sales, claiming that the widespread use of NFL stadiums should mean that ticketing and hospitality revenues “significantly exceed” the $550m forecast, which is described as “a very conservative position with significant upside potential”.
Given that the bid is forecasting a tenfold increase in revenue from the 2023 tournament based on selling two-and-a-half times more tickets, it is clear that the prices will also increase significantly from that tournament. However, lead bidders US Soccer are determined to make the event more accessible than last summer’s men’s World Cup.
“We propose a pricing table that balances what the women deserve in terms of the revenue generated from this tournament, but also access in a way that will continue to grow the game,” Cosler said. “I think there are some really good initiatives that US Soccer has done with our own national team games. We’ve partnered with local universities. We’ve offered $25 tickets that have resulted in filling stadiums and success. This isn’t a charity, but at the same time, we want this game to be accessible to fandom everywhere.”
In comparison to the men’s World Cup and other premium events in the US the pricing structure proposed in the bid looks affordable, with tickets ranging from $35 to $120 in the group stage, and $120 to $600 for the final.
